Vita, id est, Verbum Dei vivens, et vitæ principium (de quo legitur : Quoniam apud te est fons vitæ), erat lux hominum, hoc est dator luminis naturalis ingenii, atque infusor luminis gratiæ. Quidquid enim intellectualis claritatis, decoris et perfectionis in hominibus reperitur, a Verbo seu Filio Dei profluxit et datur, a quo dona naturæ et gratiæ derivantur. Dicitur ergo Verbum lux nostra, quasi causa nostræ illustrationis, illuminans nos ad divinorum cognitionem, atque perducens ad beatitudinem supernaturalem per supernaturalia dona Spiritus Sancti, sicut ait Apostolus : Gratia Dei vita æterna. Hinc dicit Psalmista : Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine.
paras.en: [[1:4|And the life was the light of men|et vita erat lux hominum]]. Here “life” is taken personally, for the hypostasis of the Word, that is, for the Word Himself as subsisting [that is, as a distinct Person, not as a quality or attribute]. The life, that is, the living Word of God and the principle of life (of whom we read: [[Ps 35:10|For with thee is the fountain of life|quoniam apud te est fons vitæ]]), was the light of men, that is, the giver of the light of natural understanding and the one who pours in the light of grace. For whatever intellectual brightness, beauty and perfection is found in men has flowed from, and is given by, the Word or Son of God, from whom the gifts of nature and of grace are derived. The Word is therefore called our light, as being the cause of our enlightenment, enlightening us to the knowledge of divine things and leading us on to supernatural beatitude through the supernatural gifts of the Holy Ghost; as the Apostle says: [[Rom 6:23|the grace of God, life everlasting|Gratia autem Dei, vita æterna]]. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 4:7|The light of thy countenance, O Lord, is signed upon us|Signatum est super nos lumen vultus tui, Domine]].

paras.t: Sed quoniam, juxta divinum Dionysium, nulla creatura sit expers participationis lucis divinæ, cur Verbum seu vita hæc appellatur specialiter lux hominum? Et respondendum dupliciter : Primo, quia in hoc libro tractatur de Verbo prout salvator est generis humani, eripiens nos a tenebris ignorantiæ et peccati, transferensque ad lumen gratiæ in præsenti, atque ad lumen gloriæ in futuro. Secundo, quoniam inter omnes creaturas corporales et inferiores, solus homo ad Deum convertitur et pertingit per intellectum et voluntatem : idcirco specialiter illustratur a Verbo, tanquam ad Dei imaginem factus.
paras.en: But since, according to the divine Dionysius, no creature is without some share in the divine light, why is the Word, or this life, called specially the light of men? The answer is twofold. First, because this book treats of the Word as He is the Saviour of the human race, snatching us from the darkness of ignorance and sin and bringing us over to the light of grace in the present[[1 Pet 2:9||]], and to the light of glory in the future. Secondly, because among all the bodily and lower creatures man alone turns to God and reaches Him by understanding and will; therefore he is specially enlightened by the Word, as being made to the image of God.

paras.t: Et lux ista, videlicet Verbum, de quo cantamus in Psalmo : In lumine tuo videbimus lumen ; in tenebris lucet, hoc est, inter perversos Judæos conversatione, prædicatione et signis resplenduit. Vel, In tenebris lucet, hoc est, in cordibus impiorum gratiæ suæ lucem diffundit, et per prædicatores fideles hominibus excæcatis ac reprobis lumen christianæ doctrinæ proponit. Potest quoque per tenebras, omnis creatura intellectualis intelligi, quæ comparatione lucis divinæ, potius reputatur caligo quam lux. Propter quod ait Psalmista : Deus meus, illumina tenebras meas.
paras.en: [[1:5|And the light|Et lux]], namely the Word, of whom we sing in the Psalm, [[Ps 35:10|in thy light we shall see light|in lumine tuo videbimus lumen]], [[1:5|shineth in darkness|in tenebris lucet]], that is, shone forth among the perverse Jews by His manner of life, His preaching and His signs. Or, [[1:5|shineth in darkness|in tenebris lucet]], that is, He pours the light of His grace into the hearts of the wicked, and through faithful preachers sets the light of Christian doctrine before blinded and reprobate men. By the darkness, too, may be understood every intellectual creature, which in comparison with the divine light is reckoned darkness rather than light. That is why the Psalmist says: [[Ps 17:29|O my God, enlighten my darkness|Deus meus, illumina tenebras meas]].

paras.t: Et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt. Infra ait S. Joannes, quod cohors et tribunus et ministri Judæorum comprehenderunt Jesum. Et in Actibus princeps Apostolorum ait de Juda : Qui fuit dux eorum qui comprehenderunt Jesum. Nonne et isti tenebræ exstiterunt, quibus dixit Salvator, Hæc est hora vestra et potestas tenebrarum? Quomodo ergo tenebræ non comprehenderunt hanc lucem? Sed hoc facillime solvitur, quoniam illa de corporali comprehensione Christi intelliguntur, nunc autem de spirituali comprehensione fit sermo.
paras.en: [[1:5|And the darkness did not comprehend it|et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt]]. Further on St. John says that [[John 18:12|the band and the tribune and the servants of the Jews took Jesus|cohors et tribunus et ministri Judæorum comprehenderunt Jesum]] [Denis plays on *comprehendere*, which means both “to seize, arrest” and “to grasp, understand”; it is the verb of v. 5 and of the two passages he cites, where the Douay-Rheims has “took” and “apprehended”]. And in the Acts the prince of the Apostles says of Judas: [[Acts 1:16|who was the leader of them that apprehended Jesus|qui fuit dux eorum qui comprehenderunt Jesum]]. Were not these too darkness, to whom the Saviour said, [[Luke 22:53|this is your hour and the power of darkness|hæc est hora vestra, et potestas tenebrarum]]? How then did the darkness not comprehend this light? But this is very easily solved: those passages are understood of the bodily seizing of Christ, whereas here the discourse is of spiritual comprehension.

paras.t: Verum tunc rursus quæstio oritur, quomodo tenebræ non comprehenderunt hanc lucem. Multi enim ad Christum conversi sunt, eumque per fidem, spem et caritatem comprehenderunt : quibus dicit Apostolus, Fuistis aliquando tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino. Sed rursus apparet oppositum. Ut enim mox subjungetur, Deum nemo vidit unquam : ergo multo amplius Deum nemo comprehendit unquam, quum spiritualis comprehensio sit perfectissima, interna ac intima visio. Et respondendum, quod Evangelista ad litteram loqui videtur de obtenebratis Judæis, et comprehensione Christi per fidem et caritatem. Sic enim excæcati et indurati Judæi Christum non comprehenderunt. Unde Salvator ad eos : Sermo (inquit) meus non capit in vobis ; et iterum, Neque me scitis, neque Patrem meum.
paras.en: But then the question arises again: how did the darkness not comprehend this light? For many were converted to Christ and comprehended Him by faith, hope and charity; to whom the Apostle says, [[Eph 5:8|you were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord|aliquando tenebræ, nunc autem lux in Domino]]. And yet the opposite appears again. For, as will be added shortly, [[1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit umquam]]: much more, then, has no man ever comprehended God, since spiritual comprehension is the most perfect, inward and intimate vision. The answer is that the Evangelist seems, according to the letter, to be speaking of the darkened Jews, and of the comprehension of Christ by faith and charity. For in this way the blinded and hardened Jews did not comprehend Christ. Hence the Saviour says to them: [[John 8:37|my word hath no place in you|sermo meus non capit in vobis]]; and again, [[John 8:19|Neither me do you know, nor my Father|Neque me scitis, neque Patrem meum]].

paras.t: Præterea, multiplex est comprehensio. Prima est comprehensio terminativa, qua res secundum se totam capitur, videtur sive cognoscitur, tam perfecte sicut cognoscibilis est. Sicque infinitum a finito comprehendi non valet. Unde hoc modo Deus est tam incomprehensibilis omni creaturæ, etiam Sanctis in patria, quam immensus : ideo hoc modo ipse solus comprehendit se ipsum. Secunda est comprehensio claræ visionis, qua essentia rei vere conspicitur. Et ita Beati comprehendunt Deum, quem facie ad faciem contuentur : propter quod comprehensores dicuntur. Tertia est comprehensio certæ adhærentiæ per fidem, atque sinceræ adhæsionis per caritatem. Sic viatores comprehendunt Deum : quod magis proprie dicitur apprehendere quam comprehendere. Tenebræ ergo, id est peccatores, quia in suis malitiis permanserunt, nullo horum modorum comprehenderunt Jesum. Qui autem conversi sunt, comprehenderunt eum tertio modo.
paras.en: Moreover, comprehension is manifold. The first is terminative comprehension [that is, comprehension that reaches the limit of its object and encloses it wholly], by which a thing is grasped, seen or known according to the whole of itself, as perfectly as it is knowable. In this way the infinite cannot be comprehended by the finite. Hence in this way God is as incomprehensible to every creature, even to the Saints in the fatherland, as He is immense; and so in this way He alone comprehends Himself. The second is the comprehension of clear vision, by which the essence of a thing is truly beheld. And so the Blessed comprehend God, whom they behold [[1 Cor 13:12|face to face|facie ad faciem]]; for which reason they are called comprehensors [the scholastic name for the blessed in heaven, who hold what they sought, as against wayfarers, *viatores*, still on the way in this life]. The third is the comprehension of firm adherence by faith and of sincere cleaving by charity. In this way wayfarers comprehend God; but this is more properly called apprehending than comprehending. The darkness, then, that is, sinners, because they remained in their wickedness, comprehended Jesus in none of these ways. But those who were converted comprehended Him in the third way.

paras.t: Denique, juxta doctrinam magni Dionysii, Deus comparatur soli materiali. Unde et Deus Sol intelligentiæ atque justitiæ appellatur ; quoniam sicut sol iste visibilis universa suæ lucis susceptiva irradiat, atque ingenita propria lucis plenitudine naturalique proprietate, sine præratiocinatione ac prævia deliberatione, cuncta disposita sua claritate perfundit, ornat impletque, et si quid est quod non illustratur hoc lumine, hoc non est ex solis defectu, sed ex propria indispositione ; sic Deus sublimis et benedictus, ex propria bonitatis infinitæ plenitudine, naturali inclinatione, et superliberalissima atque piissima communicabilitate, omnem intellectualem creaturam illuminat, implet ac perficit, si fuerit capax atque disposita. Quod si aliqua non illustratur, hoc est non ex parte Dei, sed ob propriam indignitatem ac aversionem. Quamvis enim sit Deus ubique omnibus verissime præsens ac intimus, nihilo minus passiones nostræ et vitia separant nos ab eo, ut per Isaiam inducitur : Iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter Deum vestrum et vos. Quæ utique impediunt nos a receptione gratiæ et illustrationis divinæ, secundum quod Jeremias testatur : Peccata vestra prohibuerunt bonum a vobis. Removeamus ergo obstacula ista, faciendo quod in nobis est, aptemusque nos infusioni gratiarum cœlestium ; et tunc illuminabimur atque implebimur mox a Deo, juxta illud Job : Si direxerit homo ad Deum cor suum, spiritum illius et flatum ad se trahet. Et per Zachariam : Convertimini ad me, et convertar ad vos, dicit Dominus. Hinc Jacobus admonet : Appropinquate Deo, et appropinquabit vobis.
paras.en: Lastly, according to the teaching of the great Dionysius [*On the Divine Names*, ch. 4], God is compared to the material sun. Hence God is also called the [[Wis 5:6|sun of understanding|sol intelligentiæ]] and the [[Mal 4:2|Sun of justice|sol justitiæ]]. For as this visible sun shines upon all things capable of receiving its light, and by the inborn fullness of its own light and by a natural property, without prior reasoning or previous deliberation, floods all things that are disposed with its brightness, adorns and fills them, and if there is anything that is not lit by this light, this is not from any failing of the sun but from the thing's own indisposition; so God, sublime and blessed, from the fullness of His own infinite goodness, by natural inclination and by a most superabundantly liberal and most loving communicativeness, enlightens, fills and perfects every intellectual creature, if it be capable and disposed. And if any is not enlightened, this is not on God's part, but because of its own unworthiness and turning away. For although God is everywhere most truly present and inmost to all things, nevertheless our passions and vices separate us from Him, as is set down by Isaias: [[Is 59:2|your iniquities have divided between you and your God|iniquitates vestræ diviserunt inter vos et Deum vestrum]]. And these hinder us from receiving grace and the divine enlightenment, as Jeremias testifies: [[Jer 5:25|your sins have withholden good things from you|peccata vestra prohibuerunt bonum a vobis]]. Let us therefore remove these obstacles, doing what is in us, and fit ourselves for the infusion of heavenly graces; and then we shall soon be enlightened and filled by God, according to that of Job: [[Job 34:14|If he turn his heart to him, he shall draw his spirit and breath unto himself|Si direxerit ad eum cor suum, spiritum illius et flatum ad se trahet.]] [Denis's text reads “If a man turn his heart to God”]. And by Zacharias: [[Zach 1:3|Turn ye to me|Convertimini ad me]], [[Zach 1:3|and I will turn to you, saith the Lord|et convertar ad vos, dicit Dominus]]. Hence James admonishes: [[Jas 4:8|Draw nigh to God: and he will draw nigh to you|Appropinquate Deo, et appropinquabit vobis]].

paras.t: Quæritur circa præhabita, an naturali ratione possit inveniri aut demonstrari pluralitas Personarum in Deo, et an gentiles philosophi habuerunt cognitionem de Patre et Filio per naturalem rationem. Quæstio ista præcipue oritur ob difficultatem quam habet ex verbis Augustini, septimo Confessionum dicentis: Ibi, utpote in libris Platonis vel Platonicorum, non quidem his verbis, sed omnino hoc idem quod his verbis significatur, multis ac multiplicibus rationibus reperi comprobatum quod in principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, etc., usque ibi, Et vita erat lux hominum. Trismegistus quoque invenitur dixisse: Monas gignit monadem, et in se suum reflectit ardorem.
paras.en: It is asked, concerning what has gone before, whether a plurality of Persons in God can be found out or demonstrated by natural reason, and whether the gentile philosophers had knowledge of the Father and the Son through natural reason. This question arises chiefly from the difficulty raised by the words of Augustine in the seventh book of the Confessions, where he says: There, that is, in the books of Plato or of the Platonists, I found it proved by many and manifold reasons, not indeed in these words, but altogether the same thing that is signified by these words, that [[1:1|In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God|in principio erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum]], etc., as far as [[1:4|and the life was the light of men|Et vita erat lux hominum]]. Trismegistus too is found to have said: The monad begets a monad, and reflects its own ardour back upon itself [monas = unit, unity; a saying ascribed to Hermes Trismegistus, which St Thomas cites].

paras.t: Et videtur id posse probari: Primo, ex immensitate divinæ bonitatis, quæ quum sit infinitæ communicabilitatis, processit in actum sibi proportionatum, producendo germen immensum, quod non potest esse nisi Deus. Secundo, quia nullius rei possessio jucunda est sine consortio; et quum in Deo sit amor perfectus atque immensus, habet Deus aliquem quem diligit infinito amore, eo quod amor non sit proprie ad se ipsum. Tertio, quoniam generatio est perfectissima productio: convenit ergo perfectissimo enti, Deo altissimo. Quarto, quoniam quidquid perfectionis est in creaturis, reperitur in Deo. Quum ergo in mente creata sit emanatio verbi ab intellectu, et amoris a voluntate, erit etiam in mente divina processus verbi atque amoris, seu Prolis ac Spiritus Sancti.
paras.en: And it seems that this can be proved. First, from the immensity of the divine goodness, which, since it is of infinite communicability [that is, of a nature to share itself without limit], has gone forth into an act proportioned to itself, by bringing forth an immeasurable offspring, which can be none other than God. Second, because the possession of no thing is delightful without companionship; and since in God there is perfect and immeasurable love, God has someone whom He loves with infinite love, since love is not properly directed to oneself. Third, because generation is the most perfect kind of production: it therefore befits the most perfect being, God most high. Fourth, because whatever perfection there is in creatures is found in God. Since, then, in a created mind there is an emanation of a word from the intellect, and of love from the will, there will also be in the divine mind a procession of a word and of love, that is, of an Offspring and of the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Et respondendum, quod nunquam aliquis purus philosophus agnovit, quod in Deo esset emanatio ad intra Personæ a Persona, vel quod aliquid procedens a Deo esset ei æquale et consubstantiale: imo hoc reputabant omnino impossibile, ut patet ex Elementatione Procli summi Platonici. Sed nec possibile est naturali ratione demonstrare vel invenire Deum esse in Personis trinum, vel binum, et in essentia unum: quia perfectio Creatoris relucet in creaturis eo modo quo procedunt a Creatore. Quum ergo tres Personæ sint una causa creaturarum, ita quod creatio convenit eis quantum ad id in quo conveniunt, scilicet ratione naturæ atque potentiæ, palam est quod earum distinctio ex creaturis nequeat elici, demonstrari, aut inveniri.
paras.en: And the answer must be that no mere philosopher ever acknowledged that in God there is an emanation *ad intra* [inward, within the Godhead itself, as opposed to the outward work of creation] of a Person from a Person, or that anything proceeding from God is equal and consubstantial with Him: on the contrary, they held this to be altogether impossible, as is clear from the *Elementatio* of Proclus, the greatest of the Platonists [his *Elements of Theology*]. Nor is it possible by natural reason to demonstrate or find out that God is threefold, or twofold, in Persons and one in essence: for the perfection of the Creator shines back in creatures in the manner in which they proceed from the Creator. Since, then, the three Persons are one cause of creatures, so that creating belongs to them in respect of that in which they agree, namely by reason of their nature and power, it is plain that their distinction cannot be drawn out, demonstrated, or found out from creatures.

paras.t: Verumtamen advertendum quod profundissimi philosophorum aliqua dixerunt, et in scriptis suis reliquerunt, in quibus videntur cognitionem divinitatis Patris ac Filii habuisse, propter communionem verborum quibus utuntur loquendo de Deo et processione eorum quæ producuntur ab ipso. Plato namque et ejus sequaces, multi quoque Peripatetici, disseruerunt universorum processum a primo principio fieri per quamdam assimilationem, ita quod omnia profluxerunt a Deo per rationem similitudinis, hoc est secundum similitudinem quamdam, quoniam omne agens producit sibi simile, et effectus vocatur participata similitudo suæ causæ. Quum ergo Deus sit lux pura, supersplendidissima et immensa, id quod immediate causatur ab eo, dixerunt esse ei simillimum. Unde vocabant primam intelligentiam seu primam mentem creatam, signaculum lucis divinæ, splendorem claritatis æternæ, itemque, quod esset imago evidentissima ac præclarissima majestatis divinæ, speculumque perfectionis increatæ. Et quoniam ratio filiationis in similitudine quadam consistit, idcirco dixerunt mentem illam immediate a summa divinaque mente creatam, esse Filium, imo et Unigenitum et Primogenitum Dei. Unde refert Macrobius super Somnium Scipionis, quod Platonici posuerunt a summo Deo immediate profluxisse ac conditam esse mentem quamdam Deo sublimi simillimam, omnium creaturarum speciebus ac rationibus plenam, a qua dixerunt cetera omnia esse creata.
paras.en: It must be noted, however, that the most profound of the philosophers said certain things, and left them in their writings, in which they seem to have had knowledge of the Godhead of the Father and the Son, because of the words they share with us in speaking of God and of the procession of the things that are produced by Him. For Plato and his followers, and many of the Peripatetics too, taught that the going forth of all things from the first principle comes about through a kind of likening, so that all things flowed forth from God by way of likeness, that is, according to a certain likeness, since every agent produces what is like itself, and the effect is called a participated likeness of its cause. Since, then, God is pure light, more than supremely resplendent and immeasurable, they said that what is caused by Him immediately is most like Him. Hence they called the first intelligence, or first created mind, the seal of the divine light, the splendour of the eternal brightness, and also the most evident and most glorious image of the divine majesty and the mirror of the uncreated perfection. And since the notion of sonship consists in a certain likeness, they therefore said that this mind, created immediately by the supreme and divine Mind, is the Son, indeed the Only-begotten and the First-born of God. Hence Macrobius relates, on the Dream of Scipio, that the Platonists held that from the supreme God there flowed forth immediately, and was established, a certain mind most like the sublime God, full of the forms and reasons [*rationes*: the patterns or exemplars] of all creatures, by which, they said, all other things were created.

paras.t: Hinc etiam Hermes Trismegistus, qui legitur fuisse Platonis discipulus (fuit autem et alius Hermes, qui scribitur præcessisse diluvium): ait igitur Hermes præfatus in libro suo quem intitulavit, De Verbo perfecto. Sed antequam verba Hermetis commemorem, audiamus quid in libro contra hæreticos asserat Augustinus. Hermes, qui Latine Mercurius, scripsit librum De Verbo perfecto: magnum nomen libri, quoniam magnus de quo scripsit. Audiamus quid dicat: Dominus omnium factor deorum, secundum fecit Dominum. Quoniam ergo hunc fecit primum et solum et verum, bonus ei visus est, et plenissimus omnium bonorum; et lætatus est in eo, et valde dilexit eum, tanquam unigenitum suum. Et post pauca: Hic est (inquit) Filius Dei benedicti, cujus nomen non potest humano ore narrari. Ex hoc ergo quod Hermes vocat hunc secundum Deum, elucescit quod posuit eum substantialiter distinctum a summo Deo, et per consequens puram creaturam. Itaque, quod Augustinus affirmat illum esse magnum, scilicet Verbum Dei perfectum, de quo scripsit Hermes hunc librum, indiget sano intellectu et pia interpretatione: quia secundum veritatem, liber ille scriptus non est de Filio Dei vero, sed æstimato, præsertim quoniam Filius Dei non est factus, quomodo Hermes dicit Dominum omnium deorum fecisse secundum Deum. Ex hoc dicto Hermetis et Platonicorum, orta est hæresis Arii atque Eunomii, asserentium Filium Dei esse puram creaturam, ut dicit S. Thomas in Summa contra gentiles.
paras.en: Hence also Hermes Trismegistus, who is read to have been a disciple of Plato (there was also another Hermes, who is written to have lived before the Flood): this Hermes, then, speaks in his book which he entitled *On the Perfect Word*. But before I relate the words of Hermes, let us hear what Augustine asserts in his book against the heretics [the treatise *Against Five Heresies*, then read as Augustine's]: Hermes, who in Latin is called Mercury, wrote a book *On the Perfect Word*: a great name for a book, since great is He of whom he wrote. Let us hear what he says: The Lord and maker of all the gods made a second Lord. Since, then, He made this one first, and only, and true, he seemed good to Him, and most full of all good things; and He rejoiced in him, and loved him greatly, as His only-begotten. And a little after: This (he says) is the Son of the blessed God, whose name cannot be told by human mouth. From the fact, then, that Hermes calls him a second God, it is clear that he held him to be substantially distinct from the supreme God, and consequently a mere creature. And so Augustine's statement that he is great, namely the perfect Word of God of whom Hermes wrote this book, needs a sound understanding and a devout interpretation: for in truth that book was not written of the true Son of God, but of a supposed one; especially since the Son of God was not made, in the way that Hermes says the Lord of all the gods made a second God. From this saying of Hermes and of the Platonists arose the heresy of Arius and Eunomius, who asserted that the Son of God is a mere creature, as St Thomas says in the *Summa contra Gentiles*.

paras.t: Denique, juxta Thomam in prima parte Summæ, etiam Origenes dictis Platonicorum imbutus, dixit Verbum Dei esse puram creaturam. Propter quod Thomas ait Origenem fuisse fontem Arianæ perfidiæ, quia secundum Origenem, Verbum dicitur in Deo non proprie, sed metaphorice, utpote non filius naturalis, sed imitativus. Verum, qualiter intelligendum sit dictum hoc Thomæ, ignoro. Constat nempe quod Origenes in multis locis testetur Filium Dei esse verum æternumque Deum. Imo in epistola sua ad S. Barbaram, quam instruxit, apertissime dicit quod Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti sit una divinitas et vera æqualitas, et quod sunt tres Personæ unusque Deus. Præterea Athanasius fidei propugnator, allegat Origenem pro confirmatione fidei Trinitatis; nec dubium quin sanctissimus Athanasius, qui tantæ auctoritatis exstitit in Scripturis quod nullus unquam ei contradicere ausus fuit, bene agnovit ac legit verba atque volumina Origenis, nec aliquo modo allegasset eum, disputando contra Arianos, si putasset Origenem fuisse fontem Arianæ impietatis.
paras.en: Lastly, according to Thomas in the First Part of the *Summa*, Origen too, steeped in the sayings of the Platonists, said that the Word of God is a mere creature. For this reason Thomas says that Origen was the source of the Arian faithlessness, because according to Origen the Word is spoken of in God not properly but metaphorically, as being a son not by nature but by imitation. But how this saying of Thomas is to be understood, I do not know. For it is certain that Origen in many places testifies that the Son of God is true and eternal God. Indeed, in his letter to St Barbara, whom he instructed [the letter belongs to the legend of St Barbara], he says most plainly that the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost have one Godhead and true equality, and that they are three Persons and one God. Moreover Athanasius, the champion of the faith, cites Origen in confirmation of faith in the Trinity; and there is no doubt that the most holy Athanasius, who was of such authority in the Scriptures that no one ever dared to contradict him, knew well and read the words and volumes of Origen, and would by no means have cited him in disputing against the Arians if he had thought that Origen was the source of the Arian impiety.

paras.t: Verumtamen multa inveniuntur in dictis Origenis, ex quibus videtur verum esse quod adstruit Thomas, videlicet, quod Filius Dei non comprehendat Patrem perfecte; itemque, quod hoc est Filius ad Patrem, quod Petrus vel Paulus ad Filium. Insuper, super illud Isaiæ, Seraphim stabant super illud, per Seraphim, intelligit Origenes Filium ac Spiritum Sanctum, sicut innuit S. Hieronymus, quamvis non exprimat nomen Origenis. Ad hæc atque similia diversi diversimode responderunt: quidam, quod hæretici inseruerunt alia libris Origenis, sicut libris B. Ambrosii aliqua falsa inveniuntur inserta; quidam, quod fuerunt duo Origenes, unus catholicus, alter hæreticus; quidam, quod Origenes scripsit aliqua sibi invicem contrariantia, sicut et Augustinus, propter quod tandem compulsus est facere librum Retractationum. Sed de hac materia nihil definio, Origenem indiscrete defendendo, quem certum est in multis errasse.
paras.en: Yet many things are found in the sayings of Origen from which what Thomas maintains seems to be true, namely that the Son of God does not comprehend the Father perfectly; and likewise that the Son is to the Father what Peter or Paul is to the Son. Furthermore, on that text of Isaias, [[Is 6:2|Upon it stood the seraphims|Seraphim stabant super illud]], Origen understands by the Seraphim the Son and the Holy Ghost, as St Jerome indicates, although he does not give Origen's name. To these and similar things different people have answered in different ways: some, that heretics inserted other matter into the books of Origen, just as some false things are found inserted into the books of Bl. Ambrose; some, that there were two Origens, one Catholic, the other a heretic; some, that Origen wrote some things contrary to one another, as Augustine did too, for which reason he was at last compelled to write the book of *Retractations*. But on this matter I define nothing, as one who would defend Origen indiscriminately; for it is certain that he erred in many things.

paras.t: Nunc solvendæ sunt rationes quibus videtur ostendi quod Trinitas, vel Patris ac Filii deitas, posset naturali ratione probari. Primo itaque, ad auctoritatem Augustini dicendum, quod principium evangelii S. Joannis invenitur in libris Platonicorum, non quantum ad verum ipsius intellectum, sed quantum ad aliquam communionem verborum, et quantum ad apparentiam superficialem. Posuerunt enim Platonici verbum in Deo. Unde Avicebron Platonicus in libro suo de Fonte vitæ affirmat, quod intellectus divinus ac paternalis omnia agit per verbum intus conceptum. Sed nomine verbi, intelligunt rationem idealem seu mundum archetypum. Quod vero Hermes ait monadem, id est unitatem seu unum Deum, genuisse monadem, Thomas interpretatur sic intelligendum, quod unus Deus condidit unum mundum, propter sui ipsius amorem. Tamen intelligendum id reor de generatione prædicta mentis creatæ, secundum Platonicos. Et quod dicit Trismegistus Deum in se suum reflexisse ardorem, intelligit non de processione Spiritus Sancti, sed quod Deus diligit se propter se, et ex amore sui ad se ipsum conversi diligit alia.
paras.en: Now the reasons must be answered by which it seems to be shown that the Trinity, or the Godhead of the Father and the Son, could be proved by natural reason. First, then, to the authority of Augustine it must be said that the beginning of St John's Gospel is found in the books of the Platonists, not as to its true meaning, but as to a certain sharing of words, and as to a surface appearance. For the Platonists did place a word in God. Hence Avicebron the Platonist, in his book *The Fount of Life*, affirms that the divine and fatherly intellect does all things through a word conceived within. But by the name of word they understand the ideal pattern [*ratio idealis*: the divine idea of things], or the archetypal world. As for Hermes saying that the monad, that is, unity or the one God, begot a monad, Thomas interprets it as meaning that the one God made one world for love of Himself. Yet I think it is to be understood of the generation, spoken of above, of the created mind, according to the Platonists. And when Trismegistus says that God reflected His own ardour back upon Himself, he means not the procession of the Holy Ghost, but that God loves Himself for His own sake, and from the love of Himself, turned toward Himself, loves other things.

paras.t: Ad argumentum de immensitate divinæ bonitatis, dicerent naturales, quod quamvis sit communicabilitatis immensæ, non tamen producit germen sibi æquale: non ex sua impotentia, sed propter incapacitatem procedentis, quod dicunt non posse æquari suo causali atque fontali principio. Ad aliud diceretur, quod nullius rei possessio jucunda est sine consorte, in his quorum unum indiget altero; Deus vero in se ipso summe simpliciterque perfectus est. Ad aliud de amore diceretur, quod licet amor non sit proprie ad se ipsum, nihilominus, secundum Philosophum, amor ad alium oritur ex amore ad se ipsum, et unusquisque tantum vel plus diligit se, quantum aliquem alium conditum: ideo Deus vere diligit se ipsum infinito amore atque fervore. Ad aliud diceretur, quod generatio convenit Deo altiori modo quam creaturis, per hoc quod tribuit eis vim generativam. Ad aliud quoque responderetur, quod in creatis intellectibus est emanatio verbi ac amoris, quia in eis differunt essentia et actio, nec essentia eorum in se ipsa perfecta est, quum non sit actus purus, sed verbo atque amore perficitur. In Deo autem opposito modo est, quia in eo sunt penitus idem essentia, virtus et actio, estque Deus in se absolute perfectus, et purus actus, quidquid ad beatitudinem pertinet, in se eminentissime comprehendens. Quamvis itaque præinductæ rationes non sunt demonstrativæ, pulchre tamen declarant quod fides Trinitatis non sit aliquam irrationabilitatem vel impossibilitatem complectens: nam licet sit supra rationem, non tamen est contra eam.
paras.en: To the argument from the immensity of the divine goodness, the natural philosophers would say that, although it is of immeasurable communicability, it does not produce an offspring equal to itself: not through any powerlessness of its own, but because of the incapacity of what proceeds, which, they say, cannot be made equal to its causal and fontal [that is, source-giving] principle. To the next it would be said that the possession of no thing is delightful without a companion in those things of which one needs another; but God is in Himself supremely and simply perfect. To the next, on love, it would be said that, although love is not properly directed to oneself, nevertheless, according to the Philosopher [Aristotle], love for another arises from love for oneself, and each one loves himself as much as, or more than, any other created being: and so God truly loves Himself with infinite love and fervour. To the next it would be said that generation befits God in a higher way than it does creatures, in that He gives them the power of generating. To the last, too, the answer would be that in created intellects there is an emanation of a word and of love because in them essence and action differ, and their essence is not perfect in itself, since it is not pure act, but is perfected by word and love. In God it is the opposite way, for in Him essence, power and action are altogether the same, and God is absolutely perfect in Himself, and pure act, comprehending in Himself in the most eminent manner whatever belongs to beatitude. Although, therefore, the reasons brought forward above are not demonstrative, they nevertheless show beautifully that the faith of the Trinity does not contain anything irrational or impossible: for though it is above reason, it is not against it.

1.title: Elucidatio hujus primi capituli, ab eo loco quo dicitur: Fuit homo missus a Deo.
1.title_en: Explanation of this first chapter, from the place where it says: “There was a man sent from God.”

paras.t: Hucusque tractavit sublimis Evangelista de divinitate, divinaque operatione, atque incommutabili subsistentia Verbi. Nunc vero subjungit de ejus præcursore. Quoniam enim dicturus mox est de Verbi incarnatione, et adventu ejus in hunc mundum, ceterisque operibus atque dogmatibus Salvatoris, congruenter præmisit de ejus præcursore tractatum. Pauca enim ponit de Præcursore, sciens Lucam glorioso sententiosoque stilo descripsisse genealogiam, annuntiationem, conceptionem, nativitatem conversationemque Præcursoris: de cujus etiam parcitate in victu, et duritia in vestitu, Matthæus et Marcus scripserunt. Itaque ait:
paras.en: Thus far the sublime Evangelist has treated of the divinity, the divine working, and the unchangeable subsistence of the Word. Now he goes on to speak of His forerunner. For since he is about to speak of the Incarnation of the Word, and of His coming into this world, and of the other works and teachings of the Saviour, he fittingly sets first an account of His forerunner. He says little of the Forerunner, knowing that Luke had described, in a glorious and weighty style, the lineage, the annunciation, the conception, the birth and the manner of life of the Forerunner[[Luke 1:5||]] [the margin gives only Luke i, the whole chapter]; and Matthew and Mark wrote of the sparingness of his food and the harshness of his clothing[[Matt 3:4||]][[Mark 1:6||]]. And so he says:

paras.t: Fuit homo missus a Deo. Nemo enim sapienter agens, assumit sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo, tanquam Aaron. Quocontra Dominus ait de præsumptuosis et falsis prophetis: Ipsi currebant, et ego non misi eos. Missio ista Joannis intelligi potest tunc facta, quando Deo jubente exivit a latibulis eremi ad ripam Jordanis, quatenus illic baptizando, populum congregaret, eisque de Christi adventu prædicaret. Unde Lucas ait: Anno quintodecimo imperii Tiberii Cæsaris, factum est verbum Domini super Joannem Zachariæ filium, in deserto. Fuit autem missus a Deo, vel ex sola inspiratione interna, vel ex allocutione et apparitione angelica exterius facta, quæ non est ab aliquo Evangelistarum descripta. Hanc missionem Joannis Deus prædixit per Malachiam: Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, et præparabit viam ante faciem meam. Dicitur quippe Joannes angelus, ratione officii, non naturæ, et quoniam angelicæ conversationis fuit.
paras.en: [[1:6|There was a man sent from God|Fuit homo missus a Deo]]. For no one acting wisely takes [[Heb 5:4|the honour to himself, but he that is called by God, as Aaron was|sibi honorem, sed qui vocatur a Deo, tanquam Aaron]]. Against this the Lord says of presumptuous and false prophets: [[Jer 23:21|they ran|ipsi currebant]], and I did not send them. This sending of John can be understood as having taken place when, at God's command, he went out from the hiding places of the wilderness to the bank of the Jordan, so that by baptizing there he might gather the people and preach to them of the coming of Christ. Hence Luke says: [[Luke 3:1|in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar|Anno quintodecimo imperii Tiberii Cæsaris]], [[Luke 3:2|the word of the Lord was made unto John, the son of Zachary, in the desert|factum est verbum Domini super Joannem Zachariæ filium, in deserto]]. And he was sent from God either by inward inspiration alone, or by an angelic address and apparition made outwardly, which none of the Evangelists has described. This sending of John God foretold through Malachias: [[Mal 3:1|Behold I send my angel, and he shall prepare the way before my face|Ecce ego mitto angelum meum, et præparabit viam ante faciem meam]]. For John is called an angel [*angelus*, which also means 'messenger'] by reason of his office, not of his nature, and because his manner of life was angelic.

paras.t: Cui nomen erat Joannes. Sic namque Gabriel archangelus jussit Zachariæ vocare filium suum. Et congruit nomen istud Præcursori, quia Joannes interpretatur gratia Dei, quæ præcipue fuit in homine isto, quo inter natos mulierum non surrexit major seu sanctior; qui etiam primo prædicavit: Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cælorum, hoc est gratia Salvatoris. Quum enim alicui divinitus nomen imponitur, insinuatur quod proprietas significata per nomen competit illi, quemadmodum Abram vocatus est Abraham, id est pater multarum gentium, et Jacob dictus est Israel, quum Dei angelum vidisset.
paras.en: [[1:6|whose name was John|cui nomen erat Joannes]]. For so the archangel Gabriel bade Zachary call his son[[Luke 1:13||]]. And this name befits the Forerunner, for John is interpreted 'the grace of God', which was pre-eminently in this man, than whom, [[Matt 11:11|among them that are born of women|inter natos mulierum]], there has not risen a greater or a holier; who also was the first to preach: [[Matt 3:2|Do penance: for the kingdom of heaven is at hand|Pœnitentiam agite, appropinquabit enim regnum cælorum]], that is, the grace of the Saviour. For when a name is given to anyone by God, it is intimated that the property signified by the name belongs to him; as Abram was called Abraham, that is, [[Gen 17:5|a father of many nations|multarum gentium]], and Jacob was called Israel when he had seen the angel of God[[Gen 32:28||]].

paras.t: Hic venit a secretis locis deserti ad publica loca, in testimonium perhibendum, id est ad testificandum, non ad salvandum, videlicet ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine, id est, veritatem annuntiaret de Christo, ut omnes homines, primo Judæi, deinde gentiles, crederent in Filium Dei per illum, hoc est mediante testificatione Joannis, sicque credendo, consequerentur salutem æternam. Non dicit, Ut omnes crederent in illum, quoniam fides quum sit virtus theologica, habet Deum pro objecto: concernit enim Deum sub ratione primæ veritatis. Ideo non est credendum in hominem purum. Hinc infra ait Salvator, Creditis in Deum, et in me credite: quod consequens non esset, nisi et Filius esset Deus.
paras.en: [[1:7|This man came|Hic venit]] from the hidden places of the desert to public places, [[1:7|for a witness|in testimonium]] to be borne, that is, to testify, not to save: namely, [[1:7|to give testimony of the light|ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine]], that is, to proclaim the truth about Christ, [[1:7|that all men|ut omnes]], first the Jews, then the Gentiles, [[1:7|might believe|crederent]] in the Son of God [[1:7|through him|per illum]], that is, by means of John's testimony, and so, by believing, might obtain eternal salvation. He does not say, 'That all might believe in him', because faith, being a theological virtue, has God for its object: for it regards God under the aspect [*ratio*] of the First Truth. Therefore one is not to believe in a mere man. Hence further on the Saviour says, [[John 14:1|You believe in God: believe also in me|Creditis in Deum, et in me credite]]: which would not follow unless the Son too were God.

paras.t: Non erat ille Joannes lux principalis, effective illustrans, lucem gratiæ præstans, et per essentiam lucens: erat tamen lux instrumentalis, dispositive illuminans, ad gratiam præparans, lux participata, eo modo quo Christus ait Apostolis: Vos estis lux mundi. Et ad Philippenses Apostolus: Sitis, inquit, sine querela in medio nationis pravæ, inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria in mundo. Denique, secundum Dionysium, quædam est lux illuminans, non illuminata, sicut lux prima. Alia est lux solum illuminata, ut illi qui modicam gratiam habent. Alia est lux medio modo se habens, videlicet illuminans et illuminata, ut illi qui de gratia sibi concessa alios possunt illuminare: inter quos certum est Præcursorem unum de summis fuisse. Sed ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine: hoc est, Joannes non fuit Christus in lege promissus, sed ejus minister et præco, ordinatus ad hoc, ut Christo testimonium daret. Hoc fecit Joannes dicendo: Venit fortior post me, cujus non sum dignus procumbens solvere corrigiam calceamentorum ejus. In Actibus quoque Paulus ait dixisse Joannem: Quem me arbitramini esse, non sum ego. Perhibuit etiam Joannes testimonium Christo operibus, utpote baptizando Judæos in nomine Christi venturi. Forma enim baptismi Joannis fuit, Baptizo te in nomine futuri, secundum quod in Actibus tangit Apostolus: Joannes baptizavit populum, dicens, In eum qui venturus est, ut crederent, hoc est in Jesum. Idcirco receptio baptismi Joannis erat quædam professio credendi in Christum.
paras.en: [[1:8|He was not|Non erat ille]], John was not, [[1:8|the light|lux]] in the principal sense: enlightening as the efficient cause, bestowing the light of grace, and shining by His very essence. Yet he was an instrumental light, enlightening by way of disposition, preparing for grace, a participated light, in the way that Christ says to the Apostles: [[Matt 5:14|You are the light of the world|Vos estis lux mundi]]. And the Apostle to the Philippians: [[Phil 2:15|That you may be blameless|Sitis, inquit, sine querela]], he says, [[Phil 2:15|in the midst of a crooked|in medio nationis pravæ]] generation, [[Phil 2:15|among whom you shine as lights in the world|inter quos lucetis sicut luminaria in mundo]]. Lastly, according to Dionysius, there is a light that enlightens and is not enlightened, as the First Light. Another light is only enlightened, as those who have a little grace. Another light stands in between, namely both enlightening and enlightened, as those who from the grace granted to them can enlighten others; and among these it is certain that the Forerunner was one of the highest. [[1:8|But was to give testimony of the light|sed ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine]]: that is, John was not the Christ promised in the Law, but His minister and herald, ordained for this, to bear witness to Christ. This John did by saying: [[Mark 1:7|There cometh after me one mightier than I|Venit fortior post me]], [[Mark 1:7|the latchet of whose shoes I am not worthy to stoop down and loose|cujus non sum dignus procumbens solvere corrigiam calceamentorum ejus]]. In the Acts too Paul says that John said: [[Acts 13:25|I am not he whom you think me to be|Quem me arbitramini esse, non sum ego]]. John bore witness to Christ also by works, namely by baptizing the Jews in the name of the Christ who was to come. For the form of John's baptism was, 'I baptize thee in the name of Him who is to come', as the Apostle touches on in the Acts: [[Acts 19:4|John baptized the people|Joannes baptizavit populum]], saying, [[Acts 19:4|That they should believe in him, who was to come|in eum qui venturus]], [[Acts 19:4|that is to say, in Jesus|hoc est in Jesum]]. Therefore the receiving of John's baptism was a kind of profession of belief in Christ.

paras.t: Missus est ergo Joannes ante Christum, ut homines ad Christi susceptionem aptaret, docendo, baptizando, orando, exemplariterque vivendo. Erat nempe testis idoneus, propter vitæ suæ sanctitatem omnibus manifestam, gratiam prophetalem, angelicam annuntiationem, miraculosam conceptionem ac nativitatem. Necessaria vero fuit Judæis præparatio ista: nam quum rudes fuerint, immediate capaces non erant supernaturalium atque cælestium documentorum Christi, sed pedetentim inducendi erant ad sublimiora. Joannes ergo, inducendo eos ad peccatorum confessionem, baptismi receptionem, dicendo etiam, Appropinquabit regnum cælorum, cœpit eos a terrenis abstrahere, atque ad supernorum amorem accendere, ac per hoc ad Christi legem et fidem aptare.
paras.en: John, then, was sent before Christ to make men fit to receive Christ, by teaching, baptizing, praying, and living as an example. For he was a fitting witness, because of the holiness of his life, manifest to all, his prophetic grace, the angel's announcement of him, and his miraculous conception and birth. And this preparation was necessary for the Jews: for since they were unlearned, they were not capable straight away of the supernatural and heavenly teachings of Christ, but had to be led step by step to higher things. John, therefore, by leading them to confession of their sins and to the receiving of baptism, and by saying too, [[Matt 3:2|the kingdom of heaven is at hand|regnum cælorum]], began to draw them away from earthly things and to kindle them to the love of the things above, and by this to make them fit for the law and the faith of Christ.

paras.t: Erat lux vera, hoc est non participata aut defectiva, sed plena et substantialiter clara, in qua natura lucis perfectissime reperitur. Unde Joannes in Canonica sua scribit: Deus lux est, et tenebræ non sunt in eo ullæ. Omne autem creatum habet aliquid tenebrositatis admixtum; nam ipsa minoratio lucis, ipsa ejus distantia seu dissimilitudo a luce divina, est tenebrositas quædam. Comparatione quoque lucis divinæ ac infinitæ, appellatur quasi caligo: ideo enim luna non splendet, et cæli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus. Quamvis vero istud de qualibet divina Persona sit verum, nunc tamen de Filio dicitur, cui lux appropriatur, quoniam lux spiritualis præcipue spectat ad intellectum ac sapientiam. Quum ergo Verbum seu Filius sit emanatio intellectus, sic ei appropriatur lux, sicut sapientia, veritas, ars, splendor, et species.
paras.en: [[1:9|That was the true light|Erat lux vera]], that is, not participated or deficient, but full and substantially bright, in which the nature of light is found most perfectly. Hence John writes in his Canonical Epistle: [[1 John 1:5|God is light and in him there is no darkness|Deus lux est, et tenebræ non sunt in eo ullæ]]. But every created thing has some darkness mixed in it; for the very lessening of light, its very distance or unlikeness from the divine light, is a kind of darkness. And in comparison with the divine and infinite light it is called, as it were, a mist: for this is why [[Job 25:5|the moon doth not shine|luna non splendet]], and [[Job 15:15|the heavens are not pure in his sight|cæli non sunt mundi in conspectu ejus]]. And although this is true of each divine Person, it is said here of the Son, to whom light is appropriated [that is, ascribed to Him in particular, though common to the three Persons, because of its likeness to what is proper to Him], since spiritual light belongs chiefly to understanding and wisdom. Since, then, the Word or Son is the emanation of the intellect [the Son proceeds from the Father as the Word conceived by the divine understanding], light is appropriated to Him in the same way as wisdom, truth, art, splendour and beauty [*species*].

paras.t: Quæ illuminat lumine naturalis ingenii omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, id est, qui per nativitatem ingreditur orbem terrarum vallemque lacrimarum. Vel, Illuminat lumine gratiæ omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum, id est omnem qui illuminatur gratia spirituali, quam nullus sortitur nisi a Filio. Juxta hunc sensum habetur in Psalmo, Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt, et erigit omnes elisos: non quod omnes corruentes et elisi allevantur ac eriguntur, sed quod nemo talium allevetur aut erigatur, nisi a Deo. Vel, Illuminat omnem hominem, quantum in se est, sicut vult omnes salvari, ita quod nemo excusatur si non fuerit illustratus. Illuminat quoque omnem hominem, dando unicuique angelum pro custode, qui a diversis erroribus et peccatis retrahit hominem sibi commissum. Vel, Illuminat omnem hominem, id est quosdam de omni genere hominum: nam post passionem, et prædicationem Apostolorum, illuminavit sæculum universum. Juxta quem sensum ait inferius: Si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum; et Psalmista, Benedicentur in ipso omnes tribus terræ.
paras.en: [[1:9|Which enlighteneth|Quæ illuminat]] with the light of natural understanding [[1:9|every man that cometh into this world|omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum]], that is, who by birth enters the round of the earth and the vale of tears. Or: He [[1:9|enlighteneth|illuminat]] with the light of grace [[1:9|every man that cometh into this world|omnem hominem venientem in hunc mundum]], that is, everyone who is enlightened by spiritual grace, which no one obtains except from the Son. In this sense we have in the Psalm, [[Ps 144:14|The Lord lifteth up all that fall: and setteth up all that are cast down|Allevat Dominus omnes qui corruunt, et erigit omnes elisos]]: not that all who fall and are cast down are lifted up and set up, but that none of them is lifted up or set up except by God. Or: He [[1:9|enlighteneth every man|illuminat omnem hominem]] as far as lies in Him, as He wills all to be saved[[1 Tim 2:4||]], so that no one is excused if he has not been enlightened. He also enlightens every man by giving each one an angel as guardian, who draws back the man entrusted to him from various errors and sins. Or: He [[1:9|enlighteneth every man|illuminat omnem hominem]], that is, some of every kind of men: for after the Passion and the preaching of the Apostles He enlightened the whole world. In this sense He says further on: [[John 12:32|if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself|Si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum]]; and the Psalmist, [[Ps 71:17|in him shall all the tribes of the earth be blessed|Benedicentur in ipso omnes tribus terræ]].

paras.t: In mundo erat. Hoc de Christo secundum utramque ejus naturam accipi potest, sed differenter. Primo sic: In mundo, id est in toto ente creato seu universo, erat hæc lux, id est, totum mundum ab exordio suæ creationis implevit, quum sit infinita. Propter quod ait per Jeremiam: Numquid non cælum et terram ego impleo? Deus enim ubique est per essentiam, præsentiam, atque potentiam. Ipse siquidem omnia penetrat, sua quoque potentia in omnia se extendit, et suo conspectui omnia patent. Verumtamen, juxta Salomonem, Longe est Dominus ab impiis: non utique loco, sed dissimilitudine, quia non est nec habitat in eis per gratiam. Fuit autem circa Deum triplex error: Unus Manichæorum, dicentium ista corporalia et terrena Deo lucis non esse subjecta. Contra hos dicimus Deum esse ubique per potentiam. Alius fuit error negantium divinam providentiam. De quibus dicit Psalmista: Dixerunt: Quomodo scit Deus; et, Si est scientia in Excelso? Contra hos dicimus Deum esse ubique per præsentiam, ita quod omnia sunt aperta et nuda oculis ejus. Tertius fuit error dicentium, quod Deus immediate non condidit nisi primam intelligentiam, et illa creavit secundam, secunda quoque tertiam. Cujus erroris origo, secundum Thomam, fuit auctor libri de Causis. Quem errorem Avicenna et Algazel sunt secuti. Contra istos asserimus Deum esse ubique per essentiam.
paras.en: [[1:10|He was in the world|In mundo erat]]. This can be taken of Christ according to each of His natures, but in different ways. First thus: [[1:10|in the world|In mundo]], that is, in the whole of created being, or the universe, was this light; that is, He has filled the whole world from the beginning of its creation, since He is infinite. That is why He says through Jeremias: [[Jer 23:24|do not I fill heaven and earth|Numquid non cælum et terram ego impleo]]? For God is everywhere by essence, presence and power. For He penetrates all things, by His power He extends Himself to all things, and all things lie open to His sight. Yet, according to Solomon, [[Prov 15:29|The Lord is far from the wicked|Longe est Dominus ab impiis]]: not indeed in place, but by unlikeness, because He is not in them nor dwells in them by grace. Now there was a threefold error about God. One was that of the Manichees, who said that these bodily and earthly things are not subject to the God of light. Against them we say that God is everywhere by power. Another was the error of those who deny divine providence, of whom the Psalmist says: [[Ps 72:11|they said: How doth God know? and is there knowledge in the most High|Dixerunt: Quomodo scit Deus; et, Si est scientia in Excelso?]]? [the margin reference is not legible in the scan; the words are those of Ps 72:11] Against them we say that God is everywhere by presence, so that all things are [[Heb 4:13|naked and open to his eyes|oculis ejus]]. The third was the error of those who said that God created immediately only the first intelligence, and that this created the second, and the second the third. The origin of this error, according to Thomas, was the author of the book *On Causes* [the *Liber de Causis*, drawn from Proclus]. Avicenna and Algazel followed this error. Against them we assert that God is everywhere by essence.

paras.t: Secundo exponitur sic: In mundo erat, id est, lux ista seu Christus post incarnationem in terris est visus, et cum hominibus conversatus, ita quod illum quem totus non capit orbis secundum suam divinitatem, parva pars terræ cepit et clausit secundum humanitatem assumptam.
paras.en: Secondly it is expounded thus: [[1:10|He was in the world|In mundo erat]], that is, this light, or Christ, after the Incarnation [[Bar 3:38|was seen upon earth, and conversed with men|in terris est visus, et cum hominibus conversatus]], so that He whom the whole world does not contain according to His divinity, a small part of the earth held and enclosed according to the humanity He assumed.

paras.t: Et mundus, videlicet cælum et terra, et quidquid cæli ambitu continetur, per ipsum Verbum factus est, eo sensu quo jam dictum atque expositum est: Omnia per ipsum facta sunt. Et quoniam mundus seu omnis creatura per Verbum facta est, ideo ad Verbi cognitionem naturalem inducit, videlicet ad cognoscendum suum Creatorem, quantum ad naturam, non quantum ad personam secundum relativam proprietatem. Effectus enim repræsentat suam causam.
paras.en: [[1:10|and the world|Et mundus]], namely heaven and earth and whatever is contained within the compass of heaven, [[1:10|was made by him|per ipsum factus est]], that is, by the Word, in the sense already stated and explained: [[1:3|All things were made by him|Omnia per ipsum facta sunt]]. And since the world, or every creature, was made by the Word, it therefore leads to a natural knowledge of the Word, namely to knowing its Creator as to the nature, not as to the Person according to His relative property [that is, what distinguishes the Son from the Father, His being begotten, which creatures cannot show; reason knows from creatures only the one divine nature common to the three Persons]. For an effect represents its cause.

paras.t: Et mundus eum non cognovit. In hoc sancto Joannis evangelio, mundus diversis modis accipitur: quandoque pro tota creatura; quandoque indifferenter pro bonis ac malis hominibus in mundo degentibus; interdum specialiter pro electis, ut quum dicitur, Sic Deus dilexit mundum, ut Unigenitum suum daret; interdum pro reprobis, sicut ait Salvator, Me odit mundus. Nunc ergo accipitur mundus pro perversis ac cæcis hominibus, qui Christum non cognoverunt per fidem formatam. Et licet aliqui tales agnoscant eum per fidem informem, factis tamen negant eumdem. Denique Judæi increduli, qui eum cognoverunt corporali intuitu, non cognoverunt eum interiori visu. Numquid enim cognoverunt eum, qui dixerunt, Nos scimus quia hic homo peccator est?
paras.en: [[1:10|and the world knew him not|Et mundus eum non cognovit]]. In this holy Gospel of John, "the world" is taken in various ways: sometimes for the whole of creation; sometimes for the good and the wicked alike who live in the world; at times specially for the elect, as when it is said, [[John 3:16|God so loved the world, as to give his only begotten Son|Sic enim Deus dilexit mundum, ut Filium suum unigenitum daret]]; at times for the reprobate, as the Saviour says of the world, [[John 7:7|me it hateth|me autem odit]]. Here, then, "the world" is taken for perverse and blind men, who did not know Christ by formed faith [faith "formed" by charity, that is, living faith]. And although some such men acknowledge Him by unformed faith [faith without charity, as in one in mortal sin], yet [[Tit 1:16|in their works they deny him|factis autem negant]]. Lastly, the unbelieving Jews, who knew Him by bodily sight, did not know Him by inward vision. For did they know Him who said, [[John 9:24|We know that this man is a sinner|nos scimus quia hic homo peccator est]]?

paras.t: In propria venit, hoc est, in hunc mundum inferiorem a se creatum, vel in Judæam et populum Israeliticum sibi olim peculiarem, per incarnationem descendit, quemadmodum Isaias oravit, dicendo: Utinam dirumperes cælos, et descenderes. A summo etenim cælo egressio ejus.
paras.en: [[1:11|He came unto his own|In propria venit]], that is, He came down by the incarnation into this lower world created by Him, or into Judæa and the people of Israel, once His own peculiar possession; as Isaias prayed, saying, [[Is 64:1|O that thou wouldst rend the heavens, and wouldst come down|Utinam dirumperes cælos, et descenderes]]. For [[Ps 18:7|His going out is from the end of heaven|a summo cælo egressio ejus]]. [Latin *in propria*, literally "into His own things", a neuter plural, as distinct from *sui*, "His own people", in the next clause.]

paras.t: Et sui, hoc est Judæi ad cultum Dei specialiter deputati, de quorum semine natus est Christus, eum non receperunt per fidem. Paucissimi enim Judæorum crediderunt in Christum, comparatione incredulorum. Hoc apud Isaiam apertissime invenitur prædictum, loquente Christo ad Patrem: Hæc dicit Dominus formans me ex utero servum sibi, ut reducam Jacob ad eum, et Israel non congregabitur. Hinc Dominus ait per Jeremiam: Prævaricatione prævaricata est in me domus Juda et domus Israel; negaverunt Dominum, et dixerunt, Non est ipse. Judæi igitur isti appellantur populus Christi, non ratione prædestinationis, sed creationis, et temporalis electionis atque vocationis. De quibus ait per Isaiam: Filios enutrivi et exaltavi, ipsi autem spreverunt me. Potest quoque generaliter de universis infidelibus et perversis exponi: qui dicuntur sui, quia ab ipso creati; et non receperunt eum, quia non omnium est fides, et novit Dominus qui sunt ejus per prædestinationem.
paras.en: [[1:11|and his own|et sui]], that is, the Jews, set apart in a special way for the worship of God, of whose seed Christ was born, [[1:11|received him not|eum non receperunt]] by faith. For very few of the Jews believed in Christ, compared with the unbelievers. This is found most plainly foretold in Isaias, where Christ speaks to the Father: [[Is 49:5|saith the Lord, that formed me from the womb to be his servant, that I may bring back Jacob unto him, and Israel will not be gathered together|dicit Dominus, formans me ex utero servum sibi, ut reducam Jacob ad eum, et Israël non congregabitur]]. Hence the Lord says through Jeremias: [[Jer 5:11|the house of Israel, and the house of Juda have greatly transgressed against me|Prævaricatione enim prævaricata est in me domus Israël, et domus Juda]]; [[Jer 5:12|They have denied the Lord, and said, It is not he|Negaverunt Dominum, et dixerunt: Non est ipse]]. These Jews, then, are called Christ's people not by reason of predestination, but of creation, and of election and calling in time. Of them He says through Isaias: [[Is 1:2|I have brought up children, and exalted them: but they have despised me|Filios enutrivi, et exaltavi; ipsi autem spreverunt me]]. It can also be explained in general of all unbelievers and perverse men: they are called His own because they were created by Him; and they received Him not, because [[2 Thess 3:2|all men have not faith|non enim omnium est fides]], and [[2 Tim 2:19|the Lord knoweth who are his|cognovit Dominus qui sunt ejus]] by predestination. [The margin reads I Tim. ii, 19; the words are those of 2 Tim 2:19.]

paras.t: Verum, ut Lucas ait in Actibus: Crediderunt quotquot præordinati erant ad vitam æternam. De quibus jam subditur: Quotquot autem receperunt eum per fidem formatam. Universaliter loquitur, dicendo, Quotquot, quoniam non est personarum acceptor Deus. Dedit eis potestatem, hoc est idoneitatem, seu gratiam efficacem, filios Dei fieri, hoc est per quam fiunt filii Dei adoptivi.
paras.en: But, as Luke says in the Acts, [[Acts 13:48|as many as were ordained to life everlasting believed|crediderunt quotquot erant præordinati ad vitam æternam]]. Of these it is now added: [[1:12|But as many as received him|Quotquot autem receperunt eum]] by formed faith. He speaks universally in saying "as many as", since [[Acts 10:34|God is not a respecter of persons|non est personarum acceptor Deus]]. [The margin reads "Ibid. x, 31", that is Acts 10:34.] [[1:12|he gave them power|dedit eis potestatem]], that is, fitness, or efficacious grace, [[1:12|to be made the sons of God|filios Dei fieri]], that is, the grace by which they become adopted sons of God.

paras.t: Sed quæritur, quum homines fiant filii Dei eo ipso quod credunt in Christum, quemadmodum ait Apostolus ad Galatas, Omnes vos filii Dei estis per fidem in Christo Jesu: quomodo recipientibus Christum per fidem, datur potestas filios Dei fieri, et non potius ipsa filiatio adoptiva? Et respondendum dupliciter: Primo, quod licet homo dum convertitur ad Christum per fidem et dilectionem, efficiatur adoptivus filius Dei, hoc tamen non est nisi in quantum habet propositum recipiendi Baptismum, in quo spiritualiter renascitur, et filiatio adoptiva perficitur. Omnibus ergo qui receperunt Christum, dedit ipsemet Christus secundum quod Deus, potestatem filios Dei fieri perfecte in fonte Baptismatis, quod non datur adultis nisi credentibus, imo nulli nisi fidem profiteatur, vel per se, si sit compos rationis, vel per alium, si sit infra annos discretionis. In Baptismo autem gratia augetur, character imprimitur, et homo Christo perfecte conformatur et incorporatur, atque ab omni labe peccati ac reatu pœnæ absolvitur, ut sit omnino filius Dei. Secundo respondetur, quod omnibus qui Christum nunc per fidem recipiunt, datur potestas filios Dei fieri, filiatione gloriæ consummata in patria. Per fidem enim pervenitur ad speciem. Filiatio quoque gratiæ adoptionis ordinatur ad filiationem gloriæ beatificæ fruitionis. Filiatio autem fundatur in assimilatione. Quoniam ergo per Christi adventum data est hominibus participatio divini esse, et supernaturalis similitudo cum Deo, idcirco recipientibus ipsum datur præfata potestas. Per fidem quippe inchoatur in nobis supernaturalis cognitio patriæ, quæ quantum ad suam plenitudinem, Deo est propria. Per gratiam quoque gratum facientem ponitur anima in esse supernaturali, divino ac meritorio, tamque accepta ac similis Deo efficitur, ut etiam vitam æternam de condigno mereatur.
paras.en: But it is asked: since men become sons of God by the very fact that they believe in Christ, as the Apostle says to the Galatians, [[Gal 3:26|you are all the children of God, by faith in Christ Jesus|Omnes enim filii Dei estis per fidem, quæ est in Christo Jesu]], how is it that to those who receive Christ by faith there is given power to be made sons of God, and not rather adoptive sonship itself? The answer is twofold. First: although a man, when he turns to Christ by faith and love, is made an adopted son of God, this is only in so far as he has the purpose of receiving Baptism, in which he is spiritually reborn and adoptive sonship is made perfect. To all, therefore, who received Christ, Christ Himself, as God, gave [[1:12|power to be made the sons of God|potestatem filios Dei fieri]] perfectly in the font of Baptism; which is not given to adults unless they believe, nor indeed to anyone unless faith is professed, either by himself, if he has the use of reason, or by another, if he is below the years of discretion. And in Baptism grace is increased, the character is imprinted [the indelible spiritual mark of Baptism], and the man is perfectly conformed and incorporated to Christ, and is absolved from every stain of sin and from the debt of punishment, so as to be wholly a son of God. Second, the answer is that to all who now receive Christ by faith there is given power to be made sons of God by the sonship of glory, consummated in our heavenly country. For by faith one comes to sight [Latin *species*, the vision of God face to face]. The sonship of the grace of adoption, too, is ordered to the sonship of the glory of blessed enjoyment. Now sonship is founded on likeness. Since, then, through Christ's coming a share in the divine being and a supernatural likeness to God has been given to men, the aforesaid power is given to those who receive Him. For by faith there is begun in us the supernatural knowledge of our heavenly country, which in its fulness is proper to God. And by sanctifying grace [Latin *gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes the soul pleasing to God] the soul is set in a supernatural, divine and meritorious being, and is made so acceptable to God and so like Him that it even merits eternal life condignly [*de condigno*, that is, as something truly due to its merit, not merely fitting].

paras.t: His qui credunt in nomine ejus, loquendo de nomine nominato, hoc est in ipso Christo, fide formata. Quum itaque Verbum sit Filius naturalis, qui ei per fidem uniuntur, atque per caritatem incorporantur, efficiuntur filii adoptivi. Filiatio autem adoptiva, quæ fit per gratiam, qua homines fiunt participes hæreditatis Patris adoptantis, est participatio filiationis naturalis. Hinc ad Romanos dicit Apostolus: Si filii, et hæredes, hæredes quidem Dei, cohæredes autem Christi. Et rursus: Non accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus, Abba (Pater).
paras.en: [[1:12|to them that believe in his name|his qui credunt in nomine ejus]], speaking of the name for the one named [that is, "name" stands for the person who bears it], that is, in Christ Himself, with formed faith. Since, then, the Word is the natural Son, those who are united to Him by faith and incorporated in Him by charity are made adopted sons. And adoptive sonship, which comes about through grace, by which men become sharers in the inheritance of the adopting Father, is a share in the natural sonship. Hence the Apostle says to the Romans: [[Rom 8:17|if sons, heirs also; heirs indeed of God and joint heirs with Christ|Si autem filii, et hæredes: hæredes, quidem Dei, cohæredes autem Christi]]. And again: [[Rom 8:15|you have not received the spirit of bondage again in fear: but you have received the spirit of adoption of sons, whereby we cry: Abba (Father)|Non enim accepistis spiritum servitutis iterum in timore, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis filiorum, in quo clamamus: Abba (Pater)]].

paras.t: Deinde Evangelista distinguit generationem spiritualem, per quam filiatio adoptiva acquiritur, a generatione carnali. Qui credentes et filii adoptivi, non ex sanguinibus, id est seminibus viri ac feminæ. Semen enim est superfluum alimenti sanguinei et sanguis coagulatus. Itaque, Non ex sanguinibus, id est semine viri, in quo est virtus formativa, et semine mulieris, quæ præbet in generatione materiam. Neque ex voluntate carnis, id est concupiscentia sensualitatis, vel feminæ, quæ nomine carnis exprimitur, quoniam mollior, et in ratione debilior; neque ex voluntate, id est concupiscentia, viri; sed ex Deo nati sunt, id est divina virtute et gratia spiritualiter regenerati, ac divinum esse sortiti. Nam loquendo de esse naturæ, tunc nati sunt ex seminibus parentum sicut et infideles; sed loquendo de esse gratiæ, per quod constituti sunt filii Dei adoptivi, nati sunt ex Deo, tanquam ex patre principali, hominem sibi assimilante ac deificante. Porro in generatione carnali ac naturali, semen se habet per modum causæ materialis, parentes per modum causæ efficientis; concupiscentia vero movet ad actum. Potest autem per voluntatem carnis et viri intelligi appetitus superior seu intellectivus, qui actum generationis imperat, vel ei consentit.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist distinguishes the spiritual generation, by which adoptive sonship is gained, from carnal generation. [[1:13|Who|qui]], believing and adopted sons, are born [[1:13|not of blood|non ex sanguinibus]] [Latin *ex sanguinibus*, "of bloods", a plural], that is, of the seeds of man and woman. For seed is the surplus of the blood's nourishment, and blood thickened. Thus, "not of bloods", that is, of the seed of the man, in which is the formative power, and the seed of the woman, who supplies the matter in generation. [[1:13|nor of the will of the flesh|neque ex voluntate carnis]], that is, the concupiscence of the senses, or of the woman, who is expressed by the name of flesh because she is softer and weaker in reason; [[1:13|nor of the will|neque ex voluntate]], that is, the concupiscence, [[1:13|of man|viri]]; [[1:13|but of God|sed ex Deo]] are they [[1:13|born|nati sunt]], that is, spiritually regenerated by divine power and grace, and given a share in divine being. For, speaking of natural being, they were born of the seeds of their parents just as unbelievers are; but speaking of the being of grace, by which they are made adopted sons of God, they are born of God, as of the principal Father, who makes man like Himself and deifies him. Further, in carnal and natural generation the seed stands as the material cause, the parents as the efficient cause, while concupiscence moves to the act. But "the will of the flesh and of man" can also be understood as the higher or intellective appetite, which commands the act of generation or consents to it.

1.title: Explanatio hujus primi capituli, ab eo loco quo scriptum est: Et Verbum caro factum est.
1.title_en: Explanation of this first chapter, from the place where it is written: “And the Word was made flesh.”

paras.t: Supra declaravit Evangelista quod Verbum Dei fuit ab æterno. Nunc pandit quod factum est in tempore, dicens: Et Verbum caro factum est. Item asseruit filios Dei adoptivos natos non esse ex sanguinibus. Ne quis ex hoc opinaretur quod multo minus Filius Dei naturalis natus esset ex semine seu sanguine, ideo docet quod Verbum factum est caro, nascendo ex semine Patriarcharum atque ex sanguine Virginis. Iterum, quoniam dixit homines fieri filios Dei, ostendit hoc non esse impossibile nec incredibile, quum Filius Dei factus sit filius hominis. Itaque, Verbum, id est unigenitus Filius Dei verus Deus, in se æternaliter subsistens, caro, id est homo verus, factum est, assumendo humanam naturam ad propriam personalitatem, utpote substantificando eam in semetipso, conferens ei subsistere in eodem esse in quo et Verbum subsistit, ita quod Verbi atque assumptæ humanitatis est una hypostasis, eademque suppositalitas seu subsistentia personalis: nam et ipsum Verbum est suppositum substantificans humanitatis sibi unitæ. Sumitur ergo hoc loco pars pro toto, videlicet caro pro homine, quemadmodum et in Psalmo, Ad te omnis caro veniet; in Isaia quoque, Videbit omnis caro quod os Domini locutum est; itemque, Videbit omnis caro salutare Dei nostri. Sic etiam infra ait Salvator ad Patrem: Dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis.
paras.en: Above, the Evangelist declared that the Word of God was from eternity. Now he makes known that He was made in time, saying: [[1:14|And the Word was made flesh|Et Verbum caro factum est]]. Again, he asserted that the adopted sons of God are not born of blood[[1:13||]]. Lest anyone should infer from this that much less was the natural Son of God born of seed or of blood, he therefore teaches that the Word was made flesh, being born of the seed of the Patriarchs and of the blood of the Virgin. Again, since he said that men become sons of God, he shows that this is neither impossible nor incredible, since the Son of God has become a son of man. Thus the Word, that is, the only-begotten Son of God, true God, subsisting eternally in Himself, was made flesh, that is, true man, by assuming human nature into His own personality, namely by giving it substance in Himself [substantificando: making it subsist, not in a person of its own, but in the Person of the Word], granting it to subsist in the same being in which the Word also subsists; so that the Word and the humanity assumed have one hypostasis [one individual subsisting reality, that is, here, the one Person], one and the same suppositality, or personal subsistence. For the Word Himself is the suppositum [the individual subject that exists and acts] which gives substance to the humanity united to Him. Here, then, the part is taken for the whole, namely flesh for man, as also in the Psalm: [[Ps 64:3|all flesh shall come to thee|Ad te omnis caro veniet]]; and in Isaias: [[Is 40:5|all flesh together shall see, that the mouth of the Lord hath spoken|Videbit omnis caro quod os Domini locutum est]]; and again: [[Luke 3:6|And all flesh shall see the salvation of God|Videbit omnis caro salutare Dei]] [Denis has 'of our God', as in Is 52:10; the margin gives Luke 3:6]. So too, further on, the Saviour says to the Father: [[John 17:2|thou hast given him power over all flesh|Dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis]].

paras.t: Denique Verbum factum est homo, assumendo simul in eodem instanti animam rationalem tunc primo creatam, et carnem humanam ex purissimis sanguinibus sanctissimæ atque dignissimæ Virginis sumptam, et a Spiritu Sancto formatam ac organizatam, rationalique anima informatam: sic quod in eodem instanti creata est anima Christi, et caro ejus formata ac anima copulata, et utrumque simul a Verbo assumptum. Nunquam tamen caro et anima, vel humanitas Christi, habuit propriam personalitatem aut subsistentiam; sed in momento suæ creationis ac partium suarum mutuæ unionis, assumpta est ipsa humanitas a Verbo, et supposita in ipso. Sic Virgo vere concepit Filium Dei, Deum ac hominem, præbendo materiam anima Christi informatam, ac Verbo immediate unitam. Hoc est novum et supernovum, omniumque novorum ac mirabilium novissimum ac mirabilissimum, de quo vaticinatus est Jeremias: Novum, inquiens, faciet Dominus super terram, Mulier circumdabit virum. Circumdedit enim in utero sacratissimo puerum Jesum, virum, non ætate et quantitate, sed sapientia et virtute.
paras.en: Further, the Word was made man by assuming at one and the same instant a rational soul, then first created, and human flesh taken from the most pure blood of the most holy and most worthy Virgin, formed and organized by the Holy Ghost, and informed by the rational soul [informatam: given its form, that is, made a living human body, by the soul as its form]: so that in the same instant the soul of Christ was created, and His flesh was formed and joined to the soul, and both together were assumed by the Word. Yet never did the flesh and the soul, or the humanity of Christ, have a personality or subsistence of its own; but in the moment of its creation and of the mutual union of its parts, the humanity itself was assumed by the Word, and made to subsist in Him as its suppositum. Thus the Virgin truly conceived the Son of God, God and man, by supplying the matter, informed by the soul of Christ and united immediately to the Word. This is the new thing, and more than new, the newest and most wonderful of all new and wonderful things, of which Jeremias prophesied, saying: [[Jer 31:22|the Lord hath created a new thing upon the earth: A WOMAN SHALL COMPASS A MAN|Novum, inquiens, faciet Dominus super terram, Mulier circumdabit virum]]. For she compassed in her most sacred womb the child Jesus, a man, not in age and size, but in wisdom and power.

paras.t: Incarnatus est ergo Filius Dei, ut nos efficiamur divinæ consortes naturæ, percipiendo meritis Christi copiosissimam gratiam in præsenti, æternamque beatitudinem in futuro. Inclinavit et humiliavit se ipsum, servilem formam accipiens, ut nos in cœlestibus exaltaret, et angelis pacificaret; similitudinem carnis peccati assumpsit, ut nos ab omni macula culpæ purgaret. In quibus apparet magnitudo divinæ dilectionis, atque dignatio summæ majestatis ad genus humanum. Quum enim amoris sit amantem et amatum unire, unum in alium transponere, eosque inseparabiliter colligare, constat quod Deus ineffabiliter nos amavit, quoniam nostram naturam sibi immediatissime copulavit, videlicet unione hypostatica, eamque in se quodammodo transformavit atque transposuit, et sibi indissolubiliter counivit: nam et in triduo mortis manserunt corpus et anima Verbo unita.
paras.en: The Son of God, then, became incarnate so that we might [[2 Pet 1:4|be made partakers of the divine nature|efficiamur divinæ consortes naturæ]], receiving through the merits of Christ most abundant grace in the present, and eternal beatitude in the future.
