He bowed Himself down and humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant[[Phil 2:7||]], to exalt us in the heavenly places and to make peace between us and the angels; He took [[Rom 8:3|the likeness of sinful flesh|similitudinem carnis peccati]], to cleanse us from every stain of guilt. In this appear the greatness of the divine love and the condescension of the supreme Majesty toward the human race. For since it belongs to love to unite the lover and the beloved, to carry over the one into the other, and to bind them inseparably together, it is plain that God has loved us beyond all words, since He joined our nature to Himself in the most immediate way, namely by the hypostatic union [the union of the two natures in the one Person, or hypostasis, of the Word], and in a manner transformed it and carried it over into Himself, and united it with Himself indissolubly: for even in the three days of death the body and the soul remained united to the Word.

paras.t: In Christo ergo sunt duæ naturæ, et una hypostasis seu persona; sunt quoque in eo duæ generationes, et una filiatio, puta divina. Generatio namque pertinet ad naturam, filiatio ad personam. Per hanc Verbi incarnationem, incomprehensibiliter prorsusque inenarrabiliter honorificata ac sublimata est, non solum humanitas Christi, sed totum insuper genus humanum. Quid enim tam gloriosum atque magnificum esse potest hominibus, ut hoc quod Deus noster factus est frater noster, quod Creator noster factus est noster Salvator, quod judex noster factus est noster advocatus? Nonne perfectio creaturæ est assimilari suo Creatori? Per Verbi autem incarnationem, assimilati sumus nostro Creatori similitudine speciei specialissimæ. Imo, si rite intelligo, per incarnationem hanc benedictam, facti sumus naturales fratres naturalis Filii Dei, utpote ejusdem naturæ cum Filio Patris æterni. Non tamen sumus naturales filii Patris Verbi, quia non sumus naturales fratres Verbi secundum naturam illam qua convenit ei esse naturalem Filium Dei, sed ratione naturæ assumptæ.
paras.en: In Christ, then, there are two natures and one hypostasis, or person; there are also in Him two generations and one sonship, namely the divine. For generation belongs to the nature, sonship to the person. By this incarnation of the Word not only the humanity of Christ but the whole human race besides has been honoured and exalted, incomprehensibly and altogether beyond telling. For what can be so glorious and magnificent for men as this: that our God has become our brother[[Matt 28:10||]][[Heb 2:11||]], that our Creator has become our Saviour, that our Judge has become our advocate[[1 John 2:1||]] [the margin's numeral is unclear; 1 John 2:1 speaks of Christ as our advocate]? Is not the perfection of a creature to be made like its Creator? But by the incarnation of the Word we have been made like our Creator by the likeness of the most special species [that is, by sharing with the Word made man the very same lowest species, human nature]. Indeed, if I understand rightly, by this blessed incarnation we have become natural brothers of the natural Son of God, as being of the same nature with the Son of the eternal Father. Yet we are not natural sons of the Father of the Word, because we are not natural brothers of the Word according to that nature by which it belongs to Him to be the natural Son of God, but by reason of the nature assumed.

paras.t: Amplius autem incarnatio ista sanctissima maxime auget spem nostram, caritatem quoque summe inflammat. Quomodo enim diffidere possumus de misericordia et benevolentia ejus qui propter nos in tantum exinanivit se ipsum, qui tanta dilectionis signa nobis ostendit, qui ita prævenit nos in benedictionibus suæ dulcedinis? Quid etiam ita caritatem accendere potest, sicut tantorum exhibitio beneficiorum, et quod tantum dilecti ac ante dilecti sumus a Deo nostro, quod tam propinque ac intime se nobis univit, quod una persona cum natura nostra effectus est, quod ultra omnem creaturam subcœlestem, cœlestem et supercœlestem, nostram exaltavit naturam?
paras.en: Moreover, this most holy incarnation greatly increases our hope, and sets our charity supremely aflame. For how can we distrust the mercy and goodwill of Him who for our sake so far emptied Himself[[Phil 2:7||]], who has shown us such great signs of love, who has so prevented us with the blessings of His sweetness[[Ps 20:4||]] [prevented: that is, gone before]? What, too, can so kindle charity as the showing of such great benefits, and the knowledge that we are so greatly loved, and loved beforehand, by our God; that He has united Himself to us so closely and intimately; that He has become one person with our nature; that He has exalted our nature beyond every creature beneath the heavens, in the heavens, and above the heavens?

paras.t: Magna, ni fallor, et inæstimabilis est virtus horum verborum: Verbum caro factum est. Quæ decet nos cum omni humilitate interiori et exteriori, seu corporis prostratione, inclinatione vel genuflexione proferre, ut humiliemus nos illi qui propter nos humiliavit se ipsum, quum esset Altissimus; cum summa quoque reverentia et gratitudine cordiali ac mentis fervore, ut honoremus ac diligamus eum gratissimo animo, qui prior eatenus honorificavit atque dilexit nos.
paras.en: Great, unless I am mistaken, and beyond all reckoning is the power of these words: [[1:14|the Word was made flesh|Verbum caro factum est]]. It befits us to utter them with all humility, interior and exterior, that is, with prostration of the body, a bow or a genuflexion, so that we may humble ourselves before Him who for our sake humbled Himself, though He was the Most High; and also with the deepest reverence, heartfelt gratitude and fervour of mind, so that with most grateful hearts we may honour and love Him who first so honoured and loved us[[1 John 4:10||]].

paras.t: Quæritur, cur potius Verbum quam Pater vel Spiritus Sanctus incarnatum est. Et respondendum, quod propter diversas causas. Primo: nam Verbo seu Filio appropriatur similitudo Patris cum Patre. Homo autem peccavit, Dei similitudinem inordinate appetendo: unde peccatum hominis fuit quodammodo specialiter contra Filium. Propter quod Pater zelans pro Filio, hominem condemnavit. Filius vero videns Patrem pro se zelatum, atque sui occasione honore sibi ab hominibus impendendo privatum, pro Patre quoque zelatus est. Unde ad recuperandum Patris honorem hominumque salutem, voluit incarnari. Secundo, quoniam homo habet specialem assimilationem cum Verbo. Nam Verbo appropriantur ea quæ pertinent ad intellectum; homo quoque recipit speciem a perfectione intellectuali, videlicet ab esse rationali. Tertio, quoniam incarnatio ordinatur ad beatificam visionem; visio autem hæc respicit intellectum a quo profluit, et verbum ab intellectu procedit: sicque propter convenientiam Verbi cum visione beatifica, congruebat ei incarnatio ista salvifica. Quarto, quoniam Verbum est media in Trinitate Persona: idcirco conveniebat ei incarnatio et ratio mediatoris, ut esset Deus et homo.
paras.en: It is asked why the Word, rather than the Father or the Holy Ghost, became incarnate. And the answer is: for several reasons. First, because to the Word, or Son, is appropriated [that is, attributed in a special way, though it is common to the three Persons] likeness to the Father. But man sinned by inordinately desiring the likeness of God[[Gen 3:5||]]: hence man's sin was in a manner especially against the Son. On this account the Father, zealous for the Son, condemned man. But the Son, seeing the Father zealous for Him, and, on His account, deprived of the honour that men should pay Him, was zealous for the Father in turn. Hence, to recover the Father's honour and the salvation of men, He willed to become incarnate. Second, because man has a special likeness to the Word. For to the Word are appropriated the things that belong to the intellect; and man too receives his species from an intellectual perfection, namely from his being rational. Third, because the incarnation is ordered to the beatific vision; and this vision regards the intellect from which it flows, and a word proceeds from the intellect: and so, because of the fittingness of the Word to the beatific vision, this saving incarnation was fitting to Him. Fourth, because the Word is the middle Person in the Trinity: therefore the incarnation, and the office of mediator, befitted Him, that He might be God and man.

paras.t: Postremo, protestante Simeone justo ac timorato, hoc Verbum incarnatum positum est in signum cui contradicetur. Propterea omnia loca sacræ Scripturæ plena sunt scandalis, secundum Hieronymum: non quod electi, qui sunt docibiles Dei, scandalizentur in verbis Scripturæ, sed reprobi volentes scrutari inscrutabilia Dei sacramque Scripturam proprio intellectu metiri. Unde ex hoc quod dictum est, Verbum caro factum est, homines perditissimi in intolerabiles inciderunt errores. Arius namque et Eunomius asserebant quod Verbum Dei sic factum est caro quod solam carnem assumpsit, non animam. Dicebant enim, quod Verbum esset pura creatura, carni Christi loco animæ copulata. Apollinaris hæreticus dixit, quod Verbum sic factum est caro, quod aliquid Verbi in carnem mutatum est, et quod in Christo non fuit anima rationalis, quoniam vicem animæ intellectivæ suppleverit Verbum, fuerit tamen in eo anima sensitiva: quo concesso, Christus potius esset Deus et bestia, quam Deus et homo.
paras.en: Lastly, as Simeon, the just and devout[[Luke 2:25||]], bore witness, this Word incarnate is set [[Luke 2:34|for a sign which shall be contradicted|in signum cui contradicetur]]. For this reason, according to Jerome, all the places of Sacred Scripture are full of stumbling-blocks: not that the elect, who are [[John 6:45|taught of God|docibiles Dei]], are scandalized at the words of Scripture, but the reprobate, who wish to search into the unsearchable things of God and to measure Sacred Scripture by their own understanding. Hence from this saying, [[1:14|the Word was made flesh|Verbum caro factum est]], the most abandoned men have fallen into intolerable errors. For Arius and Eunomius asserted that the Word of God was made flesh in such a way that He assumed flesh alone, not a soul. For they said that the Word was a mere creature, joined to the flesh of Christ in place of a soul. Apollinaris the heretic said that the Word was made flesh in such a way that something of the Word was changed into flesh, and that there was no rational soul in Christ, since the Word took the place of the intellective soul, though there was a sensitive soul in Him [the soul of sense and appetite, which men share with the animals]: which granted, Christ would be God and beast rather than God and man.

paras.t: Ebion autem, Cerinthus atque Photinus dixerunt, quod Verbum factum est caro per solam gratiæ unionem. Dixerunt enim, quod Christus esset purus homo, et non diceretur Deus nisi ob suæ sanctitatis et gratiæ excellentiam. Quorum errores quantum ad hoc secutus est inimicus Dei Nestorius, dicens quod Deitas non fuit in Christo nisi sicut in templo, affirmans quod ex Verbo et humana natura non constet una persona. Eutyches vero confinxit, quod Verbum sic factum est caro, quod ex natura divina et humana resultet in Christo una natura, sicut et una persona: quo dato, divina natura esset mutabilis, et Christus non esset Deus, nec homo, sed aliquid habens naturam mixtam ex divina atque humana natura. Sabellius dixit Patrem incarnatum. Manichæus asseruit Verbum carnem factum, non vere, sed tantum phantastice. Valentinus autem dixit, quod Verbum factum est caro, non assumendo corpus ex Virgine, sed secum illud portando de cœlo, ita quod corpus Christi fuerit de natura cœlestium corporum.
paras.en: Ebion, Cerinthus and Photinus said that the Word was made flesh by a union of grace alone. For they said that Christ was a mere man, and was called God only because of the excellence of His holiness and grace. Their errors on this point were followed by Nestorius, the enemy of God, who said that the Godhead was in Christ only as in a temple, and affirmed that the Word and the human nature do not make up one person. Eutyches, for his part, invented the notion that the Word was made flesh in such a way that from the divine and the human nature there results in Christ one nature, as also one person: which granted, the divine nature would be mutable, and Christ would be neither God nor man, but something having a nature mixed from the divine and the human nature. Sabellius said that the Father became incarnate. Manichæus asserted that the Word was made flesh not truly but only in appearance. And Valentinus said that the Word was made flesh, not by taking a body from the Virgin, but by bringing it with Him from heaven, so that the body of Christ was of the nature of the heavenly bodies.

paras.t: Universos errores istos stultissimos damnat Ecclesia, asserens Verbum veraciter assumpsisse totam naturam humanam, quatenus illa natura vinceret diabolum in Christo, quæ victa fuit ab eo in homine protoplasto. Denique hoc Christus assumpsit, quod sanandum redimendumque fuit. Quemadmodum ergo caro et anima rationalis infectæ erant peccato, ita utraque Verbo unitæ sunt, ita quod unio ista facta est in persona directe et immediate, tanquam in termino, non in natura hoc modo; nam utraque natura retinet suas proprietates naturales, et sine confusione, perturbatione ac commixtione unitæ sunt, una manente persona. Quum autem dicitur, Verbum caro factum, passum ac mortuum, non insinuatur aliqua mutatio facta in ipso Verbo secundum se, sed in natura assumpta, quæ tam propinque ac intime conjuncta est Verbo, ut quod est unius, prædicetur de alio, videlicet humana de Verbo, et divina de homine; sed quid propter quid dicatur, est attendendum.
paras.en: All these most foolish errors the Church condemns, asserting that the Word truly assumed the whole of human nature, so that the nature which had been overcome by the devil in the first-formed man might overcome him in Christ. Further, Christ assumed that which was to be healed and redeemed. As, then, the flesh and the rational soul had been infected by sin, so both were united to the Word; in such a way that this union was made in the person, directly and immediately, as in its term, and not in this manner in the nature [that is, not by making one nature of the two]; for each nature retains its own natural properties, and they are united without confusion, disturbance or mingling, the person remaining one. And when it is said that the Word was made flesh, suffered and died, no change is implied in the Word Himself as He is in Himself, but in the nature assumed, which is so closely and intimately joined to the Word that what belongs to the one is predicated of the other, namely human things of the Word, and divine things of the man [the 'communication of idioms']; but one must attend to what is said on account of what [that is, by reason of which nature each thing is said].

paras.t: Postremo opinor quod Spiritus Sanctus non sine præcipuis causis dixit per Evangelistam, Verbum caro factum est, potius quam, Verbum factum est homo: primo, ut magnitudo divinæ inclinationis seu exinanitionis ostenderetur; secundo, ut futurum Manichæorum errorem destrueret, incarnationisque veritatem apertissime demonstraret. Itaque Deus factus est homo, ut nos deificemur: illius ad ima descensio, nostra est ad summa promotio.
paras.en: Lastly, I think that the Holy Ghost had special reasons for saying through the Evangelist, [[1:14|the Word was made flesh|Verbum caro factum est]], rather than 'the Word was made man': first, that the greatness of the divine condescension, or self-emptying, might be shown; second, to destroy the future error of the Manichees, and to demonstrate most plainly the truth of the incarnation. And so God was made man, that we might be made godlike [deificemur, literally 'be deified': made partakers of the divine nature by grace]: His descent to the lowest is our promotion to the highest.

paras.t: Et habitavit in nobis, id est in natura nostra quam induit, quæ fuit velut templum ac tabernaculum Verbi assumentis atque Divinitatis intus latentis. Unde et dixit Judæis, Solvite templum hoc: quod dixit de templo corporis sui, prout Evangelista exposuit. In ceteris Sanctis habitat Verbum per fidem et gratiam; in Christo homine habitavit per hypostaticam unionem, et beatificam visionem, atque inseparabilem copulam. Vel sic, Habitavit in nobis, id est, inter nos commorari ac conversari dignatus est, prout dictum fuit per Baruch: Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est. Hinc quoque per Zachariam prædixit: Lauda et lætare, filia Sion, quia ecce ego venio, et habitabo in medio tui; et per Isaiam: Propter hoc sciet populus meus nomen meum in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquebar, ecce adsum.
paras.en: [[1:14|and dwelt among us|et habitavit in nobis]], that is, in our nature, which He put on, and which was as it were the temple and tabernacle of the Word who assumed it, and of the Godhead hidden within. Hence He said to the Jews: [[John 2:19|Destroy this temple|Solvite templum hoc]], which He said [[John 2:21|of the temple of his body|de templo corporis sui]], as the Evangelist explained. In the other Saints the Word dwells by faith and grace[[Eph 3:17||]]; in Christ the man He dwelt by the hypostatic union [that is, the union of the two natures in the one Person, or hypostasis, of the Word], by the beatific vision, and by an inseparable bond. Or thus: [[1:14|dwelt among us|habitavit in nobis]], that is, He deigned to abide and to converse among us, as was said through Baruch: [[Bar 3:38|Afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men.|Post hæc in terris visus est, et cum hominibus conversatus est]] Hence too He foretold through Zachary: [[Zach 2:10|Sing praise, and rejoice, O daughter of Sion: for behold I come, and I will dwell in the midst of thee|Lauda et lætare, filia Sion, quia ecce ego venio, et habitabo in medio tui]]; and through Isaias: [[Is 52:6|Therefore my people shall know my name in that day: for I myself that spoke, behold I am here|Propter hoc sciet populus meus nomen meum in die illa, quia ego ipse qui loquebar, ecce adsum]].

paras.t: Et vidimus gloriam ejus. Gloria in Scripturis diversis modis accipitur: interdum pro majestate, interdum pro clara cum laude notitia, interdum pro beatitudine seu lætitia, interdum pro quacumque excellentia seu opere magno. Apostoli ergo viderunt oculo corporali gloriam Verbi incarnati, id est magnificentiam miraculorum ipsius: et claritatem quam habuit in transfiguratione viderunt Petrus, Joannes et Jacobus; claritatem vero et excellentiam ejus post resurrectionem viderunt omnes Apostoli. Porro majestatem Divinitatis in carne latentis, et beatitudinem animæ Christi Deo semper fruentis, viderunt Apostoli oculo intellectuali seu visu interiori per fidem, præsertim post resurrectionem et Spiritus Sancti missionem. Excellentiam quoque ejus in prædicando et operando viderunt, quomodo erat docens sicut potestatem habens, et novam ac propriam legem tradens; dæmones imperiali verbo ejiciens, atque ad nutum propria virtute miracula faciens; cordium arcana aperiens, cuncta futura prænoscens; post resurrectionem clausis januis intrans, Spiritum Sanctum insufflans, in conspectu discipulorum ascendens.
paras.en: [[1:14|and we saw his glory|et vidimus gloriam ejus]]. Glory is taken in Scripture in several ways: sometimes for majesty, sometimes for a renown that is bright and joined with praise, sometimes for beatitude or joy, sometimes for any excellence or great work. The Apostles, then, saw with the bodily eye the glory of the incarnate Word, that is, the magnificence of His miracles; and the brightness that He had in the transfiguration was seen by Peter, John and James[[Matt 17:1||]]; while His brightness and excellence after the resurrection were seen by all the Apostles[[Acts 1:3||]]. Further, the majesty of the Godhead hidden in the flesh, and the beatitude of Christ's soul, which ever enjoys God, the Apostles saw with the eye of the intellect, or inward sight, through faith, above all after the resurrection and the sending of the Holy Ghost. They saw His excellence too in preaching and in working: how He was [[Matt 7:29|teaching them as one having power|docens sicut potestatem habens]], and handing down a new law, His own; casting out demons with a word of command[[Mark 1:27||]], and working miracles at His nod by His own power; laying open the secrets of hearts, foreknowing all things to come; after the resurrection entering when the doors were shut[[John 20:19||]], breathing forth the Holy Ghost[[John 20:22||]], ascending in the sight of His disciples[[Acts 1:9||]].

paras.t: Et quoniam omnia ista fuerunt supra hominem, et ultra omnem potestatem creatam, solique Deo possibilia, ideo subditur: gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre, id est, talem ejus gloriam vidimus, qualem decet videri et esse in unico naturalique Filio Patris æterni. Et ita, quod ait, Quasi, non denotat similitudinem, sed veritatem. Unde Evangelista omnem excellentiam Christi breviter innuens, dicit, Vidimus gloriam ejus quasi Unigeniti a Patre: ac si de aliquo rege cum maximo apparatu intrante, diceremus, Ipse intravit quasi rex, id est tam clare atque potenter, ut spectat ad regem.
paras.en: And since all these things were above man, and beyond every created power, and possible to God alone, there is added: [[1:14|the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father|gloriam quasi Unigeniti a Patre]], that is, we saw His glory such as it befits to be seen and to be in the only and natural Son of the eternal Father. And so the words "as it were" do not denote likeness but truth. Hence the Evangelist, briefly hinting at the whole excellence of Christ, says: [[1:14|we saw his glory, the glory as it were of the only begotten of the Father|Vidimus gloriam ejus quasi Unigeniti a Patre]]; as if, of some king making his entry with the greatest pomp, we were to say: "He came in as a king", that is, with such splendour and might as belongs to a king.

paras.t: Propter hanc visionem Christus dixit Apostolis: Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis. Hinc per Isaiam fuerat prophetatum: Simul laudabunt, quia oculo ad oculum videbunt. Et iterum dixit Isaias: Erunt oculi tui videntes præceptorem tuum; et aures tuæ audient vocem post tergum monentis. Et Psalmista: Viderunt ingressus tuos, Deus, ingressus Dei mei, regis mei, qui est in sancto.
paras.en: Because of this vision Christ said to the Apostles: [[Luke 10:23|Blessed are the eyes that see the things which you see|Beati oculi qui vident quæ vos videtis]]. Hence it had been prophesied through Isaias: [[Is 52:8|they shall praise together: for they shall see eye to eye|Simul laudabunt, quia oculo ad oculum videbunt]]. And again Isaias said: [[Is 30:20|thy eyes shall see thy teacher|Erunt oculi tui videntes præceptorem tuum]]; [[Is 30:21|And thy ears shall hear the word of one admonishing thee behind thy back|et aures tuæ audient vocem post tergum monentis]]. And the Psalmist: [[Ps 67:25|They have seen thy goings, O God, the goings of my God: of my king who is in his sanctuary.|Viderunt ingressus tuos, Deus, ingressus Dei mei, regis mei, qui est in sancto]]

paras.t: Postremo omnia, etiam humana et infima, quæ in Christo fuerunt, gloria et honore ornantur, imo supernaturalibus magnificentiis decorantur, divinisque plena fuerunt præconiis. Nam conceptus et natus est ex muliere; sed mulier ista ante partum, in partu, et post partum virgo permansit, omnique macula caruit, tota pulchra ineffabiliterque sanctissima: et hoc utique gloriosissimum fuit. Denique hanc conceptionem ac nativitatem prædixerunt Prophetæ ac Patriarchæ, quam nuntiaverunt et Angeli. Turpissima quoque et acerbissima morte occisus est: sed tempore passionis sola voce omnes adversarios suos dejecit in terram; et quum in cruce penderet, supernaturaliter obscuratus est sol, mota est terra; et cum resurgente multi Sancti dudum mortui surrexerunt.
paras.en: Lastly, all the things that were in Christ, even the human and the lowliest, are adorned with glory and honour[[Ps 8:6||]], nay, are decked with supernatural splendours, and were full of divine praises. For He was conceived and born of a woman[[Gal 4:4||]]; but that woman remained a virgin before the birth, in the birth and after the birth, and was free from every stain, [[Cant 4:7|all fair|tota pulchra]] and holy beyond all telling; and this indeed was most glorious. Again, this conception and birth the Prophets and Patriarchs foretold, and the Angels too announced it[[Luke 2:9||]] [the margin is read as Luc. i, 9–14, probably Luke ii, 9–14, the angels' announcement of the Nativity]. He was also put to a most shameful and most bitter death; but in the time of His passion He cast all His adversaries to the ground by His voice alone[[John 18:6||]]; and while He hung on the cross the sun was supernaturally darkened[[Matt 27:45||]], the earth quaked[[Matt 27:51||]]; and with Him as He rose many Saints long dead rose again[[Matt 27:52||]].

paras.t: Vidimus etiam eum, plenum gratiæ. De plenitudine gratiæ Christi multa possem inducere; sed breviter perstringendo, sciendum quod secundum doctores, fuit et est in Christo triplex gratia, utpote gratia unionis, gratia habitualis, et gratia capitis. Alii dividunt sic, quod in Christo fuit gratia unionis, gratia singularis personæ, et gratia capitis. Sed redit in idem, quoniam gratia singularis personæ fuit habitualis, sicut et gratia capitis: ideo illi per gratiam habitualem intelligunt gratiam illius personæ singularis, hominis Christi. Gratia autem unionis in Christo, non est quid creatum, sed ipsemet Deus gratiose, gratis et pie uniens naturam humanam divinæ, vel esse personale Verbi humanitati unitum. De hac gratia intelligendum est verbum Augustini, dicentis, quod sola gratia factum est ut homo sit Deus, et quod humana natura unita est Verbo. Quum enim unio Verbi ac hominis sit summa et propinquissima, scilicet personalis, certum est quod non sit facta per aliquam gratiam creatam ac habitualem intermediam.
paras.en: We saw Him also [[1:14|full of grace|plenum gratiæ]]. On the fullness of Christ's grace I could bring in much; but to touch on it briefly, it must be known that, according to the doctors, there was and is in Christ a threefold grace: the grace of union, habitual grace, and the grace of headship [that is, the grace He has as Head of the Church, flowing from Him into its members]. Others divide it thus: that in Christ there was the grace of union, the grace of the individual person, and the grace of headship. But it comes to the same, since the grace of the individual person was habitual grace, as was the grace of headship; so these understand by habitual grace the grace of that individual person, the man Christ. The grace of union in Christ is not something created, but God Himself graciously, freely and lovingly uniting the human nature to the divine; or it is the personal being of the Word united to the humanity. Of this grace is to be understood the saying of Augustine, that it was by grace alone that man is God, and that the human nature was united to the Word. For since the union of the Word and the man is the highest and closest, namely personal, it is certain that it was not brought about through any created and habitual grace in between.

paras.t: Gratia vero habitualis in Christo, est donum supernaturale, personalem consequens unionem, operationes Christi perficiens. Quæ gratia tanta fuit in Christo, quod major gratia communicari non potest creaturæ. Tota nempe capacitas intellectualis creaturæ vel rationalis, quantum ad gratiæ receptionem, fuit in anima Christi repleta. Eratque gratia ista summe perfecta atque plenissima, ratione immediatæ ac hypostaticæ unionis hominis Christi cum Verbo. Quanto enim intellectualis creatura fonti gratiarum Deo sublimi vicinius copulatur, tanto gratia ampliori perfunditur. Quemadmodum ergo humanitas Christi incomparabiliter præ ceteris omnibus vicinius unita est Verbo, sic gratia ejus omnium electorum gratiam incomparabiliter pene, non tamen simpliciter infinite, excedit.
paras.en: Habitual grace in Christ, on the other hand, is a supernatural gift, following upon the personal union and perfecting the operations of Christ. This grace was so great in Christ that no greater grace can be communicated to a creature. For the whole capacity of the intellectual or rational creature, as regards the receiving of grace, was filled in the soul of Christ. And this grace was supremely perfect and most full, by reason of the immediate and hypostatic union of the man Christ with the Word. For the more closely an intellectual creature is joined to God, the sublime fount of graces, the more abundantly is it flooded with grace. As, then, the humanity of Christ is united to the Word more closely than all others, beyond compare, so His grace exceeds the grace of all the elect almost beyond compare, yet not absolutely infinitely.

paras.t: Insuper, quoniam Christus est salvator, mediator et caput totius Ecclesiæ militantis ac triumphantis, ideo habet omnibus de sua plenitudine communicare, spiritualem sensum atque vivificum motum influere, sicut et caput influit membris sensum ac motum. Idcirco ponitur in Christo gratia capitis, hoc est exuberans habitus gratiæ, ex cujus redundantia alii gratiam sortiuntur. Gratia tamen immediate a Deo creatur; sed gratia Christi asseritur causa gratiæ aliorum per modum causæ instrumentalis, exemplaris, seu meritoriæ. Unumquodque autem operatur per id per quod est in actu. Quoniam ergo Christus per gratiam habitualem seu personalem, est in actu gratiæ perfectissimo, ideo per eamdem gratiam influit aliis. Unde gratia habitualis et gratia capitis non distinguuntur in Christo realiter, sed gratia capitis superaddit gratiæ habituali rationem superabundantis. — Patet ergo, quod gratia unionis in Christo sit simpliciter infinita, quum sit ipsemet Deus, qui est gratia effective gratificans, sicut appellatur natura naturans. Alia gratia, quum sit quid creatum, non est simpliciter infinita in Christo.
paras.en: Moreover, since Christ is the saviour, the mediator[[1 Tim 2:5||]] and the head of the whole Church, militant and triumphant[[Eph 1:22||]], He has therefore to communicate to all from His fullness[[Eph 1:23||]], and to pour into them spiritual sense and life-giving movement, as the head too pours sense and movement into the members. Therefore there is placed in Christ the grace of headship, that is, an overflowing habit of grace, from whose overflow others receive grace. Grace, it is true, is created immediately by God; but the grace of Christ is said to be the cause of the grace of others by way of an instrumental, exemplary or meritorious cause. Now each thing acts through that by which it is in act. Since, then, Christ through habitual or personal grace is in the most perfect act of grace, He therefore pours into others through that same grace. Hence habitual grace and the grace of headship are not really distinct in Christ, but the grace of headship adds to habitual grace the character of superabundance. — It is clear, then, that the grace of union in Christ is absolutely infinite, since it is God Himself, who is grace effectively making gracious, as He is called nature naturing [*natura naturans*: a scholastic name for God as the source that produces all natures]. The other grace, since it is something created, is not absolutely infinite in Christ.

paras.t: Quæritur, quid magnum est Christo, quod dicitur plenus gratia, quum de Joanne Baptista prædixerit angelus: Spiritu Sancto replebitur ex utero matris. Stephanus quoque plenus gratia et fortitudine fuisse describitur; et de Apostolis legitur, quod repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto. Dicendum, quod gratia dicitur plena dupliciter: Primo, ex parte gratiæ, quum tanta est intensive ac virtualiter, quod major esse non valet: sicque plenitudo gratiæ est propria Christo. Secundo, ex parte subjecti, ut quum quis habeat gratiam tantam, quod operationes ad quas divinitus ordinatur, facile exsequi potest: et ita Sancti dicuntur fuisse gratia pleni, secundum exigentiam sui status ac propriæ conditionis. Tanto enim gratia dicitur plenior, quanto redundare potest in plures. Plenum autem opponitur vacuo. Unde quemadmodum aliqua nuncupantur diversimode vacua, sic multipliciter plena dicuntur.
paras.en: It is asked what great thing it is for Christ that He is said to be full of grace, since the angel foretold of John the Baptist: [[Luke 1:15|he shall be filled with the Holy Ghost, even from his mother's womb|Spiritu Sancto replebitur ex utero matris]]. Stephen too is described as having been [[Acts 6:8|full of grace and fortitude|plenus gratia et fortitudine]]; and of the Apostles we read that [[Acts 2:4|they were all filled with the Holy Ghost|repleti sunt omnes Spiritu Sancto]]. The answer is that grace is called full in two ways. First, on the side of the grace, when it is so great in intensity and power that it cannot be greater; and thus fullness of grace is proper to Christ. Secondly, on the side of the subject, as when someone has grace so great that he can readily carry out the works to which he is ordained by God; and thus the Saints are said to have been full of grace, according to the requirements of their state and of their own condition. For grace is called the fuller, the more people it can overflow into. Now the full is opposed to the empty. Hence, just as things are called empty in different ways, so they are called full in many ways.

paras.t: Præterea fuerunt in Christo gratiæ gratis datæ, quæ ordinantur ad fidei manifestationem et aliorum utilitatem, videlicet gratia prophetiæ et miraculorum, donum linguarum, etc. Dona vero Spiritus Sancti fuerunt in eo excellentissimo modo; virtutes quoque morales et intellectuales, eo modo quo, secundum Plotinum magnum Platonicum, virtutes heroicæ insunt hominibus purgati defæcatique animi. Quædam tamen virtutes imperfectionem includunt circa objectum, ut fides et spes; vel circa subjectum, ut pœnitentia. Fides namque includit defectum et obscuritatem notitiæ, spes vero absentiam et exspectationem boni optati. Hæ ergo virtutes non fuerunt in Christo, cujus anima a suæ creationis principio vidit Deum per speciem, plenamque sortita est felicitatem.
paras.en: There were besides in Christ the graces freely given [*gratiæ gratis datæ*: gifts given for the good of others rather than for the sanctification of the one who has them], which are ordained to the manifestation of the faith and the benefit of others[[1 Cor 12:7||]], namely the grace of prophecy and of miracles, the gift of tongues[[1 Cor 12:10||]], etc. The gifts of the Holy Ghost were in Him in the most excellent manner; and the moral and intellectual virtues too, in the way in which, according to Plotinus, the great Platonist, the heroic virtues are present in men of purified and cleansed soul. Some virtues, however, include an imperfection: as to their object, as faith and hope; or as to their subject, as penance. For faith includes a lack and obscurity of knowledge, and hope the absence and the awaiting of the good desired. These virtues, therefore, were not in Christ, whose soul from the first moment of its creation saw God by sight [*per speciem*, that is, face to face, not through faith], and obtained full happiness.

paras.t: Et veritatis. Verbum incarnatum plenum fuit veritate, id est Divinitate, secundum Augustinum et Bedam, quia in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter, secundum Apostolum. Veritas quoque increata appropriatur Filio ab intellectu Patris profluenti. Fuit etiam plenum veritate, id est omni cognitione et sapientia, quia in ipso sunt omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi. Fuit etiam et est in Christo sapientia increata, quæ realiter idem est quod Verbum ac divina essentia; item, sapientia Beatorum seu patriæ, quoniam anima ejus vidit semper Deum per speciem, cognovitque omnia in Verbo, quæ Deus cognoscit notitia visionis, videlicet universa præterita, præsentia, et futura.
paras.en: [[1:14|and truth|et veritatis]]. The incarnate Word was full of truth, that is, of the Godhead, according to Augustine and Bede, because, as the Apostle says, [[Col 2:9|in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead corporeally|in ipso habitat omnis plenitudo Divinitatis corporaliter]]. Uncreated truth, too, is appropriated to the Son [that is, attributed to Him in particular, though common to the three Persons], who proceeds from the intellect of the Father. He was also full of truth, that is, of all knowledge and wisdom, because in Him are [[Col 2:3|all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge|omnes thesauri sapientiæ et scientiæ absconditi]] hidden. There was and is in Christ, moreover, uncreated wisdom, which is really the same as the Word and the divine essence; and also the wisdom of the Blessed, or of the homeland [Latin *patriæ*; the OCR reads *patris*: the knowledge of those who already see God in heaven], since His soul always saw God by sight, and knew in the Word all the things that God knows by the knowledge of vision [that is, His knowledge of all that actually is, was or will be], namely all things past, present and to come.

paras.t: Est quoque in Christo scientia indita seu infusa, qua per species sibi concreatas agnoscit res in propriis naturis, ordinibus atque generibus: quemadmodum angeli, secundum Augustinum, cognoscunt res cognitione vespertina, et Adam cognovit creata in paradiso ante ruinam. Præter istas scientias ponunt quidam in Christo scientiam acquisitam, ita quod intellectus possibilis animæ Christi abstraxit ab intellectu suo agente species rerum sensatarum. Nulla enim naturalis perfectio defuit Christo: unde ad ejus perfectionem pertinuit, quod easdem res diversis modis atque scientiis novit. De hac scientia dicunt loqui Apostolum ad Hebræos: Didicit ex his quæ passus est obedientiam. Insuper Christus plenus fuit veritate vitæ, veritate doctrinæ, et veritate justitiæ.
paras.en: There is also in Christ an implanted or infused knowledge, by which, through species created together with His soul, He knows things in their own natures, orders and kinds; as the angels, according to Augustine, know things by evening knowledge [that is, knowledge of things in themselves, as against "morning" knowledge of them in the Word], and as Adam knew created things in paradise before the fall[[Gen 2:19||]]. Besides these kinds of knowledge some place in Christ an acquired knowledge, in that the possible intellect of Christ's soul abstracted, by its agent intellect, the species of things perceived by the senses [in scholastic teaching the agent intellect draws the intelligible likeness out of what the senses present, and the possible intellect receives it]. For no natural perfection was lacking to Christ; hence it belonged to His perfection that He knew the same things in different ways and by different kinds of knowledge. Of this knowledge, they say, the Apostle speaks to the Hebrews: [[Heb 5:8|he learned obedience by the things which he suffered|Didicit ex his quæ passus est obedientiam]]. Furthermore, Christ was full of the truth of life, the truth of doctrine, and the truth of justice.

paras.t: Huic autem verbo Joannis, consonat illud Lucæ: Puer Jesus crescebat plenus sapientia, et gratia Dei erat in eo. Imo tam plenus fuit gratia a principio suæ conceptionis in Virgine, quod nunquam profecit in gratia habituali, sicut nec in sapientia, nisi ponamus in eo sapientiam acquisitam. Unde quod Lucas dicit, profecisse gratia et sapientia apud Deum et homines, intelligendum est quantum ad manifestationem, sicut post resurrectionem dicitur ei data omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra; vel quantum ad usum. — Postremo dicitur Christus plenus veritate, quoniam implevit et verificavit ea quæ scripta erant de ipso.
paras.en: With this word of John agrees that of Luke: [[Luke 2:40|the child grew and waxed strong, full of wisdom: and the grace of God was in him|Puer Jesus crescebat plenus sapientia, et gratia Dei erat in eo]]. Nay, He was so full of grace from the first moment of His conception in the Virgin that He never advanced in habitual grace, as neither in wisdom, unless we place in Him acquired wisdom. Hence what Luke says, that He advanced in grace and wisdom with God and men[[Luke 2:52||]], is to be understood as regards its showing forth, just as after the resurrection it is said: [[Matt 28:18|All power is given to me in heaven and in earth|data omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra]]; or as regards its use. — Lastly, Christ is called full of truth because He fulfilled and made true the things that were written of Him.

paras.t: Deinceps Evangelista confirmat quæ dixit de excellentia Verbi incarnati, testimonio Præcursoris. Joannes Baptista testimonium perhibet de ipso: quemadmodum dictum atque expositum est, Hic venit in testimonium, ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine. Et clamat magno affectu, sublimique voce, tanquam certus de veritate, nec metuens prædicare eminentiam Filii Dei. Dicit autem Evangelista de Præcursore principaliter, Perhibet, et, Clamat: nam quamvis verba ore Joannis Baptistæ prolata diu transierint, tamen verba ejus incessabiliter repetuntur, et ipse in Evangelio indesinenter testimonium perhibet Christo et clamat. Quid ergo de Christo testetur, subjungitur.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist confirms what he has said of the excellence of the incarnate Word by the testimony of the Forerunner. [[1:15|John beareth witness of him|Joannes testimonium perhibet de ipso]], as was said and explained above: [[1:7|This man came for a witness, to give testimony of the light|Hic venit in testimonium, ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine]]. [[1:15|And crieth out|Et clamat]], with great affection and a loud voice, as one certain of the truth and not afraid to proclaim the pre-eminence of the Son of God. Now the Evangelist says of the Forerunner, in the present tense [the scan reads *principaliter*, “chiefly”, probably for *præsentialiter*, “in the present”, which the reason that follows requires], [[1:15|beareth witness|Perhibet]] and [[1:15|crieth out|Clamat]]: for although the words spoken by the mouth of John the Baptist passed away long ago, yet his words are repeated without ceasing, and in the Gospel he unceasingly bears witness to Christ and cries out. What, then, he testifies of Christ is added next.

paras.t: Hic Unigenitus Patris plenus gratia et veritate, erat ab æterno, quia in principio erat Verbum, et etiam nunc est, semperque erit ille, quem dixi esse regem Messiam, Salvatorem mundi; vel, Quem dixi, id est, futurum prænuntiavi, et de quo testificatus sum verba sequentia: Qui post me, id est post meam prædicationem ac baptizationem, venturus est in publicum, manifeste docendo, miracula faciendo, atque per suos discipulos baptizando. Non utique loquitur Joannes de adventu Christi in mundum, quoniam incarnatio et nativitas Christi humana jam diu fuerunt præteritæ; sed Christus, qui usque ad tricesimum suæ ætatis annum latuit, post prædicationem Joannis venit in publicum. Ante me factus est, id est mihi præpositus et prælatus seu dignior factus, etiam secundum naturam assumptam, cujus dignitas et gratia omnium creaturarum simul sumptarum dignitatem gratiamque excellit, per hypostaticam ejus unionem cum Verbo. Unde ratio prælationis subjungitur: quia prior me erat, secundum divinitatem, in qua coæternus est Patri. Quoniam ergo persona Verbi æterna est, idcirco ipsa secundum naturam assumptam omni creaturæ præficitur. Nec obstat illud Psalmistæ, quod Apostolus ad Hebræos allegat de Christo: Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis. Quamvis enim Christus, quantum ad corporis passibilitatem et assumptæ humanitatis naturalem seu specificam dignitatem, minor angelis fuit, absolute tamen loquendo major exstitit illis, secundum suam humanitatem, imo secundum corpus et animam, ut Verbo unita omniumque gratiarum charismatibus adimpleta.
paras.en: [[1:15|This|Hic]], the Only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth, [[1:15|was|erat]] from eternity, since [[1:1|In the beginning was the Word|in principio erat Verbum]]; and He is also now, and ever will be, [[1:15|he of whom I spoke|quem dixi]], that is, whom I declared to be the King Messias, the Saviour of the world; or, [[1:15|of whom I spoke|Quem dixi]], that is, whom I foretold as one to come, and to whom I bore witness in the words that follow: [[1:15|He that shall come after me|Qui post me]], that is, after my preaching and baptizing, [[1:15|shall come|venturus est]] into public view, teaching openly, working miracles, and baptizing through His disciples. John is certainly not speaking of Christ’s coming into the world, since the incarnation and human birth of Christ were long past; but Christ, who lay hidden until the thirtieth year of His age, came into public view after John’s preaching. [[1:15|Is preferred before me|Ante me factus est]] [literally “was made before me”], that is, He is set over me and placed above me, or made worthier than I, even according to the nature He assumed, whose dignity and grace surpass the dignity and grace of all creatures taken together, through its hypostatic union with the Word [that is, the union of the human nature with the Word in the one Person, or hypostasis, of the Son]. Hence the reason for this precedence is added: [[1:15|because he was before me|quia prior me erat]], according to the divinity, in which He is coeternal with the Father. Since, then, the Person of the Word is eternal, therefore according to the nature assumed it is set over every creature. Nor is this contradicted by the words of the Psalmist, which the Apostle applies to Christ in Hebrews[[Heb 2:7||]]: [[Ps 8:6|Thou hast made him a little less than the angels|Minuisti eum paulo minus ab angelis]]. For although Christ, as regards the passibility of His body [that is, its capacity to suffer] and the natural or specific dignity of the humanity He assumed, was less than the angels, yet, absolutely speaking, He was greater than they even according to His humanity, indeed according to body and soul, as united to the Word and filled with the gifts of all graces.

paras.t: Ex hoc verbo vitali quo ait Joannes de Christo, Ante me factus est, sumpsit Arius occasionem letalis erroris, asserens Verbum secundum naturam Verbi factum, quum certum sit quod Joannes præcessit ipsum Verbum secundum quod incarnatum: unde Verbum non potest dici factum ante Joannem, nisi secundum propriam naturam. Sed argumentum istud facillime solvitur, quia laborat in æquivocis: non enim jam sumitur factum esse, pro productione rei quantum ad esse de non esse, sed sicut expositum est. Juxta quem sensum Manasses primogenitus filius Joseph patriarchæ, dicere potuit de fratre suo Ephraim, Qui post me venit seu natus est, ante me factus est, quia sublimius benedictus, atque præpositus mihi a patriarcha Jacob: ut patet in Genesi. Juxta hunc modum Baruch ait: Facti sumus subtus, et non supra. Potest nihilo minus exponi de Christo secundum assumptam humanitatem, et factione proprie dicta. Eritque sensus: Ante me, id est ante generationem seu nativitatem meam ex utero, factus est, id est quantum ad corporis sui perfectam organizationem quoad lineamentorum distinctionem, quamvis non quoad debitam quantitatem; et item, Ante me factus est, quoad animæ suæ perfectionem in omni sapientia, dono, virtute et gratia Spiritus Sancti. Christus enim in primo suæ conceptionis instanti habuit corpus et animam prædictis modis perfecta, et tunc Joannes nondum factus fuit his modis.
paras.en: From this life-giving word, in which John says of Christ, [[1:15|is preferred before me|Ante me factus est]], Arius took occasion for his deadly error, asserting that the Word was made according to the nature of the Word: for it is certain that John came before the Word as incarnate, so that the Word cannot be said to have been made before John except according to His own nature. But this argument is very easily answered, for it labours under an equivocation [that is, it takes one word in two different senses]: “to be made” is not taken here for the production of a thing into being from non-being, but as has been explained. In this sense Manasses, the first-born son of the patriarch Joseph, could have said of his brother Ephraim: He that came, or was born, after me was made before me, because he was more highly blessed and set over me by the patriarch Jacob, as is plain in Genesis[[Gen 48:13||]]. In this way Baruch says: [[Bar 2:5|we are brought under, and are not uppermost|Facti sumus subtus, et non supra]] [literally “we were made beneath, and not above”, with the same verb as *factus est* here]. It can nevertheless be explained of Christ according to the humanity He assumed, and of making in the proper sense. The sense will then be: [[1:15|before me|Ante me]], that is, before my generation or birth from the womb, He was made, that is, as to the perfect organization of His body in the distinction of its features, though not as to its due size; and again, [[1:15|is preferred before me|Ante me factus est]], that is, He was made before me as to the perfection of His soul in all wisdom, gift, virtue and grace of the Holy Ghost. For in the first instant of His conception Christ had body and soul perfect in the ways just described, and at that time John was not yet made in these ways.

paras.t: Porro quæ sequuntur, Et de plenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus, dicit Origenes esse verba Joannis Baptistæ. Et hoc videtur: primo, ex ordine vel serie textus; secundo, ex parte conjunctionis copulativæ et, connectentis sequentia præcedentibus; tertio, quia post verba sequentia immediate subjungitur: Et hoc est testimonium Joannis, quando miserunt Judæi ab Jerosolymis sacerdotes ad eum. Secundum Hieronymum vero, Augustinum et Bedam, sunt verba Joannis evangelistæ redeuntis, et exsequentis post introductionem testimonii Joannis Baptistæ, quod supra dixit: Et Verbum caro factum est, et vidimus gloriam ejus. Itaque, secundum istos, Evangelista prosequitur quid de Christi humanitate sentit, et quomodo Apostoli viderunt gloriam ejus, quum dicitur:
paras.en: Now the words that follow, [[1:16|And of his fulness we all have received|Et de plenitudine ejus nos omnes accepimus]], Origen says are the words of John the Baptist. And so it seems: first, from the order or sequence of the text; secondly, from the copulative conjunction *and*, which joins what follows to what goes before; thirdly, because immediately after the words that follow it is added: [[1:19|And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent from Jerusalem priests|Et hoc est testimonium Joannis, quando miserunt Judæi ab Jerosolymis sacerdotes]] to him. But according to Jerome, Augustine and Bede, they are the words of John the Evangelist, returning, after bringing in the testimony of John the Baptist, to carry on what he said above: [[1:14|And the Word was made flesh|Et Verbum caro factum est]], [[1:14|and we saw his glory|et vidimus gloriam ejus]]. So, according to them, the Evangelist goes on to say what he holds of Christ’s humanity, and how the Apostles saw His glory, when it is said:

paras.t: Et de plenitudine ejus, id est de plena et superabundanti gratia Christi, nos omnes accepimus aliquam portionem, seu gratiam particularem: quemadmodum ait Apostolus, Divisiones gratiarum sunt, idem autem Spiritus; itemque, Alii datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ, alii gratia sanitatum, etc.; et iterum, Unicuique (inquit) nostrum data est gratia, secundum mensuram donationis Christi. Accepimus ergo de plenitudine ejus gratiam subsequentem et bene agendo adeptam ac meritam, pro gratia primo infusa pure gratis collata. Nemo enim primam gratiam gratificantem valet mereri, quum sine gratia nihil sit meritorium, et tanta est dignitas gratiæ, quod ex puris naturalibus mereri non potest; sed ea gratis accepta, potest homo per eam adipisci gratiam ampliorem, imo de condigno mereri gratiæ incrementum. Quoniam ergo gratia sequens, seu major vel aucta, datur pro actu meritorio procedente a gratia prima, ob id dicimur accipere gratiam pro gratia.
paras.en: [[1:16|And of his fulness|Et de plenitudine ejus]], that is, of the full and superabounding grace of Christ, [[1:16|we all have received|nos omnes accepimus]] some portion, or a particular grace; as the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 12:4|there are diversities of graces, but the same Spirit|Divisiones gratiarum sunt, idem autem Spiritus]] [the margin gives 1 Cor. xii, 5; the words are those of verse 4]; and again: [[1 Cor 12:8|To one indeed, by the Spirit, is given the word of wisdom: and to another, the word of knowledge|Alii datur sermo sapientiæ, alii sermo scientiæ]], [[1 Cor 12:9|to another, the grace of healing|alii gratia sanitatum]], etc.; and once more: [[Eph 4:7|to every one of us is given grace, according to the measure of the giving of Christ|Unicuique (inquit) nostrum data est gratia, secundum mensuram donationis Christi]]. We have received of His fulness, then, the grace that follows, obtained and merited by acting well, for the grace first infused, conferred purely gratis. For no one can merit the first grace that makes pleasing [*gratia gratificans*, that is, sanctifying grace], since without grace nothing is meritorious, and so great is the dignity of grace that it cannot be merited from purely natural powers; but once it has been freely received, a man can through it obtain a fuller grace, and indeed merit an increase of grace *de condigno* [that is, by merit in the strict sense, which deserves its reward in justice, as opposed to merit *de congruo*, of fittingness]. Since, then, the grace that follows, that is, greater or increased grace, is given for a meritorious act proceeding from the first grace, we are therefore said to receive [[1:16|grace for grace|gratiam pro gratia]].

paras.t: Vel, Accepimus de plenitudine ejus, id est de sapientia, pietate et gratia Christi, gratiam novi Testamenti, id est evangelicam legem et gratiam, pro gratia veteris Testamenti, id est loco Mosaicæ legis. Utraque autem lex gratia appellatur, quoniam gratis et misericorditer data. Vel sic: Accepimus gratiam membrorum, videlicet gratiam nobis concessam, pro gratia capitis, id est merito et efficacia gratiæ Christi, qui quolibet vitæ suæ actu quem habuit ut viator, ex gratia profluente meruit nobis gratiam in præsenti, et gloriam in futuro. Sibi ipsi enim non meruit gratiam gratum facientem, nec beatificam visionem, sed membris suis, quæ participant gratiam capitis per fidem et sacramenta Ecclesiæ. Secundum Magistrum vero Sententiarum, quoniam nostra merita et præmia sunt Dei dona, eo quod ex gratia sola liberalitate Dei infusa dependeant, ideo potest sic accipi: Accepimus gratiam, id est meritum vel præmium, pro gratia, quæ est causa meriti vel mercedis. Quum ergo Deus remunerat nostra merita, remunerat sua dona, donatque gratiam super gratiam, juxta illud: Habenti dabitur, et abundabit. Augustinus quoque et Beda exponunt sic: Accepimus jam in spe, gratiam pro gratia, id est vitam æternam pro fide.
paras.en: Or: we [[1:16|have received|Accepimus]] [[1:16|of his fulness|de plenitudine ejus]], that is, of the wisdom, loving-kindness and grace of Christ, the grace of the New Testament, that is, the law and grace of the Gospel, [[1:16|for grace|pro gratia]] of the Old Testament, that is, in place of the law of Moses. Both laws are called grace, since both were given freely and in mercy. Or thus: we have received the grace of the members, namely the grace granted to us, for the grace of the Head, that is, by the merit and efficacy of the grace of Christ, who by every act of His life that He performed as a wayfarer [*viator*, one still on the way to the heavenly homeland], from the grace that flowed from Him, merited for us grace in the present and glory in the future. For He did not merit for Himself sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes a man pleasing to God], nor the beatific vision, but merited them for His members, who share in the grace of the Head through faith and the sacraments of the Church. But according to the Master of the Sentences [Peter Lombard], since our merits and rewards are gifts of God, because they depend on grace infused by the liberality of God alone, it can be taken thus: we have received grace, that is, merit or reward, for grace, which is the cause of the merit or of the recompense. When, therefore, God rewards our merits, He rewards His own gifts, and gives grace upon grace, according to the saying: [[Matt 25:29|to every one that hath shall be given, and he shall abound|Habenti dabitur, et abundabit]]. Augustine and Bede also explain it thus: we have received already in hope [[1:16|grace for grace|gratiam pro gratia]], that is, eternal life for faith.

paras.t: Quæritur, quum gratia Christi sit accidens, quod non migrat de subjecto in subjectum, et quum solus Deus sit gratiæ dator, quomodo dicimur de plenitudine gratiæ Christi accepisse. Rursus, quomodo gratia gratis confertur, si datur merito Christi. — Et respondendum ad primum, quod non dicimur accepisse de plenitudine Christi, quasi particulam gratiæ ejus acceperimus, ita quod gratia Christi sit divisibilis, et eadem numero sit primo in Christo, deinde in nobis; sed quia plenitudo gratiæ Christi est causa instrumentalis, dispositiva ac meritoria, per quam singulis electis hominibus datur gratia secundum aliquem gradum, sola vero Divinitas est causa efficiens gratiæ. De plenitudine autem gratiæ Christi omnes, præsertim Apostoli, acceperunt, acceptando gratiam non dumtaxat pro habitu gratiæ gratum facientis, quæ ponitur in essentia animæ, sed pro quocumque dono supernaturali vel supernaturaliter dato, quamvis sit naturale in se. Nam de plenitudine sapientiæ Christi, accepimus evangelicam legem; de plenitudine vero sanctissimæ conversationis suæ, accepimus boni exempli exhibitionem; de plenitudine suæ gratiæ interioris, essentiam animæ perficientis, accepimus gratiam pro gratia, id est gratiam habitualem deiforme esse præstantem, pro gratia secundum modos præhabitos. Maxime autem de plenitudine Christi receperunt Apostoli, aliique cum eis in conclavi collecti, quando in die sancto Pentecostes receperunt Spiritum Sanctum in signo visibili; repletique sunt omnes, non solum gratia gratificante, sed gratiis etiam gratis datis. Nec mirum si de plenitudine Christi dicimur accepisse, quum Petrus universos fideles hortetur, dicendo: Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei.
paras.en: It is asked: since the grace of Christ is an accident, which does not pass from one subject into another [an accident, in the language of the schools, is a quality that exists only in a subject and cannot be handed on from one to another], and since God alone is the giver of grace, how are we said to have received of the fulness of Christ’s grace? And again: how is grace given gratis, if it is given through the merit of Christ? — To the first it must be answered that we are not said to have received of the fulness of Christ as though we had received a particle of His grace, so that the grace of Christ were divisible, and one and the same in number were first in Christ and then in us; but because the fulness of Christ’s grace is the instrumental, dispositive and meritorious cause through which grace is given to each of the elect in some degree, while the Godhead alone is the efficient cause of grace. Of the fulness of Christ’s grace all have received, and the Apostles above all, taking grace not only for the habit of sanctifying grace, which is placed in the essence of the soul, but for any gift that is supernatural or supernaturally given, even if it be natural in itself. For of the fulness of Christ’s wisdom we have received the law of the Gospel; of the fulness of His most holy way of life, the showing of a good example; of the fulness of His interior grace, which perfects the essence of the soul, we have received [[1:16|grace for grace|gratiam pro gratia]], that is, habitual grace, which bestows a godlike being, for grace in the senses given above. But the Apostles above all received of the fulness of Christ, and the others gathered with them in the upper room, when on the holy day of Pentecost they received the Holy Ghost under a visible sign[[Acts 2:1||]]; and they were all filled, not only with sanctifying grace, but also with graces freely given [*gratiæ gratis datæ*: gifts such as prophecy or tongues, given for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the one who receives them]. Nor is it any wonder that we are said to have received of the fulness of Christ, since Peter exhorts all the faithful, saying: [[1 Pet 4:10|As every man hath received grace, ministering the same one to another: as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.|Unusquisque sicut accepit gratiam, in alterutrum illam administrantes, sicut boni dispensatores multiformis gratiæ Dei]]

paras.t: Ad secundum dicendum, quod gratia fertur dari sine præviis meritis, quoniam datur sine præviis meritis recipientis, non sine meritis Salvatoris; vel datur sine meritis quantum ad primam radicem, quia et Christo collata est absque meritis ejus (sola enim bonitate Dei datum est humanæ naturæ Christi, esse unitam Verbo, et gratia adimpleri), et quoniam Deus decrevit hominibus gratiam dare ex sua largitate per meritum Christi, sive futurum, sive præsens, sive præteritum.
paras.en: To the second it must be said that grace is said to be given without preceding merits because it is given without preceding merits of the one who receives it, not without the merits of the Saviour; or it is given without merits as regards its first root, since it was conferred on Christ too without any merits of His (for by the goodness of God alone was it given to the human nature of Christ to be united to the Word and to be filled with grace), and because God decreed of His bounty to give grace to men through the merit of Christ, whether future, present or past.

paras.t: Consequenter subditur causa, signum vel declaratio, quod de plenitudine Christi accepimus. Quia lex veteris Testamenti, in qua erant præcepta moralia, judicialia, ac cæremonialia, per Moysen data est, tanquam per servum populo Israel. Data est quoque per angelos, quemadmodum in Actibus loquitur Stephanus ad Judæos incredulos: Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum, et non custodistis. Unde ad Galatas dicit Apostolus: Lex propter transgressiones posita est, ordinata per angelos in manu mediatoris. Ex quibus elicitur, quod data sit lex ministerio angelorum multorum, quamvis communiter non fiat mentio nisi de angelo uno, qui frequentius apparuit Moysi. Lex ergo data est a Deo principaliter, per angelum ministerialiter Moysi, et per Moysen tanquam per ministrum secundarium, data est populo Israel.
paras.en: Next is added the cause, sign or declaration of our having received of the fulness of Christ: [[1:17|For the law|Quia lex]] of the Old Testament, in which were the moral, judicial and ceremonial precepts, [[1:17|was given by Moses|per Moysen data est]], as by a servant, to the people of Israel. It was also given by angels, as Stephen says in the Acts to the unbelieving Jews: you [[Acts 7:53|have received the law by the disposition of angels and have not kept it|Accepistis legem in dispositione angelorum, et non custodistis]]. Hence the Apostle says to the Galatians that the law [[Gal 3:19|was set because of transgressions|propter transgressiones posita est]], [[Gal 3:19|being ordained by angels in the hand of a mediator|ordinata per angelos in manu mediatoris]]. From this it is gathered that the law was given by the ministry of many angels, although commonly mention is made of only one angel, who appeared more often to Moses. The law, then, was given by God as its principal author, by an angel as minister to Moses, and through Moses, as a secondary minister, to the people of Israel.

paras.t: Gratia, id est liberatio a peccatis, justificatio generis humani, supernaturale donum Spiritus Sancti perficiens animam, eamque Deo acceptam et ad promerendum idoneam faciens, et veritas, id est doctrina evangelicæ legis, vel impletio legis ac Prophetarum, per Jesum Christum facta est. Christus namque ut Deus, causa est principalis atque efficiens gratiæ hujus; sed ut homo talis, est causa instrumentalis ac meritoria ejus. Ipse quoque per assumptam humanitatem implevit et verificavit quæ de ipso prænuntiabantur in lege et Prophetis per figuras seu verba prophetica. Ipse etiam exposuit nobis Scripturas veteris legis per se ipsum, quando aperuit discipulis sensum ut intelligerent Scripturas, et quando misit eis Spiritum Sanctum, prout apud Joannem promisit: Quum venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem.
paras.en: [[1:17|Grace|Gratia]], that is, deliverance from sins, the justification of the human race, the supernatural gift of the Holy Ghost that perfects the soul and makes it acceptable to God and fit to merit, [[1:17|and truth|et veritas]], that is, the teaching of the law of the Gospel, or the fulfilment of the Law and the Prophets, [[1:17|came by Jesus Christ|per Jesum Christum facta est]]. For Christ as God is the principal and efficient cause of this grace, but as man He is its instrumental and meritorious cause. He also, through the humanity He assumed, fulfilled and made true what had been foretold of Him in the Law and the Prophets by figures or prophetic words. He also expounded to us Himself the Scriptures of the old law, when [[Luke 24:45|he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures|aperuit discipulis sensum ut intelligerent Scripturas]], and when He sent them the Holy Ghost, as He promised in John: [[John 16:13|when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will teach you all truth|Quum venerit ille Spiritus veritatis, docebit vos omnem veritatem]].

paras.t: Præterea Moyses dedit legem, multa jubendo; sed non dedit gratiam qua implerentur quæ jussit. Lex quoque Mosaica habuit umbram futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum, ut dicit Apostolus. Christus vero præstitit gratiam adimplendi quæ jussit, et pro umbra legalium figurarum, proposuit lucem veritatis, atque imaginem rerum, id est evidentem similitudinem bonorum cœlestium. Propter quod, secundum Dionysium, lex evangelica media est inter legem Mosaicam et statum Beatorum in patria. Hinc tempus Christi novæque legis, vocatur tempus gratiæ: quoniam lex nova dat gratiam, in quantum includit sacramenta Ecclesiæ, quæ faciunt quod designant; et propter copiosissimam gratiam quam Christus nobis promeruit; et item propter ineffabilem magnitudinem beneficiorum Dei, et pronitatem ejus ad dandam gratiam tempore evangelicæ legis. Unde philosophis dicitur innotuisse divina majestas; Judæis, justitia. Christianis vero misericordia innotescit, prout ad Titum protestatur Apostolus: Apparuit benignitas et humanitas Salvatoris nostri Dei; et alibi, Apparuit gratia Salvatoris. Hoc per Zachariam legitur prophetatum, quum dicitur: Et erit qui offenderit ex eis in die illa sicut domus David, et domus David quasi Dei, sicut angelus Domini.
paras.en: Moreover, Moses gave the law, commanding many things; but he did not give the grace by which what he commanded might be fulfilled. The Mosaic law also had [[Heb 10:1|a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things|umbram futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum]], as the Apostle says. But Christ gave the grace to fulfil what He commanded, and in place of the shadow of the figures of the law He set forth the light of truth and the image of the things, that is, a clear likeness of the heavenly goods. For this reason, according to Dionysius, the law of the Gospel stands midway between the law of Moses and the state of the Blessed in the homeland. Hence the time of Christ and of the new law is called the time of grace: because the new law gives grace, inasmuch as it contains the sacraments of the Church, which effect what they signify; and because of the most abundant grace that Christ merited for us; and also because of the unspeakable greatness of God’s benefits, and His readiness to give grace in the time of the law of the Gospel. Hence it is said that to the philosophers the divine majesty was made known, to the Jews His justice; but to Christians His mercy is made known, as the Apostle declares to Titus: [[Tit 3:4|the goodness and kindness of God our Saviour appeared|Apparuit benignitas et humanitas Salvatoris nostri Dei]]; and elsewhere: [[Tit 2:11|the grace of God our Saviour hath appeared|Apparuit gratia Salvatoris]]. This we read was prophesied by Zacharias, where it is said: [[Zach 12:8|he that hath offended among them in that day shall be as David: and the house of David, as that of God, as an angel of the Lord|Et erit qui offenderit ex eis in die illa sicut domus David, et domus David quasi Dei, sicut angelus Domini]].

paras.t: Deinde ostendit Joannes certitudinem horum quæ hic recitantur. Deum nemo vidit unquam. Verba evangelistæ Joannis, sicut in stilo simplicissima sunt, sic in sensu vere profundissima exstant. Sic nempe decuit scribi Evangelium humillimi atque altissimi Jesu Christi, ut esset in stilo simplicitas summa, et in sensu profunditas maxima: quatenus sermonis inculta simplicitas corresponderet, tam humilitati humanitatique Christi, de quo conscriptum est Evangelium, quam humilitati Evangelistarum scribentium, qui omnem curiositatem stilique pompam vitarunt; profunditas vero sententiæ corresponderet, tam majestati ac divinitati Christi, quam altæ illuminationi Evangelistarum. Ait ergo nunc Evangelista aquilinus ac deificatus: Deum nemo vidit unquam. Quid quantum ad verba simplicius? quid in sensu profundius? Quomodocumque enim exponatur, habet instantiam, et requirit idoneam responsionem.
paras.en: Next John shows the certainty of the things related here: [[1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit unquam]]. The words of John the Evangelist, as they are most simple in style, so in sense they are truly most profound. For so it was fitting that the Gospel of Jesus Christ, most humble and most high, should be written: that there should be the utmost simplicity in its style and the greatest depth in its sense; so that the unadorned simplicity of the language might answer both to the humility and humanity of Christ, of whom the Gospel was written, and to the humility of the Evangelists who wrote it, who shunned all affectation and pomp of style; while the depth of its meaning might answer both to the majesty and divinity of Christ and to the lofty illumination of the Evangelists. So now the eagle-like and deified Evangelist says: [[1:18|No man hath seen God at any time|Deum nemo vidit unquam]]. What could be simpler as to the words? What more profound in sense? For however it is explained, it meets an objection [Latin *instantia*: in scholastic usage, a counter-instance raised against a statement] and calls for a fitting answer.

paras.t: Potest autem exponi quatuor modis, secundum quod quadriformis est visio, et etiam visio Dei. Est enim corporalis visio Dei, non tamen secundum divinitatem. De qua ait sanctus Job: In carne mea videbo Deum salvatorem meum, quem visurus sum ego ipse, et oculi mei conspecturi sunt. Ex qua auctoritate ostendit Thomas in Summa contra gentiles, quod beatus Job noverat Deum incarnandum. Alia est visio Dei imaginaria, de qua communiter eloquuntur Prophetæ: ut Isaias, quum dicit, Vidi Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum et elevatum; Daniel quoque, Adspiciebam donec throni positi sunt, et Antiquus dierum sedit. Tertia est visio Dei per speciem, qua Deum vident Sancti in patria. Quarta est visio perfectæ comprehensionis, qua res cognoscitur totaliter, tamque perfecte sicut ex sua natura cognoscibilis est: qua solus Deus videt se ipsum.
paras.en: It can be explained in four ways, according as vision is fourfold, and so too the vision of God. For there is a bodily vision of God, though not according to His divinity; of which holy Job says: [[Job 19:26|in my flesh I shall see my God|In carne mea videbo Deum salvatorem meum]] [Denis's text reads "God my Saviour"], [[Job 19:27|Whom I myself shall see, and my eyes shall behold|quem visurus sum ego ipse, et oculi mei conspecturi sunt]]. From this authority Thomas shows in the *Summa contra Gentiles* that blessed Job knew that God was to become incarnate. Another is the imaginary vision of God [that is, one formed in the imagination, through bodily likenesses], of which the Prophets commonly speak: as Isaias, when he says, [[Is 6:1|I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated|Vidi Dominum sedentem super solium excelsum et elevatum]]; Daniel also, [[Dan 7:9|I beheld till thrones were placed, and the ancient of days sat|Adspiciebam donec throni positi sunt, et Antiquus dierum sedit]]. The third is the vision of God by sight [*per speciem*: open sight of His essence, as against faith], by which the Saints see God in the fatherland. The fourth is the vision of perfect comprehension, by which a thing is known wholly, and as perfectly as it is knowable by its own nature: by this God alone sees Himself.

paras.t: Si ergo hæc verba exponantur de visione corporali, occurrit objectio de Jacob, qui de visione tempore vigiliæ habita, ait in Genesi: Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem. Sed hoc facile solvitur, ut dicamus cum Augustino, quod non vidit Deum in propria persona, sed per creaturam subjectam, hoc est per angelum, Dei præconem: quo modo Manue pater Samsonis, viso angelo, locutus est conjugi suæ, Morte moriemur, quia vidimus Dominum. Sed tunc occurrit objectio de his qui Christum in carne viderunt, qui utique divinam Personam verumque Deum corporali visu intuiti sunt, sicut Joannes ait: Quod perspeximus oculis nostris, et manus nostræ contrectaverunt de Verbo vitæ. Sed hoc rursus de facili solvitur, quoniam non viderunt Deum secundum divinitatis essentiam, sed quoad naturam assumptam; divinitatem vero non viderunt, nisi per fidem. Porro, si verba hæc exponantur de visione imaginaria, certum est quod Prophetæ frequenter asserant se hoc modo Deum vidisse. Si autem exponatur de visione comprehensionis, habet instantiam de Sanctis in patria, qui Deum comprehendere perhibentur, unde et comprehensores dicuntur. Si vero exponatur de comprehensione omnino perfecta, occurrit instantia de Christo, qui quum homo esset, comprehendit Deum perfecte, quemadmodum ait Joannes: Nemo novit Patrem, nisi Filius.
paras.en: If, then, these words are understood of bodily vision, an objection arises from Jacob, who, of a vision he had while awake, says in Genesis: [[Gen 32:30|I have seen God face to face|Vidi Dominum facie ad faciem]]. But this is easily resolved if we say with Augustine that he did not see God in His own person, but through a creature subject to Him, that is, through an angel, God's herald: in the way that Manue, the father of Samson, on seeing the angel, said to his wife, [[Judg 13:22|We shall certainly die, because we have seen God|Morte moriemur, quia vidimus Dominum]]. But then an objection arises from those who saw Christ in the flesh, who certainly beheld with bodily sight a divine Person and true God, as John says: [[1 John 1:1|which we have seen with our eyes, which we have looked upon and our hands have handled, of the word of life|Quod perspeximus oculis nostris, et manus nostræ contrectaverunt de Verbo vitæ]]. But this again is easily resolved, since they did not see God according to the essence of the Godhead, but as to the nature He assumed; the Godhead they did not see, except by faith. Further, if these words are understood of imaginary vision, it is certain that the Prophets often assert that they saw God in this way. And if it is understood of the vision of comprehension, it meets an objection from the Saints in the fatherland, who are said to comprehend God, and hence are called comprehensors [*comprehensores*: the blessed, who have reached God, as against *viatores*, wayfarers still on the way]. And if it is understood of altogether perfect comprehension, an objection arises from Christ, who, being man, comprehended God perfectly, as John says: [[Matt 11:27|neither doth any one know the Father, but the Son|Nemo novit Patrem, nisi Filius]][[John 6:46||]] [the words are those of Matthew, though Denis names John; the margin cites Matth. xi and John 6:46, where John says the like].

paras.t: Verum breviter respondendo dicendum, quod verbum Evangelistæ his quatuor modis intelligi potest. Primo sic: Deum Trinitatem, vel quamcumque divinam Personam, nemo vidit, videt, videbit videreve potest unquam visu corporali, quantum ad Divinitatis naturam, quum Deus secundum propriam essentiam sit incorporalis, incircumscriptus, simplicissimus, atque purissimus actus. Unde dicit Apostolus: Quem nemo hominum vidit, sed nec videre potest. — Secundo sic: Deum in sua essentia, nemo vidit unquam, visione imaginaria. Quamvis enim in tali visione dicatur Deus videri, hoc tamen non est, nisi in quantum in sensu interiori formantur corporales similitudines, ad repræsentandum Deum.
paras.en: But to answer briefly, it must be said that the Evangelist's word can be understood in these four ways. First thus: God the Trinity, or any divine Person, no man has seen, sees, will see, or can ever see with bodily sight, as to the nature of the Godhead, since God in His own essence is incorporeal, uncircumscribed, most simple, and most pure act [*actus purus*: wholly in act, with no potency at all]. Hence the Apostle says: [[1 Tim 6:16|whom no man hath seen, nor can see|Quem nemo hominum vidit, sed nec videre potest]]. Second thus: God in His essence no man hath seen at any time by imaginary vision. For although in such a vision God is said to be seen, this is so only in so far as bodily likenesses are formed in the inner sense to represent God.

paras.t: Tertio sic: Deum in sua essentia, seu per speciem, nemo, hoc est nullus homo purus viator, vivens vita humana ac sensitiva, vidit unquam. Sic enim Deus videri non potest, nisi per speciem increatam, quum omnis species, forma ac similitudo creata, in infinitum deficiat a clara repræsentatione divinæ essentiæ, sicut et omnis creatura in infinitum deficit a plena repræsentatione perfectionis divinæ.
paras.en: Third thus: God in His essence, or by sight, no man, that is, no man who is a mere wayfarer [*viator*: one still on the way, in this life], living a human and sensitive life, hath seen at any time. For God cannot be seen in this way except through an uncreated species [*species*: the likeness through which the mind knows a thing; here God's own essence must serve as it], since every created species, form and likeness falls infinitely short of clearly representing the divine essence, as every creature too falls infinitely short of fully representing the divine perfection.

paras.t: Denique, quum secundum Philosophum, intellectus noster se habeat ad cognitionem intelligentiarum, quemadmodum oculus noctuæ ad intuitum lucis solaris, patet quod incomparabiliter impotentior sit ad claram ac immediatam divinæ essentiæ visionem, loquendo de statu ejus in præsenti, et naturali virtute. Hoc cognoverunt atque professi sunt omnes subtiliores philosophi. Unde Alphorabius, Avicenna, Theophrastus, alii quoque innumerabiles dixerunt, quod de Deo melius cognoscimus quid non sit, quam quid sit, et quod de eo solum cognoscimus quia est, non quid est. Hoc princeps theologorum beatissimus Dionysius plenius docet, affirmans quod perfectissima cognitio quam habemus de Deo in vita præsenti, est per puram ac meram abnegationem omnium rerum a Deo, ita ut uniamur ei tanquam prorsus ignoto.
