Unde tertio capitulo Mysticæ Theologiæ: Hoc est (inquit) Deum vere cognoscere, supersubstantialem supersubstantialiter per omnium entium ablationem laudare. Et in epistola ad Dorotheum: Invisibilis est Deus propter excedentem suæ lucis claritatem. Lux autem divina, immensa et increata, secundum quod inaccessibilis seu incomprehensibilis, hoc modo vocatur a Dionysio divina caligo. De qua in epistola sua ad Caium monachum contestatur: Divinæ tenebræ cooperiuntur omni lumini, et absconduntur omni visioni, propter incircumscriptibilem propriæ claritatis splendorem. Omnia hæc in Elementatione theologica Procli, et in libro de Causis, subtilissime inveniuntur probata.
paras.en: Moreover, since, according to the Philosopher, our intellect stands toward the knowledge of the intelligences [that is, the separate, purely spiritual substances] as the eye of the owl toward gazing at the light of the sun, it is plain that it is incomparably more powerless for a clear and immediate vision of the divine essence, speaking of its state in the present life and of its natural power. All the more acute philosophers knew and professed this. Hence Alphorabius, Avicenna, Theophrastus, and countless others besides said that we know better of God what He is not than what He is, and that of Him we know only that He is, not what He is. This the prince of theologians, the most blessed Dionysius, teaches more fully, affirming that the most perfect knowledge we have of God in the present life is by the pure and sheer denial of all things of God, so that we are united to Him as to one wholly unknown. Hence in the third chapter of the *Mystical Theology* he says: This is truly to know God: to praise the Supersubstantial One supersubstantially by the removal of all beings. And in the letter to Dorotheus: God is invisible because of the surpassing brightness of His light. Now the divine light, immense and uncreated, in so far as it is inaccessible or incomprehensible[[1 Tim 6:16||]], is in this way called by Dionysius the divine darkness. Of this he testifies in his letter to Caius the monk: The divine darkness is veiled from all light and hidden from all vision, because of the uncircumscribable splendour of its own brightness. All these things are found most subtly proved in the *Elements of Theology* of Proclus and in the *Book of Causes*.

paras.t: Hinc quoque Dominus ait ad Moysen: Non poteris videre faciem meam; non enim videbit me homo et vivet. Veruntamen, quoniam in libro Numerorum de Moyse legitur, Palam, et non per ænigmata et figuras, videt Deum; et quoniam Paulus de se ipso fatetur, quod raptus est usque ad tertium cælum, audivitque arcana verba quæ non licet homini loqui: propterea Augustinus in libro de Videndo Deum, et Thomas, dicunt quod Moyses Judæorum magister, et Paulus gentium doctor, viderunt Deum in hac vita per speciem. Sed hoc non est contra prædicta, quia pro tunc non vixerunt vita humana, nec quidquam senserunt. Quod ergo legitur Moysi negatum in Exodo, postea concessum est ei, ut legitur in libro Numerorum.
paras.en: Hence also the Lord says to Moses: [[Ex 33:20|Thou canst not see my face: for man shall not see me, and live|Non poteris videre faciem meam; non enim videbit me homo et vivet]]. Nevertheless, since in the book of Numbers we read of Moses, [[Num 12:8|plainly, and not by riddles and figures doth he see the Lord|Palam, et non per ænigmata et figuras, videt Deum]]; and since Paul confesses of himself that he was [[2 Cor 12:2|caught up to the third heaven|raptus est usque ad tertium cælum]], and [[2 Cor 12:4|heard secret words which it is not granted to man to utter|audivitque arcana verba quæ non licet homini loqui]]: therefore Augustine in the book *On Seeing God*, and Thomas, say that Moses, the master of the Jews, and Paul, the teacher of the Gentiles, saw God in this life by sight [that is, in His essence]. But this is not against what was said above, since at that time they were not living a human life, nor perceiving anything by the senses. What we read was denied to Moses in Exodus, then, was afterwards granted him, as we read in the book of Numbers.

paras.t: Quarto sic: Deum nemo, hoc est nulla creatura, vidit visione perfectæ comprehensionis unquam. Sic enim nec anima Christi videt Deum, qui sicut est infinitæ actualitatis, sic est infinitæ cognoscibilitatis: propter quod perfecte atque totaliter cognosci et comprehendi non valet nisi ab intellectu infinitæ virtutis. Hanc ultimam expositionem multi putant amplius ad propositum pertinere. Sicque Damascenus in principio sui libri disseruit, quod non solum nullus hominum, sed nec aliquis supermundanorum animorum, Deum vidit unquam. Sed advertendum, quod res dicitur a cognoscente comprehendi dupliciter: Primo, quoniam ejus essentia cernitur, et sic ipsa immediate attingitur. Hoc modo Sancti in patria comprehendunt Deum, et comprehensores dicuntur, quoniam vident, hoc est, intelligunt et agnoscunt Deum sicuti est, secundum Joannem, seu facie ad faciem, juxta Paulum. Secundo, res dicitur comprehendi, quia in tantum cognoscitur sicut ex sua natura cognoscibilis est, ita quod nil ejus latet, sed quasi infra certos terminos continetur in animo cognoscentis. Hoc modo infinitum a finito comprehendi non potest: sicque Apostolus loquitur, Quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit, nisi Spiritus ejus. Præter modos commemoratos, videmus Deum tripliciter: per fidem, per naturalem rationem, per anagogicam illustrationem.
paras.en: Fourth thus: God no man, that is, no creature, hath seen at any time with the vision of perfect comprehension. For in this way not even the soul of Christ sees God, who, as He is of infinite actuality, so is He of infinite knowability; wherefore He cannot be perfectly and wholly known and comprehended except by an intellect of infinite power. Many think this last explanation more to the purpose. And so Damascene argued at the beginning of his book that not only no man, but not any of the supermundane minds either, has ever seen God. But it should be noted that a thing is said to be comprehended by the knower in two ways. First, because its essence is beheld, and so it is reached immediately. In this way the Saints in the fatherland comprehend God and are called comprehensors, because they see, that is, understand and know, God [[1 John 3:2|as he is|sicuti est]], according to John, or [[1 Cor 13:12|face to face|facie ad faciem]], according to Paul. Second, a thing is said to be comprehended because it is known as fully as it is knowable by its own nature, so that nothing of it is hidden, but it is held, as it were, within fixed bounds in the mind of the knower. In this way the infinite cannot be comprehended by the finite; and so the Apostle says, [[1 Cor 2:11|the things also that are of God, no man knoweth, but the Spirit of God|Quæ sunt Dei, nemo novit, nisi Spiritus ejus]]. Besides the ways mentioned, we see God in three ways: by faith, by natural reason, and by anagogical illumination [that is, an illumination that lifts the mind upward to God].

paras.t: Consequenter pandit Evangelista, quis nos instruxit de invisibilibus Dei. Unigenitus Filius, Patri consubstantialis, consempiternus et coæqualis, qui est invariabiliter ab æterno, in sinu Patris, id est Patri intime atque affectuosissime inseparabiliterque conjunctus, ipse enarravit, id est, in Evangelio docuit quid de Divinitatis unitate, et Personarum trinitate, quid de Creatoris providentia, omnipotentia, ceterisque secretis divinis, et ad salutem pertinentibus, sentire debemus. Hinc infra loquitur: Pater, manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus quos dedisti mihi de mundo. Et ut ait Joannes: Scimus quoniam Filius Dei venit, et dedit nobis sensum, ut cognoscamus Deum verum. Hoc utique insuperabiliter ac ineffabiliter roborat fidem nostram, quod a Filio Dei unigenito vero Deo sumus edocti. Itaque, quod ait, Filium esse in sinu Patris, non est materialiter intelligendum, sed per sinum intelligitur cor paternum, in quo Verbum æternaliter manet. Loquitur tamen Evangelista more humano, quatenus per exsistentiam Filii in sinu Patris, insinuet superdulcem affectum, amorosissimamque unionem Patris ac Filii, sicut apud nos parentes ponunt filios in sinu ex magno affectu.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist makes known who has instructed us about the invisible things of God. [[1:18|the only begotten Son|Unigenitus Filius]], consubstantial with the Father, co-eternal and co-equal, [[1:18|who is|qui est]] unchangeably from eternity [[1:18|in the Bosom of the Father|in sinu Patris]], that is, joined to the Father intimately, most lovingly and inseparably, [[1:18|he hath declared him|ipse enarravit]], that is, has taught in the Gospel what we ought to hold concerning the unity of the Godhead and the trinity of Persons, concerning the Creator's providence and omnipotence, and the other divine secrets and the things that pertain to salvation. Hence He says further on: Father, [[John 17:6|I have manifested thy name to the men whom thou hast given me out of the world|manifestavi nomen tuum hominibus quos dedisti mihi de mundo]]. And as John says: [[1 John 5:20|we know that the Son of God is come. And he hath given us understanding that we may know the true God|Scimus quoniam Filius Dei venit, et dedit nobis sensum, ut cognoscamus Deum verum]]. This indeed strengthens our faith insuperably and ineffably, that we have been taught by the only begotten Son of God, true God. So, when he says that the Son is [[1:18|in the Bosom of the Father|in sinu Patris]], it is not to be understood materially: by the bosom is understood the Father's heart, in which the Word abides eternally. Yet the Evangelist speaks in a human way, so as to suggest, by the Son's being in the Father's bosom, the most sweet affection and most loving union of the Father and the Son, as among us parents hold their children in their bosom out of great affection.

paras.t: Quoniam ergo fides et lex christiana ab unigenito Filio Dei pronuntiata ac data est nobis, idcirco gravius est non credere et obedire Evangelio, quam olim fuit non credere ac parere Pentateucho et Scripturis veteris Testamenti. Ad quod insinuandum dicit Apostolus ad Hebræos: Si illi (puta Judæi) non effugerunt, recusantes eum qui super terram loquebatur (puta Moysen), multo magis nos qui de cælis loquentem nobis avertimus, scilicet Filium Dei, non effugiemus. — De hac sua enarratione Christus ait apud Isaiam: Ad annuntiandum mansuetis misit me.
paras.en: Since, then, the Christian faith and law was proclaimed and given to us by the only begotten Son of God, it is therefore a graver thing not to believe and obey the Gospel than it once was not to believe and obey the Pentateuch and the Scriptures of the Old Testament. To suggest this the Apostle says to the Hebrews: if they (namely, the Jews) [[Heb 12:25|escaped not|non effugerunt]], [[Heb 12:25|who refused him that spoke upon earth|recusantes eum qui super terram loquebatur]] (namely, Moses), [[Heb 12:25|much more shall not we that turn away from him that speaketh to us from heaven|multo magis nos qui de cælis loquentem nobis avertimus]], namely the Son of God, escape. Of this His declaring [*enarratio*, from the verse's *enarravit*, "he hath declared"] Christ says in Isaias: [[Is 61:1|he hath sent me to preach to the meek|Ad annuntiandum mansuetis misit me]].

paras.t: Deinde Evangelista prosequitur plenius testificationem Joannis de Christo, ostendens locum et tempus, ubi et quando perhibuit testimonium Christo. Et hoc est testimonium Joannis, id est, verba Joannis Baptistæ jam introducta, sunt quæ testificando dixit de Christo. Aliqui referunt hoc ad verba sequentia, in quibus Præcursor testatur veritatem de Christo. Quando miserunt Judæi ab Jerosolymis, urbe sacerdotali ac regia atque metropoli in Judæa, in qua studium Prophetarum ac legis vigebat, sacrificia quoque fiebant, et principes Judæorum demorabantur, sacerdotes et Levitas, videlicet nuntios solennes et eruditos, qui magis videbantur zelare pro lege ac divino honore, ad eum, ut interrogarent eum: Tu quis es, id est qua vel qualis persona, cujus auctoritatis aut dignitatis? Unde moti fuerunt Judæi ad hanc legationem et interrogationem Joannis? Nisi enim putassent eum esse aliquem magnum, non misissent ad eum tales legatos, nec tam magna petissent ab ipso.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist sets out more fully John's testimony of Christ, showing the place and the time, where and when he gave testimony to Christ. [[1:19|And this is the testimony of John|Et hoc est testimonium Joannis]], that is, the words of John the Baptist already brought forward are those which he spoke of Christ in bearing witness. Some refer this to the words that follow, in which the Forerunner testifies to the truth about Christ. [[1:19|when the Jews sent from Jerusalem|Quando miserunt Judæi ab Jerosolymis]], the priestly and royal city and metropolis in Judea, in which the study of the Prophets and of the law flourished, where sacrifices also were offered, and where the princes of the Jews dwelt, [[1:19|priests and Levites|sacerdotes et Levitas]], that is, solemn and learned messengers, who seemed the more zealous for the law and for the honour of God, [[1:19|to him, to ask him: Who art thou|ad eum, ut interrogarent eum: Tu quis es]], that is, what or what manner of person, of what authority or dignity? What moved the Jews to this embassy and this questioning of John? For had they not thought him to be someone great, they would not have sent such envoys to him, nor asked such great things of him.

paras.t: Et respondendum, quod Judæi, baptizante Joanne, magnam æstimationem habebant quod Messias venisset in mundum, ex causis diversis, videlicet: propter testimonium pastorum, Annæ prophetissæ et justi Simeonis, trium quoque Magorum, et propter occisionem infantium: quorum testimoniorum memoria adhuc in Judæis permansit. Item, quia viderunt sibi regnum ablatum, et alienigenæ traditum, quod Jacob dedit eis pro signo adventus Christi; et quia viderunt hebdomadas illas impletas, de quibus cecinit Daniel quod intra illas Christus veniret. Istud de hebdomadibus dicit quidam, quod non videtur certum, vel multum probabile, quia apud Matthæum Christus improperat Pharisæis, quod ex vaticinio Danielis prædicto, non adverterunt tempus adventus Messiæ instare: Faciem (inquit) cœli judicare nostis, signa autem temporum non potestis? Et in Luca planius ait: Hypocritæ, faciem cœli et terræ nostis probare, hoc autem tempus quomodo non probatis? Quoniam itaque æstimabant tempus Messiæ adesse, opinati sunt Joannem esse Christum, propter miraculosam ejus nativitatem, quæ super omnia montana Judææ divulgabatur; item, propter vitæ suæ abstractionem, rigorem ac sanctitatem, genealogiæ nobilitatem. Quum enim fuerit natus de tribu sacerdotali, probabile est quod etiam fuit de tribu regali vel Juda, quoniam hæ duæ tribus pene semper contraxerunt ad invicem. Quærendo autem, Tu quis es? non intendebant sciscitari vel certificari de nomine et origine, hæc enim sciebant; sed de dignitate et gratia.
paras.en: The answer is that while John was baptizing the Jews held it very likely that the Messias had come into the world, for various reasons: because of the testimony of the shepherds[[Luke 2:20||]], of Anna the prophetess and of just Simeon[[Luke 2:25||]], and also of the three Magi[[Matt 2:1||]], and because of the slaying of the infants[[Matt 2:16||]]; the memory of these testimonies still remained among the Jews. Again, because they saw the kingdom taken from them and handed over to a foreigner, which Jacob had given them as a sign of the coming of Christ[[Gen 49:10||]]; and because they saw fulfilled those weeks of which Daniel sang, that within them the Christ would come[[Dan 9:24||]]. This about the weeks is said by a certain writer, but it does not seem certain, or very probable, since in Matthew Christ reproaches the Pharisees that, from the aforesaid prophecy of Daniel, they had not noticed that the time of the Messias's coming was at hand: [[Matt 16:3|You know then how to discern the face of the sky|Faciem (inquit) cœli judicare nostis]] (He says), [[Matt 16:3|and can you not know the signs of the times|signa autem temporum non potestis]]? And in Luke He says more plainly: [[Luke 12:56|You hypocrites, you know how to discern the face of the heaven and of the earth: but how is it that you do not discern this time?|Hypocritæ, faciem cœli et terræ nostis probare, hoc autem tempus quomodo non probatis?]] Since, then, they reckoned that the time of the Messias was at hand, they supposed John to be the Christ, because of his miraculous birth, which was noised abroad [[Luke 1:65|over all the hill country of Judea|super omnia montana Judææ]]; and also because of his withdrawal from the world, the rigour and holiness of his life, and the nobility of his lineage. For since he was born of the priestly tribe[[Luke 1:5||]], it is probable that he was also of the royal tribe, that is, of Juda, since these two tribes almost always intermarried. But in asking, Who art thou? they did not mean to inquire or make sure of his name and origin, for these they knew, but of his dignity and grace.

paras.t: Et confessus est Joannes veritatem, tanquam Veritatis præco, amicus et paranymphus, et non negavit eam. Os enim quod mentitur, occidit animam. Et Psalmista ait Deo: Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium. Quamvis namque sæpe sit licitum veritatem silere, propter audientium improbitatem, vel propriam pacem, seu aliam piam seu rationabilem causam (juxta illud Psalmistæ: Posui ori meo custodiam, dum consisteret peccator adversum me; obmutui, et humiliatus sum, et silui a bonis), nunquam tamen licet veritatem negare, quamvis possit aliquando pia cautela abscondi. Et confessus est. Quia, id est quod, non sum ego Christus, id est non judex, non sponsus, non Salvator, non unigenitus Filius Dei, sed Christi minister, judicis præco, sponsi paranymphus, Salvatoris præcursor, Filii Dei minister. Sacerdotes ergo primo quæsierunt explicite vel saltem implicite a Joanne, an esset Christus. Idcirco Joannes respondit vel ad verba, vel ad mentem eorum.
paras.en: [[1:20|And he confessed|Et confessus est]], John, the truth, as the herald, friend and groomsman [paranymphus: the friend who leads the bride to the bridegroom] of the Truth, [[1:20|and did not deny|et non negavit]] it. For [[Wis 1:11|the mouth that belieth, killeth the soul|Os enim quod mentitur, occidit animam]]. And the Psalmist says to God: [[Ps 5:7|thou wilt destroy all that speak a lie|Perdes omnes qui loquuntur mendacium]]. For although it is often lawful to keep silent about the truth, because of the wickedness of the hearers, or for the sake of one's own peace, or for some other devout or reasonable cause (according to that word of the Psalmist: [[Ps 38:2|I have set a guard to my mouth, when the sinner stood against me|Posui ori meo custodiam, dum consisteret peccator adversum me]]; [[Ps 38:3|I was dumb, and was humbled, and kept silence from good things|obmutui, et humiliatus sum, et silui a bonis]]), yet it is never lawful to deny the truth, though it may at times be hidden with devout caution. [[1:20|and he confessed|Et confessus est]]: That [quia, here meaning quod, introducing his words], [[1:20|I am not the Christ|non sum ego Christus]], that is, not the judge, not the bridegroom, not the Saviour, not the only-begotten Son of God, but the minister of Christ, the herald of the judge, the groomsman of the bridegroom, the forerunner of the Saviour, the minister of the Son of God. So the priests first asked John, explicitly or at least implicitly, whether he was the Christ; and therefore John answered either their words or their mind.

paras.t: Et interrogaverunt eum: Quid ergo es? et quid restat? Elias es tu? Putabant autem Judæi Joannem esse aliquem valde magnum. Quum ergo audissent quod non esset Christus, sciscitati sunt an esset Elias, qui fuit unus de maximis Sanctis veteris Testamenti. Multa vero induxerunt sacerdotes atque Judæos ad opinandum quod Joannes esset Elias, scilicet: solitaria vita, duritia vestium, zelus justitiæ contra Herodem. Omnia enim hæc in Elia fuerunt. Item, quoniam adventus Eliæ fuit Judæis promissus per Malachiam. Propter quod discipuli dixerunt Christo, apud Matthæum: Quomodo dicunt Pharisæi, quod Eliam oportet prius venire? Sed quoniam isti Judæi sciebant Joannem esse Zachariæ filium atque Elisabeth, circa triginta annos habentem, intra quos ex infante crevit in virum, mirum est quomodo interrogaverunt, an Joannes esset Elias, qui per tot centenos annos translatus fuit in paradisum, et rediturus est in forma ac statu virili. Et respondendum, quod multi Judæorum tunc, sicut et nunc, posuerunt animas transcorporari: sicque æstimare poterant quod Joannes esset Elias in alio corpore, sicut et multi eorum dixerunt quod Elias esset Phinees, propter zelum utriusque contra iniquos. Vel, sicut quidam dixerunt Jesum esse Eliam, aliique Jeremiam, aut unum ex Prophetis, sic isti æstimabant de Joanne.
paras.en: [[1:21|And they asked him: What then|Et interrogaverunt eum: Quid ergo]] art thou, and what remains? [[1:21|Art thou Elias|Elias es tu]]? For the Jews thought John to be someone very great. So when they had heard that he was not the Christ, they inquired whether he was Elias, who was one of the greatest Saints of the Old Testament. Many things led the priests and the Jews to suppose that John was Elias: namely his solitary life[[Luke 1:80||]], the roughness of his clothing[[Matt 3:4||]], his zeal for justice against Herod[[Matt 14:4||]]. For all these things were in Elias[[3 Kings 19:4||]][[4 Kings 1:8||]][[3 Kings 19:10||]]. Again, because the coming of Elias had been promised to the Jews through Malachias[[Mal 4:5||]]. That is why the disciples said to Christ, in Matthew: Why do the Pharisees say [[Matt 17:10|that Elias must come first|quod Eliam oportet prius venire]][[Mark 9:10||]]? But since these Jews knew that John was the son of Zachary and Elizabeth, about thirty years old, in which years he had grown from an infant into a man, it is a wonder how they asked whether John was Elias, who so many hundreds of years before had been translated into paradise[[4 Kings 2:11||]], and is to return in the form and state of a grown man[[Mal 4:5||]]. The answer is that many of the Jews then, as now, held that souls pass from body to body [transcorporari: the transmigration of souls]; and so they could think that John was Elias in another body, just as many of them said that Elias was Phinees, because of the zeal of each against the wicked[[Num 25:11||]][[3 Kings 19:10||]]. Or, just as some said that Jesus was Elias, and others [[Matt 16:14|Jeremias, or one of the prophets|Jeremiam, aut unum ex Prophetis]], so these thought of John.

paras.t: Et dixit: Non sum Elias in persona, quia non idem homo. Joannes tamen dici potest Elias, propter similitudinem operationis, parilitatem officii, conformitatem conversationis, sanctitatis et gratiæ cum Elia. Præcessit enim primum Christi adventum, sicut ille præcedet secundum; redarguit Herodem et Herodiadem, sicut ille Achab et Jezabel; uterque eremita; et in aliis multis conveniunt. Propter quod ait Christus discipulis: Elias jam venit, et si vultis scire, Joannes ipse est Elias. Hinc Gabriel de Joanne prædixit: Ipse præcedet ante illum in spiritu et virtute Eliæ.
paras.en: [[1:21|And he said: I am not|Et dixit: Non sum]] Elias in person, for he is not the same man. Yet John can be called Elias, because of the likeness of his work, the equality of his office, and the conformity of his manner of life, holiness and grace with Elias. For he went before the first coming of Christ, as the other will go before the second; he rebuked Herod and Herodias[[Matt 14:4||]], as the other did Achab and Jezabel[[3 Kings 21:20||]]; each was a hermit; and in many other things they agree. That is why Christ says to the disciples: [[Matt 17:12|Elias is already come|Elias jam venit]], and if you will know it, John himself [[Matt 11:14|is Elias|est Elias]]. Hence Gabriel foretold of John: [[Luke 1:17|he shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias|Ipse præcedet ante illum in spiritu et virtute Eliæ]].

paras.t: Tertio quæsierunt: Propheta es tu? Et respondit: Non. Aliqui dicunt, quod sacerdotes isti per prophetam, intellexerunt non simplicem vatem, sed Prophetam quemdam præcipuum, illum videlicet de quo Moyses scripsit in Deuteronomio: Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus de fratribus vestris tanquam me. Et dicunt, quod Judæi per istum Prophetam, intellexerunt non ipsum Christum, sed ejus præcursorem.
paras.en: Thirdly they asked: [[1:21|Art thou the prophet|Propheta es tu]]? [[1:21|And he answered: No|Et respondit: Non]] [these words of the text are printed in the margin]. Some say that by the prophet these priests understood not a simple seer, but a certain pre-eminent Prophet, namely the one of whom Moses wrote in Deuteronomy[[Deut 18:15||]]: [[Acts 3:22|A prophet shall the Lord your God raise up unto you of your brethren, like unto me|Prophetam suscitabit vobis Dominus de fratribus vestris tanquam me]] [Denis gives the words as Peter cites them in Acts]. And they say that by this Prophet the Jews understood not Christ Himself, but His forerunner.

paras.t: Hoc autem non videtur rationabiliter dictum. Joannes enim respondendo, dicit se non esse Prophetam illum de quo ipsi loquuntur. Si igitur ipsi nomine prophetæ, intelligunt Prophetam illum præcipuum, Christi præcessorem, negaret se esse quod veraciter erat. Et si quis dicat, quod negat se esse illum Prophetam de quo præallegata Scriptura loquitur, quæ ad litteram intelligenda est de Christo, tunc responsio Joannis non absolveret quæstionem interrogantium: imo ipse et illi laborarent in æquivocis. Illi enim, secundum istos, quæsierunt an esset præcipuus Propheta Christum præcessurus; et ipse, secundum istos, respondit se non esse Prophetam de quo Moyses loquitur, secundum veritatem, scilicet, quod non esset Christus: sicque illi per prophetam, intelligerent alium quam Joannes. Imo sic responsio ista Joannis non differret a prima, qua se dixit non esse Christum, quum tamen Joannes optime sciret quod sacerdotes in tertia quæstione, nomine prophetæ non intelligebant Christum. Denique ex textu præsenti elici nequit, quod sacerdotes intendebant quærere de Propheta illo præcipuo de quo Moyses fuit locutus, sed potius de aliquo Propheta inferiore Elia, quia paulatim descenderant. Non est etiam consuetudo Scripturæ novi vel veteris Testamenti, ut nomine prophetæ simpliciter pronuntiati, intelligatur ille Propheta præcipuus. Melius igitur reor, ut per prophetam, intelligatur quicumque Propheta indistincte, eo modo quo in veteri Testamento communiter fit sermo de propheta.
paras.en: But this does not seem reasonably said. For John in answering says that he is not that Prophet of whom they speak. If, then, by the name of prophet they understand that pre-eminent Prophet, the one who goes before Christ, he would be denying that he was what he truly was. And if someone says that he denies being that Prophet of whom the Scripture cited above speaks, which is to be understood literally of Christ, then John's answer would not settle the question of those asking: rather, he and they would be caught up in equivocation [that is, using one word in two different senses]. For according to these writers, they asked whether he was the pre-eminent Prophet who was to go before Christ; and he, according to them, answered that he was not the Prophet of whom Moses speaks in truth, namely, that he was not the Christ: and so by the prophet they would understand someone other than John did. Indeed, in that case this answer of John's would not differ from the first, in which he said he was not the Christ, although John knew perfectly well that the priests, in the third question, did not understand Christ by the name of prophet. Finally, it cannot be drawn from the present text that the priests meant to ask about that pre-eminent Prophet of whom Moses had spoken, but rather about some Prophet lower than Elias, since they had been coming down step by step. Nor is it the custom of the Scripture of the New or the Old Testament that by the name of prophet, said simply, that pre-eminent Prophet should be understood. I think it better, therefore, that by the prophet any Prophet whatever should be understood, without distinction, in the way that the Old Testament commonly speaks of a prophet.

paras.t: Sed tunc dubitatio oritur, quomodo Joannes neget se esse prophetam, quum certum sit ipsum fuisse prophetam, Zacharia testante: Tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis. Christus quoque vocat eum plus quam prophetam. Dicit enim de eo: Major inter natos mulierum propheta Joanne Baptista nemo est. Ex quibus patet quod fuit propheta. Ad hoc respondent Gregorius et Beda, quod quia Joannes fuit plus quam propheta, non solum futura de Christo prænuntiando, sed etiam Christum præsentialiter ostendendo, dum dixit, Ecce Agnus Dei; quantum ad id se negat prophetam, quo fuit plus quam propheta. Aliter dici potest, quod quia Joannes fuit medius inter Prophetas et Apostolos, et quasi horizon ac medius utriusque Testamenti, ita quod sua ultimata, formalis ac propria gratia gratis data, non fuit cum Prophetis veteris Testamenti Christum futurum in mundum prædicere, sed eum jam demonstrare, et cum Apostolis annuntiare quoniam venit, ideo negat se esse prophetam: non quia nequaquam propheta fuit, sed quoniam suum ultimatum, formale ac proprium officium, non fuit futura prædicere, sed Christum præcurrere, prædicando, baptizando, ejusque semitas disponendo. Unumquodque enim denominationem sortitur a sua formali et propria ratione. Potest quoque aliter dici, videlicet, quod Joannes dicit se non esse prophetam, eo modo quo ait Amos propheta: Non sum propheta: et quo modo Christus dicit in Psalmo, Ego autem sum vermis, et non homo.
paras.en: But then a doubt arises: how can John deny that he is a prophet, since it is certain that he was a prophet, as Zachary testifies: [[Luke 1:76|And thou, child, shalt be called the prophet of the Highest|Tu, puer, Propheta Altissimi vocaberis]]. Christ too calls him [[Matt 11:9|more than a prophet|plus quam prophetam]]. For He says of him: [[Luke 7:28|Amongst those that are born of men, there is not a greater prophet than John the Baptist|Major inter natos mulierum propheta Joanne Baptista nemo est]]. From which it is plain that he was a prophet. To this Gregory and Bede answer that, since John was more than a prophet, not only foretelling things to come concerning Christ but also showing Christ present, when he said, [[1:29|Behold the Lamb of God|Ecce Agnus Dei]], he denies that he is a prophet in that respect in which he was more than a prophet. It can be put another way: John was midway between the Prophets and the Apostles, a kind of horizon, as it were, standing between the two Testaments, so that his final, formal and proper gratia gratis data [a grace freely given, that is, a gift such as prophecy, granted for the good of others rather than for the holiness of the one who receives it] was not, as with the Prophets of the Old Testament, to foretell that Christ would come into the world, but to point Him out as already here and, with the Apostles, to announce that He had come; therefore he denies that he is a prophet: not because he was in no way a prophet, but because his final, formal and proper office was not to foretell things to come, but to run before Christ, by preaching, by baptizing, and by preparing His paths. For each thing takes its name from its formal and proper character [ratio]. It can also be put another way: John says he is not a prophet in the way that the prophet Amos says: [[Amos 7:14|I am not a prophet|Non sum propheta]]; and in the way that Christ says in the Psalm: [[Ps 21:7|But I am a worm, and no man|Ego autem sum vermis, et non homo]].

paras.t: Dixerunt ergo ei: Quis es, id est cujus auctoritatis, gratiæ, vel officii? Non enim quærebant solum quis esset per naturam sive personam, sed quis esset per gratiam et missionem divinam. Ut responsum demus his qui miserunt nos ad te ad hunc finem, ut reportaremus eis certam responsionem de hoc quis sis: et frivolum esset nos sine absolutione quæstionum et affirmativa responsione reverti. Quid dicis de te ipso? qui tantæ excellentiæ es, ut proprio testimonio tuo de te ipso prolato credendum sit: quamvis secundum communem legem, homo non reputetur idoneus testis de se ipso, nisi forte cum juramento. Unde infra Judæi dicunt ad Christum: Tu de te ipso testimonium perhibes, testimonium tuum non est verum. Hinc Paulus ad Corinthios, quum sibi ipsi et propriæ gratiæ testimonium perhibuisset propria bona describendo, adjecit: Factus sum insipiens, vos me coegistis.
paras.en: [[1:22|They said therefore unto him: Who art thou|Dixerunt ergo ei: Quis es]], that is, of what authority, grace or office? For they were not asking only who he was by nature or person, but who he was by grace and by divine mission. [[1:22|that we may give an answer to them that sent us|Ut responsum demus his qui miserunt nos]] to thee for this end, that we should bring back to them a sure answer about who thou art: and it would be idle for us to return without the questions settled and without an answer that says what thou art. [[1:22|What sayest thou of thyself|Quid dicis de te ipso]]? who art of such excellence that thy own testimony, given of thyself, is to be believed: although by the common law a man is not reckoned a fit witness concerning himself, unless perhaps on oath. Hence later on the Jews say to Christ: [[John 8:13|Thou givest testimony of thyself. Thy testimony is not true|Tu de te ipso testimonium perhibes, testimonium tuum non est verum]]. Hence Paul, writing to the Corinthians, when he had borne witness to himself and to his own grace by describing the good things he had, added: [[2 Cor 12:11|I am become foolish. You have compelled me|Factus sum insipiens, vos me coegistis]].

paras.t: Ait Joannes sacerdotibus et Levitis ad se missis: Ego vox, per proprietatem, non per essentiam, id est præco et vociferator, clamantis, id est Christi vel Spiritus Sancti per me loquentis, in deserto, hoc est solitudine Judææ, in qua habitavit ac prædicavit Joannes. Dicitur autem Joannes vox, secundum Gregorium, quia sicut vox præcedit verbum, ut audiatur, sic Joannes præcessit Christum, ut cognosceretur. Sed quum verbum et vox sint idem realiter, quomodo vox dicitur verbum præcedere? Dicendum, quod Christus est verbum intellectuale. Quemadmodum ergo in nobis vox oris præcedit verbum mentis, ut audiatur, sic Joannes Christum præcessit. Vel dicendum, quod licet verbum oris et vox idem sint, vox tamen præcedit hoc verbum, secundum rationem, eo modo quo, secundum auctorem libri Causarum, genus præcedit speciem. Secundo, Joannes Baptista appellatur vox Christi, quoniam sicut vox rem ipsam significat, sic Joannes Christum ostendit. Tertio, propter efficaciam suæ prædicationis, altæ atque tubalis, qua Christo testimonium perhibebat. Unde vocatur non solum prænuntiator, sed etiam vox Christi, sicut de homine multum dilecto dicimus, Amor meus.
paras.en: [[1:23|He said|Ait]], John, to the priests and Levites sent to him: [[1:23|I am the voice|Ego vox]], by a property, not by essence [that is, he is called a voice from what he does, not because that is what he is], that is, the herald and crier, [[1:23|of one crying|clamantis]], that is, of Christ or of the Holy Ghost speaking through me, [[1:23|in the wilderness|in deserto]], that is, the desert of Judea, in which John lived and preached. John is called a voice, according to Gregory, because just as the voice goes before the word, so that it may be heard, so John went before Christ, so that He might be known. But since the word and the voice are really the same thing, how is the voice said to go before the word? The answer is that Christ is the word of the intellect. As, then, in us the voice of the mouth goes before the word of the mind, so that it may be heard, so John went before Christ. Or the answer is that although the word of the mouth and the voice are the same thing, yet the voice goes before this word in concept [secundum rationem: in the order of thought, not in reality], in the way that, according to the author of the Book of Causes [the Liber de causis], the genus goes before the species. Secondly, John the Baptist is called the voice of Christ because, as the voice signifies the thing itself, so John showed Christ. Thirdly, because of the power of his preaching, loud and like a trumpet, by which he bore witness to Christ. So he is called not only the one who announced Christ beforehand, but even the voice of Christ, as we say of a man much loved, My love.

paras.t: Quid autem Christus clamaverit per Joannem, subjungitur: Dirigite viam Domini, id est, recte et vere exercete opera bona, et sancta desideria in vobis habete, per quæ Deus ingreditur cor humanum: hoc est, vitiorum obliquitates fugite, vos ipsos ad gratiam præparate, atque ad Christi prædicationem ac fidem mentes vestras disponite; sicut dixit, hoc est de me prophetavit, Isaias propheta, qui prædixit de me quod essem futurus vox clamantis, etc. Prædicationem istam Joannis Baptistæ, evangelista Joannes non prosequitur, quam Matthæus et Lucas plenius prosequuntur.
paras.en: What Christ cried out through John is then added: [[1:23|make straight the way of the Lord|Dirigite viam Domini]], that is, do good works rightly and truly, and have holy desires in you, through which God enters the human heart: that is, flee the crookedness of vices, prepare yourselves for grace, and dispose your minds to the preaching of Christ and to faith in Him; [[1:23|as said|sicut dixit]], that is, as prophesied of me, [[1:23|the prophet Isaias|Isaias propheta]], who foretold of me that I would be [[Is 40:3|The voice of one crying|vox clamantis]], etc. This preaching of John the Baptist the Evangelist John does not set out; Matthew and Luke set it out more fully[[Matt 3:1||]][[Luke 3:3||]].

paras.t: Et qui missi fuerant, id est prædicti sacerdotes atque Levitæ, erant ex Pharisæis, hoc est de numero Pharisæorum, imo et Pharisæi: ex quo patet quod erant solennissimi nuntii. Triplici quippe exsistente secta inter Judæos (videlicet: Essæorum, qui rigorosissimam, castam et sobriam vitam duxerunt; Sadducæorum, qui dixerunt animas hominum esse mortales, et nec angelum, nec spiritum, nec resurrectionem esse; ac Pharisæorum, qui posuerunt animas immortales, et futuram esse resurrectionem universalem, et spirituales esse substantias), secta Pharisæorum, de qua et Paulus se fuisse testatur, erat famosior. Videbantur enim specialem zelum legis habere, et religiose incedere. Aliqui autem sacerdotes, Levitæ ac Scribæ, fuerant Pharisæi, sicut nunc multi sacerdotes, clerici et doctores, sunt claustrales seu religiosi.
paras.en: [[1:24|And they that were sent|Et qui missi fuerant]], that is, the aforesaid priests and Levites, [[1:24|were of the Pharisees|erant ex Pharisæis]], that is, of the number of the Pharisees, nay, Pharisees themselves: from which it is plain that they were envoys of the highest dignity. For there being three sects among the Jews (namely: the Essenes, who led a most austere, chaste and sober life; the Sadducees, who said that the souls of men are mortal, and that there is neither angel, nor spirit, nor resurrection[[Acts 23:8||]]; and the Pharisees, who held that souls are immortal, and that there will be a general resurrection, and that there are spiritual substances[[Acts 23:8||]]), the sect of the Pharisees, to which Paul too testifies that he belonged[[Acts 23:6||]], was the more famous. For they seemed to have a special zeal for the Law, and to walk religiously. And some of the priests, Levites and Scribes were Pharisees, just as now many priests, clerics and doctors are cloistered men, that is, religious.

paras.t: Præterea advertendum, quod secundum sanctos doctores communiter, Gregorium, Chrysostomum, Bedam, et alios, nuntii isti insidianter ac malitiose interrogaverunt Joannem, quærentes occasionem adversus eum. Ad quod insinuandum, asserunt nunc dixisse Evangelistam: Et qui missi fuerant, erant ex Pharisæis. Pharisæi namque, quamvis foris sanctitatem prætenderunt, intus tamen replebantur hypocrisi, ambitione atque invidia. Origenes vero dicit, quod simplici animo quæsierunt, optantes veritatem agnoscere: Primo, quoniam dictum est nunc, quod ex dubitatione moti sunt ad interrogandum. Secundo, quoniam tam magnifice senserunt de Joanne, quod suspicabantur eum esse Christum. Tertio, quoniam maximam reverentiam ei exhibuerunt in ipso interrogationis processu. Quarto, quia Judæi communiter primo multum bene senserunt de Joanne, scientes mirabilem ejus nativitatem, atque sanctissimam vitam. Unde et apud Marcum habetur, quod exibat ad eum omnis Judææ regio, et Jerosolymitæ universi, et baptizabantur ab eo. Sed et in Matthæo legitur, quod multi Pharisæorum veniebant ad baptismum Joannis. Postremo, quia Joannes fuit de genere sacerdotali, et magni sacerdotis filius, non apparet quod sacerdotes prima facie insidiati sint ei: imo, si Joannes dixisset se esse Christum, aliud nihil videtur nisi quod credidissent sic esse. Quod ergo ait Evangelista, Et qui missi fuerant, additum est ad innuendum solennitatem ac idoneitatem nuntiorum.
paras.en: Further, it is to be noted that according to the holy doctors generally, Gregory, Chrysostom, Bede and others, these envoys questioned John insidiously and with malice, seeking an occasion against him. To hint at this, they say, the Evangelist has now said: [[1:24|And they that were sent were of the Pharisees|Et qui missi fuerant, erant ex Pharisæis]]. For the Pharisees, though they made an outward show of holiness, were within full of hypocrisy, ambition and envy. But Origen says that they asked with a simple mind, wishing to know the truth. First, because it has just been said that they were moved to ask by doubt. Secondly, because they thought so highly of John that they suspected him to be the Christ. Thirdly, because they showed him the greatest reverence in the very course of their questioning. Fourthly, because the Jews generally thought very well of John at first, knowing of his wondrous birth and most holy life. Hence in Mark too we have it that [[Mark 1:5|there went out to him all the country of Judea and all they of Jerusalem and were baptized by him|exibat ad eum omnis Judææ regio, et Jerosolymitæ universi, et baptizabantur ab eo]]. And in Matthew too we read that many of the Pharisees came to John's baptism[[Matt 3:7||]]. Lastly, since John was of priestly stock, and the son of a great priest, it does not appear that the priests laid snares for him at first sight; nay, had John said that he was the Christ, it seems they would have done nothing else than believe it to be so. What the Evangelist says, then, [[1:24|And they that were sent|Et qui missi fuerant]], was added to suggest the dignity and fitness of the envoys.

paras.t: Et interrogaverunt eum, et dixerunt ei: Quid ergo baptizas, id est, homines in aquis Jordanis lavas, si tu non es Christus, neque Elias, neque propheta? id est, cur novum ritum præsumis inducere, si non es aliquis horum? Nullus enim ante Joannem ausus est baptizare. Unde Judæi videntes Joannem aliquid novi inducere, voluerunt scire qua auctoritate hoc faceret: et nunc, quia se dixit non esse Christum, neque Eliam, neque prophetam, incipiunt eum de præsumptione notare.
paras.en: [[1:25|And they asked him and said to him: Why then dost thou baptize|Et interrogaverunt eum, et dixerunt ei: Quid ergo baptizas]], that is, wash men in the waters of the Jordan, [[1:25|if thou be not Christ, nor Elias, nor the prophet?|si tu non es Christus, neque Elias, neque propheta?]] that is, why dost thou presume to bring in a new rite, if thou art none of these? For no one before John had dared to baptize. Hence the Jews, seeing John bring in something new, wished to know by what authority he did it; and now, since he has said that he is not the Christ, nor Elias, nor the prophet, they begin to tax him with presumption.

paras.t: Respondit eis Joannes dicens: Ego baptizo in aqua, id est, exterius lavo corpora vestra, non intus purgo a culpa, nec gratiam præsto; medius autem vestrum stetit, id est, inter vos apparere, conversari, et communiter vivere dignatus est, quem vos non scitis, id est, non cognoscitis esse Christum, Filium Dei, quamvis forte sciatis quod sit filius Mariæ. Non enim agnoverant Christum secundum suam divinitatem, nec etiam secundum suam humanitatem, per comparationem ad unionem cum Verbo, atque ad cetera Spiritus Sancti charismata.
paras.en: [[1:26|John answered them, saying: I baptize with water|Respondit eis Joannes dicens: Ego baptizo in aqua]], that is, I wash your bodies outwardly; I do not cleanse within from guilt, nor bestow grace; [[1:26|but there hath stood one in the midst of you|medius autem vestrum stetit]], that is, He has deigned to appear among you, to converse with you and to live in common with you, [[1:26|whom you know not|quem vos non scitis]], that is, whom you do not recognise to be the Christ, the Son of God, though perhaps you know that He is the son of Mary. For they had not known Christ according to His divinity, nor even according to His humanity as regards its union with the Word and the other gifts of the Holy Ghost.

paras.t: Quæritur, quomodo Christus stetit medius horum, vel inter hos medius fuit, qui forsitan nunquam fuit inter nuntios istos, sacerdotes et Levitas. Dicendum, quod Christus secundum suam deitatem stat, id est, firmiter invariabiliterque subsistit, medius omnium, quia in omnibus est. Dicitur enim stare, juxta illud in Psalmo: Deus stetit in synagoga deorum. Et Isaias ait: Stat ad judicandum Dominus. Porro, secundum humanitatem, stetit Christus medius horum dupliciter: Primo, quia in terra et populo eorum communiter vixit. Secundo, quia singulis annis ascendit Jerosolymam in solennitate paschali, secundum legem, intravitque templum, et ibi inter sacerdotes et alios stetit in templo. Nam et quum esset annorum duodecim, inventus est in templo in medio doctorum. Sed non videtur Jesus corporaliter adfuisse, et inter istos stetisse, quando locutus est hæc verba Joannes.
paras.en: It is asked how Christ stood in the midst of these men, or was in the midst among them, when perhaps He was never among these envoys, the priests and Levites. The answer is that Christ, according to His Godhead, stands, that is, subsists firmly and unchangeably, in the midst of all things, because He is in all things. For He is said to stand, according to that in the Psalm: [[Ps 81:1|God hath stood in the congregation of gods|Deus stetit in synagoga deorum]]. And Isaias says: [[Is 3:13|The Lord standeth up to judge|Stat ad judicandum Dominus]]. Moreover, according to His humanity, Christ stood in their midst in two ways. First, because He lived in common in their land and among their people. Secondly, because every year He went up to Jerusalem at the paschal solemnity, according to the Law, and entered the temple, and there stood among the priests and others in the temple. For when He was twelve years old, too, He was found in the temple in the midst of the doctors[[Luke 2:42||]][[Luke 2:46||]]. But it does not seem that Jesus was bodily present, standing among these men, when John spoke these words.

paras.t: Ipse quem vos non scitis, videlicet Christus, est qui post me venturus est, qui ante me factus est. Hoc jam paulo ante expositum est. Cujus ego non sum dignus, id est, cujus præsentia et famulatu dignus non sum in minimis rebus, videlicet, ut solvam ejus corrigiam calceamenti, id est, in rebus corporalibus et vilibus ei deserviam. Improportionabiliter namque fuit Christus major Joanne Baptista. Multo minus dignus sum ipsum contingere, vel ejus nomine appellari seu æstimari quod ego sim ille, videlicet Christus. Matthæus et Lucas plenius recitant verba Joannis Baptistæ. Nam præinductis verbis suis, adjecit de Christo: Ipse vos baptizabit Spiritu Sancto et igni. Quæ verba apud Matthæum, prout Dominus dedit, diligenter exposui.
paras.en: [[1:27|The same|Ipse]] [[1:26|whom you know not|quem vos non scitis]], namely Christ, [[1:27|is he that shall come after me, who is preferred before me|est qui post me venturus est, qui ante me factus est]]. This has already been explained a little earlier. [[1:27|whose shoe I am not worthy|Cujus ego non sum dignus]], that is, of whose presence and service I am not worthy in the least things, namely, [[1:27|to loose|ut solvam]] [[1:27|the latchet|ejus corrigiam calceamenti]] of His shoe, that is, to serve Him in bodily and lowly things. For Christ was greater than John the Baptist beyond all proportion. Much less am I worthy to touch Him, or to be called by His name, or to be thought to be He, namely the Christ. Matthew[[Matt 3:11||]][[Matt 3:12||]] and Luke[[Luke 3:16||]][[Luke 3:17||]] give the words of John the Baptist more fully [the margin's second reference prints only "iii, 16, 17", evidently Luke 3:16–17]. For after the words set down here, he added of Christ: [[Matt 3:11|he shall baptize you in the Holy Ghost and fire|Ipse vos baptizabit Spiritu Sancto et igni]]. These words I have carefully explained on Matthew, as the Lord granted.

paras.t: Prædictis itaque verbis Joannes Baptista satisfecit quæstioni Judæorum. Dicens enim se esse vocem Domini, quemadmodum Isaias prænuntiavit, et quod Dominus, cujus ipse vox fuit, tantum excelleret eum quod non esset dignus solvere corrigiam calceamenti ejus, fassus est se esse Christi præcursorem. Item, dicendo quod baptizaret in aqua dumtaxat, ostendit insufficientiam sui baptismi, ita quod sicut prædicando disponebat homines ad Christi prædicationem salubriter audiendam, sic baptizando disponebat ad suscipiendum Christi Baptisma: Primo, quoniam susceptio baptismi Joannis fuit quædam professio credendi in Christum. Baptizavit namque in nomine Christi venturi. Secundo, quoniam qui baptizabantur a Joanne, confitebantur sua peccata: sicque aptabantur ad fidem et gratiam Christi. Tertio, quia Joannes baptizando congregavit populum multum, et ita potuit pluribus annuntiare Christi adventum. Hanc rationem ipsemet sanctus Baptista post pauca commemorat, sicut patebit. Patet ergo quod Joannes baptizando, non usurpavit indebitum sibi officium, sed ejus inspiratione hoc fecit quem præcurrebat.
paras.en: By the aforesaid words, then, John the Baptist answered the question of the Jews. For in saying that he was the voice of the Lord, as Isaias foretold[[Is 40:3||]], and that the Lord, whose voice he was, so far excelled him that he was not worthy to loose the latchet of His shoe, he confessed himself to be the forerunner of Christ. Again, by saying that he baptized only in water, he showed the insufficiency of his baptism; so that, as by preaching he disposed men to hear Christ's preaching to their salvation[[Matt 3:1||]], so by baptizing he disposed them to receive Christ's Baptism. First, because the receiving of John's baptism was a kind of profession of belief in Christ; for he baptized in the name of the Christ who was to come[[Acts 19:4||]]. Secondly, because those who were baptized by John confessed their sins[[Matt 3:6||]], and so were made fit for the faith and grace of Christ. Thirdly, because by baptizing John gathered a great multitude[[Matt 3:5||]], and so was able to announce Christ's coming to many. This reason the holy Baptist himself mentions a little further on, as will appear[[1:31||]]. It is plain, then, that in baptizing John did not usurp an office not due to him, but did this by the inspiration of Him whose forerunner he was.

paras.t: Denique, quod ait Joannes se esse indignum ad solvendum cingulum calceamentorum Christi, non est sic intelligendum, quod Christus tulerit calceamenta. Ipse enim cœpit facere et docere. Ipse vero discipulis jussit ne calceis uterentur, ut legitur in Matthæo. Sed Joannes conformat se communi modo loquendi, quo aliquis volens se multum humiliare sub alio, asserit se indignum ad solvendum ligaturam calceorum ipsius.
paras.en: Lastly, when John says that he is unworthy to loose the strap of Christ's shoes, this is not to be understood as though Christ wore shoes. For He [[Acts 1:1|began to do and to teach|cœpit facere et docere]] [that is, He first practised what He taught]; and He bade His disciples not to wear shoes, as we read in Matthew[[Matt 10:10||]]. But John conforms himself to the common way of speaking, by which one who wishes to humble himself greatly beneath another declares himself unworthy to undo the fastening of his shoes.

paras.t: Sed quomodo Joannes fuit indignus ad hoc, qui dignus fuit Christum baptizare? Et quum homo exsistens in gratia mereatur de condigno vitam æternam, hoc est claram et immediatam divinæ essentiæ visionem, ita quod dignus fit Divinitati fruendo uniri, quomodo Joannes non fuit dignus Christo in corporalibus ministrare? Et respondendum dupliciter: Primo, quod loquendo de Joanne secundum sua naturalia tantum, non fuit dignus Christum baptizare, vel ei in minimo ministrare, propter infinitam dignitatem Christi secundum suam deitatem, et propter plenitudinem gratiæ suæ humanitatis: et sic loquitur de se Joannes. Vel loquitur de se, secundum quod aliquo modo fuit peccator, quantum ad venialia minutissima: juxta quem modum Paulus, Non sum (inquit) dignus vocari apostolus. Loquendo autem de Joanne secundum magnitudinem gratiæ sibi collatæ, dignus fuit ad hæc, præsertim ob suam profundissimam humilitatem. Secundo dicendum, quod aliquis dicitur dignus per comparationem ad Christum, dupliciter: Primo, simpliciter: sic Joannes ad ista dignus non exstitit. Secundo, juxta modum humanæ conditionis ac possibilitatis: sic Joannes dignus erat ad ista. Imo sic homo dignus est corpus Christi consecrare et manducare. Aliter omnes damnaremur, dicente Apostolo: Quicumque manducaverit corpus Domini indigne, judicium sibi manducat, et reus erit corporis Domini. Hoc modo Virgo benedicta digna fuit Filium Dei concipere et lactare. Sic quoque justus dignus est vita æterna. Et videtur dignitas ista fundari in quadam benevola acceptatione voluntatis divinæ, qua libere voluit homines taliter dignificari per gratiam.
paras.en: But how was John unworthy of this, who was worthy to baptize Christ? And since a man in grace merits eternal life de condigno [that is, by condign merit, merit in the strict sense, and not merely by fittingness], that is, the clear and immediate vision of the divine essence, so that he becomes worthy to be united to the Godhead in enjoying it, how was John not worthy to minister to Christ in bodily things? The answer is twofold. First, speaking of John according to his natural endowments alone, he was not worthy to baptize Christ, or to minister to Him in the least thing, because of the infinite dignity of Christ according to His Godhead, and because of the fulness of grace of His humanity; and it is in this way that John speaks of himself. Or he speaks of himself inasmuch as he was in some way a sinner, as regards the slightest venial sins; in which way Paul says: I am [[1 Cor 15:9|not worthy to be called an apostle|Non sum (inquit) dignus vocari apostolus]]. But speaking of John according to the greatness of the grace conferred on him, he was worthy of these things, especially because of his most profound humility. Secondly, it must be said that someone is called worthy in comparison with Christ in two ways. First, simply; and so John was not worthy of these things. Secondly, according to the measure of the human condition and of human capability; and so John was worthy of them. Nay, in this way a man is worthy to consecrate and to eat the body of Christ; otherwise we should all be damned, since the Apostle says: [[1 Cor 11:27|whosoever shall eat|Quicumque manducaverit]] the body of the Lord unworthily, eateth [[1 Cor 11:29|judgment to himself|judicium sibi manducat]], and [[1 Cor 11:27|shall be guilty of the body|reus erit corporis]] of the Lord. In this way the blessed Virgin was worthy to conceive and to suckle the Son of God. So too the just man is worthy of eternal life. And this worthiness seems to be founded on a certain benevolent acceptance on the part of the divine will, by which God freely willed that men should be made worthy in this way through grace.

paras.t: In omnibus his commendatur et imitanda relinquitur nobis eximia humilitas S. Joannis, qui quum tantæ sanctitatis reputationisque esset ut Christus putaretur, se ipsum profundissime humiliavit. Noverat enim scriptum: Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus, et invenies gratiam coram Deo et hominibus. Noverat quod homo tanto sit coram Deo sublimior, quanto in oculis propriis fuerit vilior atque declivior. Et si Joannes reputavit se indignum solvere corrigiam calceamentorum Christi, quum esset amicus paranymphusque Sponsi, consanguineus Domini, et breviter, talis ac tantus quod inter natos mulierum non fuerit major eo: quomodo nos pusilli, tam irreverenter, et intimorate, et inaffectuose accedimus venerandum Dei altare, et Christum consecramus aut sumimus? Humiliemur igitur sub potenti manu Dei: et faciamus quidquid præceptum est nobis et quidquid valemus, tuncque ex corde dicamus, Servi inutiles sumus; et Christi sacramentis cum omni puritate ac reverentia propinquemus. Præstet hoc mihi et ceteris indigentibus Christus.
paras.en: In all these things the surpassing humility of St John is commended to us and left for our imitation: who, though he was of such holiness and repute that he was thought to be the Christ, humbled himself most profoundly. For he knew that it is written: [[Ecclus 3:20|The greater thou art, the more humble thyself in all things, and thou shalt find grace before God|Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus, et invenies gratiam coram Deo]] and men[[Ecclus 10:7||]] [the margin also cites Ecclus 10:7, where the words "before God and men" occur]. He knew that a man is the higher before God, the viler and lowlier he is in his own eyes. And if John reckoned himself unworthy to loose the latchet of Christ's shoes, though he was the friend and groomsman of the Bridegroom, a kinsman of the Lord, and, in short, such and so great that [[Matt 11:11|among them that are born of women|inter natos mulierum]] there was none greater than he: how do we little ones approach the venerable altar of God, and consecrate or receive Christ, so irreverently, so fearlessly and so coldly? Let us be humbled, therefore, [[1 Pet 5:6|under the mighty hand of God|sub potenti manu Dei]]; and let us do whatever is commanded us and whatever we are able, and then say from the heart: [[Luke 17:10|We are unprofitable servants|Servi inutiles sumus]] [the margin prints Luc. xv; the words are those of Luke 17:10]; and let us draw near to the sacraments of Christ with all purity and reverence. May Christ grant this to me and to the others who are in need.

paras.t: Mystice per calceamenta, intelligitur Christi humanitas a Verbo induta; per pedem, divinitas humanitate tecta quodammodo et velata; per corrigiam vero, unio utriusque. Joannes ergo non fuit dignus corrigiam calceamentorum pedis Christi dissolvere, quia non potuit perfecte mysterium Incarnationis, seu modum hypostaticæ unionis humanæ naturæ cum Verbo, explicare. Imo hoc excedit intellectum non solum omnium viatorum, sed et angelicorum spirituum.
paras.en: Mystically, by the shoes is understood the humanity of Christ, put on by the Word; by the foot, the divinity, in a manner covered and veiled by the humanity; and by the latchet, the union of the two. John, then, was not worthy to undo the latchet of the shoes of Christ's foot, because he could not perfectly unfold the mystery of the Incarnation, or the manner of the hypostatic union [the union of the two natures in the one Person of the Word] of human nature with the Word. Nay, this surpasses the understanding not only of all wayfarers [viatores: those still on their pilgrimage in this life], but even of the angelic spirits.

paras.t: Hæc, scilicet interrogatio Judæorum, et responsio testificatioque Joannis de Christo, in Bethania facta sunt trans Jordanem, hoc est in illa Bethania quæ est ultra Jordanem, in terra duarum tribuum ac dimidiæ. Estque Bethania illa supra Jordanem sita. Ubi erat Joannes baptizans, non in Bethania, sed in aquis prope currentibus. Hoc dicitur, ad differentiam alterius Bethaniæ citra Jordanem, in qua Martha, Maria et Lazarus commorati sunt. Verumtamen, secundum Origenem, textus vitio scriptorum corruptus est, quia, ut asserit, sic textus haberet: Hæc in Bethabora facta sunt.
paras.en: [[1:28|These things|Hæc]], namely the questioning of the Jews and John's answer and testimony concerning Christ, [[1:28|were done in Bethania, beyond the Jordan|in Bethania facta sunt trans Jordanem]], that is, in that Bethania which is on the far side of the Jordan, in the land of the two tribes and a half. And that Bethania is situated on the Jordan. [[1:28|where John was baptizing|Ubi erat Joannes baptizans]]: not in Bethania, but in the waters flowing close by. This is said to distinguish it from the other Bethania, on this side of the Jordan, in which Martha, Mary and Lazarus dwelt[[John 11:1||]]. However, according to Origen, the text has been corrupted by the fault of scribes, since, as he asserts, the text should read: These things were done in Bethabora [the place usually called Bethabara].

20.title: PROSECUTIO EXPOSITIONIS PRÆSENTIS VICESIMI CAPITULI : QUUM SERO ESSET DIE ILLA, UNA SABBATORUM.
20.title_en: Continuation of the exposition of this twentieth chapter: When it was late that same day, the first of the week

paras.t: HOC loco describit Evangelista quintam Christi apparitionem, factam in die Paschæ, et etiam sextam, quæ facta est præsente Thoma, in octava Paschæ. Quinquies enim apparuit Christus in die Paschæ : Primo, Magdalenæ, quemadmodum in Marco legitur : Surgens Jesus mane prima sabbati, apparuit primo Mariæ Magdalene. Secundo, mulieribus redeuntibus a sepulcro, juxta illud Matthæi : Ecce Jesus occurrit illis, dicens, Avete. Tertio, Petro, quamvis locus ignoretur; creditur tamen quod redeunti a monumento. Quarto, duobus discipulis euntibus in Emmaus, secundum quod recitat Lucas. Quinto, undecim Apostolis in conclavi, sicut nunc contestatur Joannes.
paras.en: In this place the Evangelist describes the fifth appearance of Christ, made on the day of the Pasch, and also the sixth, which was made with Thomas present, on the octave of the Pasch. For Christ appeared five times on the day of the Pasch. First, to Magdalen, as is read in Mark: [[Mark 16:9|But he rising early the first day of the week, appeared first to Mary Magdalen|Surgens Jesus mane prima sabbati, apparuit primo Mariæ Magdalene]]. Second, to the women returning from the sepulchre, according to that of Matthew: [[Matt 28:9|behold, Jesus met them, saying: All hail|Ecce Jesus occurrit illis, dicens, Avete]]. Third, to Peter[[Luke 24:34||]][[1 Cor 15:5||]], though the place is unknown; yet it is believed that it was as he returned from the tomb. Fourth, to the two disciples going to Emmaus, as Luke recounts[[Luke 24:13||]]. Fifth, to the eleven Apostles in the closed room, as John now bears witness.

paras.t: Quum sero esset, hoc est hora vespertina, et nocte incipiente, die illa, in qua apparuit Magdalenæ, una sabbatorum, id est, quæ dies fuit una dierum illius hebdomadæ, qui omnes dicebantur sabbata, quia festivi, et fores, id est januæ, essent clausæ, ubi erant discipuli, hoc est Apostoli, et etiam alii, secundum Lucam, congregati propter metum Judæorum : in quo patet eorum infirmitas, qui timebant eos qui corpus potuerunt occidere. Dicunt quidam, quod Apostoli erant dispersi in die propter metum Judæorum, sed de sero conveniebant ad locum unum. Evangelista vero nunc dicit, quod erant congregati propter metum prædictum. Lucas quoque habet, quod mulieres regressæ a monumento, nuntiaverunt quæ audierunt illis undecim : quod fuit clara die, quia post hoc Petrus et Joannes cucurrerunt ad monumentum. Ex quibus patet, quod discipuli etiam in die sederunt collecti januis clausis, propter metum Judæorum : imo minus audebant exire diebus quam noctibus.
paras.en: [[20:19|Now when it was late|Cum ergo sero esset]], that is, at the evening hour, as night was beginning, [[20:19|the same day|die illo]], on which He appeared to Magdalen, [[20:19|the first of the week|una sabbatorum]], that is, the day which was one of the days of that week, all of which were called sabbaths because they were festal, [[20:19|and the doors were shut, where the disciples were|et fores essent clausæ, ubi erant discipuli]], that is, the Apostles, and others too, according to Luke[[Luke 24:33||]], [[20:19|gathered together, for fear of the Jews|congregati propter metum Judæorum]]: in which their weakness is plain, who feared those who could kill the body[[Matt 10:28||]]. Some say that the Apostles were scattered by day for fear of the Jews, but in the evening came together to one place. But the Evangelist now says that they were gathered together for the said fear. Luke also has it that the women, returning from the tomb, told what they had heard to the eleven[[Luke 24:9||]]: which was in broad day, since after this Peter and John ran to the tomb[[Luke 24:12||]]. From which it is plain that the disciples sat gathered with the doors shut even by day, for fear of the Jews: indeed they dared go out less by day than by night.

paras.t: Venit Jesus ostio clauso, per penetrationem dimensionum. Corpora enim glorificata omnia penetrant per dotem subtilitatis, secundum quosdam : non tamen sine grandi miraculo, prout Thomas super quartum Sententiarum satis demonstrat. Quemadmodum igitur Jesus exivit uterum Matris, ea integra remanente, sic intravit et exiit domum non apertam, divina omnipotente virtute. Et stetit in medio discipulorum. Ipse namque est mediator, doctor reconciliatorque noster, ideo competebat ei esse in medio, sicut et ante passionem locutus est : Ego in medio vestrum sum. Magister quippe virtutum, medium semper elegit, quia in medio virtus consistit. Quomodo autem factum sit quod nunc refert Joannes, Lucas plenius edocet : quo legitur, quod quum Jesus cognitus fuisset a duobus discipulis in fractione panis, et disparuisset, illi surgentes regressi sunt in Jerusalem eadem hora, inveneruntque undecim congregatos, et eos qui cum illis erant, quibus dixerunt quomodo Jesus apparuisset eis in via, et qualiter eum cognoverunt : quibus ista narrantibus, venit Jesus, et stetit in medio discipulorum.
paras.en: [[20:19|Jesus came|venit Jesus]] with the door shut, by penetration of dimensions [[that is, two bodies occupying the same place]]. For glorified bodies penetrate all things by the endowment of subtlety, according to some: yet not without a great miracle, as Thomas amply shows on the fourth book of the Sentences. As therefore Jesus came forth from His Mother's womb while she remained intact, so He entered and left the unopened house by the almighty power of God. [[20:19|And stood in the midst|et stetit in medio]] of the disciples. For He is our mediator, teacher and reconciler, and so it befitted Him to be in the midst, as He also said before the passion: [[Luke 22:27|I am in the midst of you|Ego in medio vestrum sum]]. For the Master of the virtues always chose the mean, since virtue consists in the mean. How what John now relates came about, Luke teaches more fully: where it is read that when Jesus had been known by the two disciples in the breaking of bread and had vanished[[Luke 24:30||]], they rose up and returned to Jerusalem the same hour, and found the eleven gathered together, [[Luke 24:33|and those that were with them|et eos qui cum illis erant]], to whom they told how Jesus had appeared to them on the way and how they knew Him[[Luke 24:35||]]: and as they were telling these things, Jesus came and stood in the midst of the disciples[[Luke 24:36||]].

paras.t: Et dixit eis : Pax vobis. Quod docuit Christus, hoc fecit. Præcepit autem discipulis : In quamcumque domum intraveritis, primum dicite : Pax huic domui. Hinc ipse domum ingrediens in qua erant carissimi sui electissimique discipuli, ait : Pax vobis. Rursus, sic eos salutavit, quoniam paulo ante, in qua nocte tradebatur, disseruit : Pacem relinquo vobis. Quod igitur tunc reliquit, nunc attulit, dedit et auxit. Discipuli quoque pace maxime indigebant, quoniam multipliciter conturbati erant, ac territi, videlicet propter præteritam Christi passionem, propter Judæorum crudelitatem, et proprii cordis quamdam hæsitationem de Christi resurrectione, de cujus veritate nondum fuerant roborati. Insuper sic salutavit discipulos, quoniam pax est maximum bonum, omnique Christiano præcipue appetendum : per quam homines fiunt filii Dei, quemadmodum scriptum est : Beati pacifici, quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur. Propter quod ait Dionysius, quod omnia appetunt pacem, et propter hanc agunt omne quod agunt. Ex quo concluditur, quod pax est vel ipsa beatitudo, vel proxima ad beatitudinem dispositio.
paras.en: [[20:19|and said to them: Peace be to you|et dixit eis: Pax vobis]]. What Christ taught, that He did. For He commanded the disciples: [[Luke 10:5|Into whatever house you enter, first say: Peace be to this house|In quamcumque domum intraveritis, primum dicite : Pax huic domui]]. Hence He Himself, entering the house in which were His dearest and most chosen disciples, says: Peace be to you. Again, He so greeted them because a little before, on the night He was betrayed, He had said: [[John 14:27|Peace I leave with you|Pacem relinquo vobis]]. What He left then, therefore, He now brought, gave and increased. The disciples too were in the greatest need of peace, since they were troubled and frightened in many ways: by the passion of Christ now past, by the cruelty of the Jews, and by a certain hesitation of their own hearts about Christ's resurrection, of whose truth they had not yet been made firm. Moreover, He so greeted the disciples because peace is the greatest good, to be sought above all by every Christian: through which men become sons of God, as it is written: [[Matt 5:9|Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.|Beati pacifici: quoniam filii Dei vocabuntur.]]. Wherefore Dionysius says that all things seek peace, and for its sake do all that they do. From which it is concluded that peace is either beatitude itself, or the disposition nearest to beatitude.

paras.t: Christus autem præsertim nunc loquitur de pace interna, quæ est tranquillitas animi, utpote quies a motibus propriis inordinatis, videlicet a timore immoderato, a tristitia sæculi, quæ secundum Apostolum, mortem operatur, a dolore rationem impediente. Non enim optavit discipulis quietem ab exterioribus persecutionibus ad tempus, quos in medio luporum erat missurus, sed ut in omni turbatione extrinseca conservarent pacem internam. Propterea ad Hebræos monet Apostolus : Pacem sequimini et sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo Deum videbit.
paras.en: But Christ is here speaking chiefly of inward peace, which is tranquillity of mind, namely rest from one's own disordered motions: from immoderate fear, from the sorrow of the world, which, according to the Apostle, worketh death[[2 Cor 7:10||]], from grief that hinders reason. For He did not wish His disciples rest from outward persecutions for the time, since He was about to send them into the midst of wolves[[Matt 10:16||]], but that amid every outward disturbance they might keep inward peace. Hence the Apostle admonishes the Hebrews: [[Heb 12:14|Follow peace with all men and holiness: without which no man shall see God|Pacem sequimini et sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo Deum videbit]].

paras.t: Et quum hoc dixisset, ostendit eis manus et latus, forte et pedes : imo et pedes, ut infra ex verbis Lucæ evangelistæ patebit. In his quinque vulnerum remanserunt cicatrices, in testimonium identitatis corporis passi, resuscitati, et glorificati, itemque in signum victoriæ Salvatoris. Ostendit ergo discipulis manus perfossas, et latus lancea perforatum, ut scirent quod ipse esset qui paulo ante pendebat in ligno, et quod idem numero corpus resumpsisset. — Multa hoc loco omittit Joannes, quæ recitat Lucas; ea quoque quæ Lucas omisit, supplevit Joannes. Itaque Luca testante, Christus discipulis dixit : Videte manus meas et pedes meos; palpate et videte, quoniam spiritus carnem et ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere. Et alia multa in hac apparitione dicta et facta recitat Lucas.
paras.en: [[20:20|And when he had said this, he shewed them his hands and his side|Et cum hoc dixisset, ostendit eis manus et latus]], perhaps the feet too: indeed the feet too, as will appear below from the words of Luke the Evangelist. In these the scars of the five wounds remained, in witness of the identity of the body that suffered, was raised and was glorified, and also as a sign of the Saviour's victory. He showed the disciples, then, the pierced hands and the side opened by the lance, that they might know that He was the one who a little before hung on the wood, and that He had taken again the body numerically the same. — Many things John omits in this place which Luke recounts; and what Luke omitted, John supplied. So, by Luke's witness, Christ said to the disciples: [[Luke 24:39|See my hands and feet, that it is I myself. Handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me to have|Videte manus meas et pedes meos; palpate et videte, quoniam spiritus carnem et ossa non habet, sicut me videtis habere]]. And Luke recounts many other things said and done in this appearance[[Luke 24:36||]].

paras.t: Gavisi sunt ergo discipuli, viso Domino dominorum, qui in femore suo scriptum habet : Rex regum et Dominus dominantium. Gaudium nempe est diffusio animi in conceptione boni, oriturque ex unione potentiæ cum bono convenienti. Quoniam ergo discipuli viderunt Jesum, summum et convenientissimum bonum, quem maxime diligebant, de cujus passione vehementer dolebant, cujus beatitudini cordialiter congratulabantur : ideo viso eo, ultra quam æstimari posset aut exprimi, lætabantur. Gavisi sunt autem propter Jesum, et propter se ipsos : quia magistro suo intime congaudebant ; et de suo profectu exhilarati sunt, videntes se non esse deceptos sequendo Jesum, propter quem omnia sua reliquerunt, et multa perpessi fuerunt ac patiebantur.
paras.en: [[20:20|The disciples therefore were glad, when they saw the Lord|Gavisi sunt ergo discipuli, viso Domino]] of lords, who hath on His thigh written: [[Apoc 19:16|KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS|Rex regum et Dominus dominantium]]. For joy is the expansion of the mind in the conceiving of a good, and arises from the union of a power with a fitting good. Since, then, the disciples saw Jesus, the highest and most fitting good, whom they loved most, for whose passion they grieved vehemently, in whose beatitude they heartily rejoiced with Him: therefore, seeing Him, they were glad beyond what could be reckoned or expressed. They rejoiced for Jesus' sake and for their own: because they rejoiced inwardly with their Master; and they were cheered at their own advancement, seeing that they had not been deceived in following Jesus, for whom they had left all they had[[Matt 19:27||]], and had suffered and were suffering much.

paras.t: Dixit ergo eis iterum : Pax vobis. Siquidem viso Domino Jesu, conturbati fuerunt atque conterriti, juxta Lucam : ideo repetit, Pax vobis. Quæ etiam repetitio, confirmationis indicium est, dilectionisque signum, et admonitio discipulorum ut pacem jugiter appetant, præcipueque exquirant. Vel, ideo bis ait, Pax vobis, quia optavit eis pacem gratiæ in præsenti, et pacem gloriæ in futuro. Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos : id est, quemadmodum Pater misit me ex vera caritate et pietate, ad prædicandum Evangelium vitæ Judæis, a quibus multas persecutiones, et tandem amarissimam perpessus sum mortem, quorum tamen hominum nonnullos converti; sic ego nunc mittam vos ad prædicandum evangelicam legem Judæis ac gentibus, ex caritate et pietate ad vos, et item ad illos, a quibus multa adversa et mortem sustinebitis, quosdam vero eorum convertetis.
paras.en: [[20:21|He said therefore to them again: Peace be to you|Dixit ergo eis iterum: Pax vobis]]. For on seeing the Lord Jesus they were troubled and terrified, according to Luke[[Luke 24:37||]]: therefore He repeats, Peace be to you. This repetition too is a token of confirmation and a sign of love, and an admonition to the disciples to seek peace constantly and to pursue it above all. Or, He says Peace be to you twice because He wished them the peace of grace in the present and the peace of glory in the future. [[20:21|As the Father hath sent me, I also send you|Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos]]: that is, as the Father sent Me out of true charity and loving-kindness to preach the Gospel of life to the Jews, from whom I suffered many persecutions and at last a most bitter death, and yet some of whom I converted; so I now will send you to preach the law of the Gospel to Jews and Gentiles, out of charity and loving-kindness towards you and likewise towards them, from whom you will endure many adversities and death, but some of whom you will convert.

paras.t: Hæc quum dixisset, insufflavit, et dixit eis : Accipite Spiritum Sanctum. Postquam Salvator dixit discipulis, Sicut misit me Pater, et ego mitto vos, infudit discipulis Spiritum Sanctum, quia officium prædicationis quod eis commisit, sine speciali gratia Spiritus Sancti expleri non valuit. Oportet enim ut prædicator verbi cœlestis, in se ipso abundet caritatis fervore, et sapientia divinorum, quatenus ignita proferat verba, motiva et penetrativa, sitque sententiosus, discretus et instructivus in sermonibus suis. Denique, per corporalem illam insufflationem et inspirationem, evidenter signavit superintellectualem atque æternam processionem seu spirationem qua Spiritus Sanctus ab ipso procedit, prout plenius probat Anselmus in libro de Processione Spiritus Sancti. Rursus, dicendo, Accipite Spiritum Sanctum, insinuavit se per auctoritatem dare Spiritum Sanctum : quod nequaquam sic esset, nisi Spiritus Sanctus ab ipso procederet. Sed nonne Apostoli ante hanc horam habuerunt Spiritum Sanctum? Habuerunt utique, non autem tam copiose et efficaciter, seu ad tot tantosque effectus, ut ex hac hora, quia et nunc data est omnibus eis potestas ligandi atque solvendi, sicut mox introducetur.
paras.en: [[20:22|When he had said this, he breathed on them; and he said to them: Receive ye the Holy Ghost|Hæc cum dixisset, insufflavit, et dixit eis: Accipite Spiritum Sanctum]]. After the Saviour had said to the disciples, As the Father hath sent me, I also send you, He poured the Holy Ghost into them, because the office of preaching which He committed to them could not be fulfilled without a special grace of the Holy Ghost. For the preacher of the heavenly word must abound in himself with the fervour of charity and with wisdom in divine things, so that he may utter fiery words, moving and piercing, and be weighty, discerning and instructive in his sermons. Further, by that bodily breathing and inbreathing He plainly signified the supra-intellectual and eternal procession or spiration by which the Holy Ghost proceeds from Him, as Anselm proves more fully in his book On the Procession of the Holy Ghost. Again, by saying, Receive ye the Holy Ghost, He intimated that He gives the Holy Ghost by authority: which would by no means be so unless the Holy Ghost proceeded from Him. But did not the Apostles have the Holy Ghost before this hour?
